🤖 Offline decode of the [September 15 missing-peer dump](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/441) narrows the stall to a self-deadlocked CTA inside QuACK 0.6.4's SM100 grouped GEMM, and identifies the one code path that separates the warps that retired from the warps that did not. QuACK is not exonerated: the rank stops inside this kernel with no external dependency left, and the deadlock is structural to its CLC scheduler. The initiating condition is still unproved, and two reproduction attempts at production shape did not trigger it.

The stuck kernel is the `dh` backward GEMM (`quack_grouped_gemm(dy, w2, cu, b_major="k")`, tile 256x256, cluster 2x2x1, CLC on). Both resident clusters show the same state in every CTA: the MMA warp and all four epilogue warps have exited, the TMA load warp waits on an A/B empty barrier that the exited MMA warp will never release, and the scheduler warp is still inside its CLC loop. The scheduler ring holds three valid grants (work indices 3996/4032/4068 in one cluster, 4011/4047/4083 in the other), and the ring's barrier words show every warp released grants 1-4 while only the four scheduler warps released grant 5. So the MMA and epilogue warps decoded grant 4 as "no more work" and retired, while the load and scheduler warps decoded the same grant as a valid batch-1 tile and kept going. The load warp's registers hold the batch-1 window `[2214, 4182)` (369 and 328 M-clusters for the first two groups), inside which index 4032 is valid; the retired warps must have used a window ending in `(4011, 4032]`. No invalid CLC response was ever in the ring, so this is not the spurious-cancel failure fixed in 0.6.4.

Every warp role decodes its own tile from `cu_seqlens` in global memory (`VarlenMTileScheduler._delinearize_work_idx`, with a per-warp cached batch window). Only the load and scheduler warps execute `griddepcontrol.wait` first (SASS `ACQBULK` at kernel offsets +2272 and +10528); the MMA and epilogue warps' `cu_seqlens` loads (+15408, +21696) come before any wait, and upstream main still has the same placement (`336a5ca` "Enable PDL"). The kernel is launched with PDL (`use_pdl=True` default) and the XLA fusion after it was already resident at its `ACQBULK`, so the sequence is PDL-chained. Under the hero's `save_moe` remat, `cu` is recomputed in the backward by a small fusion, so a predecessor that writes `cu` is plausible. That is the only per-role difference in the decode path and the natural explanation for a role-consistent split, but a one-time stale read at kernel start does not by itself produce the observed state: the retired warps rescan the window at later grants, and a fresh rescan resynchronizes them. The observed state requires those warps to keep seeing stale group boundaries for the whole kernel, which I could not reproduce.

Two probes on `cw-us-east-08a` (2 nodes, production priority, both clean, `/mwittmann/8870-quack-pdl-repro-2` and `/mwittmann/8870-quack-moe-bwd-probe-1`): (1) `experiments/grug/recovery/quack_pdl_repro.py`, the production `dh` GEMM at 601,088 rows with the routing alternating every launch so a stale decode is visibly wrong, six arms (production config, PDL off, CLC off, QuACK patched to wait in the MMA/epilogue warps, constant routing, and the `cu` writer as the immediate predecessor), 600 launches per GPU per arm on 8 GPUs, 28,800 launches, zero hangs and zero output mismatches; (2) `experiments/grug/recovery/quack_moe_bwd_probe.py`, the full `_expert_mlp_quack_wgrad` forward plus backward with a fresh random routing every iteration, 1,500 iterations per GPU on 8 GPUs, 72,000 GEMM launches, zero hangs, zero non-finite values. The hero rate is roughly one hang per 1e6 GPU-steps, about 3e-9 per GEMM launch, so a clean 1e5 launches neither confirms nor excludes the PDL path. In probe (1) the PDL-off arm ran at the same speed as production (27 ms versus 27 ms per launch), so disabling PDL on these launchers costs nothing measurable at this shape.

What this changes: the pooled-wave backend runs dense einsums and never touches this kernel, which matches its clean record. CLC off alone removes the per-grant decode (the scheduler warp decodes once and broadcasts) but leaves the initial-tile decode per warp, so it converts most of this failure into wrong or missing tiles rather than a hang, at the 5-12% GEMM cost recorded in `sonic_cute.py`. The cheap, targeted mitigation for the next hero restart is `use_pdl=False` on the three `quack_moe_cute` launchers (or the two-line wait in the MMA and epilogue warps, arm `patched`, to propose upstream); its efficacy can only be judged by the hang recurrence interval, currently one to two thousand steps.

🤖 Decoding the step-108711 dump (`/tmp/8870-watch-108711/`, task 90) the same way as the step-107501 one adds two facts that the earlier dump could not give, because this one has seven stuck clusters instead of two.

Six of the seven clusters split at a shared threshold. Their scheduler rings hold grants 4305-4404, the load and scheduler warps hold the fresh windows (group 1 is work indices `[2220, 4398)`, group 2 is `[4398, 6558)`; both are in the load warps' `R7/R8/R9` and the scheduler warps' `R8/R9`), and the ring barrier counts show which grant the MMA and epilogue warps retired on: 4358, 4363, 4365, 4340, 4362, 4367 after accepting 4324, 4328, 4332, 4305, 4327, 4333. The retired warps' end of work therefore sits in `(4333, 4340]` in all six clusters, one value, 58-64 indices short of the real end of group 1. That is one stale set of group boundaries shared by 24 CTAs on 24 SMs, not per-CTA noise.

The seventh cluster (blocks 12-13, initial work index 6) is stuck on its very first tile. Its load warp holds the fresh group-0 window `[0, 2220)` and has filled six A/B stages of tile 6 that were never consumed (A/B full parity 1, empty parity 0 in every stage), its scheduler ring holds one grant (index 13, released by the four scheduler warps only), and its MMA and epilogue warps are gone. The MMA warp exited before issuing a single MMA, so it decoded the initial tile, `idx 6 < 2220`, as no work. That is a decode from `cu_seqlens` that says the kernel has fewer than seven clusters of work, taken in the first microseconds of the kernel, by exactly the warps that do not execute `griddepcontrol.wait`. This case needs no persistence argument at all, which was the gap in the previous comment: a stale read at kernel start deadlocks the CTA on its first tile directly. The six other clusters show the same read at a slightly later moment, with `cu_seqlens[1]` already current and the later boundaries not, which fits a buffer being written while the non-waiting warps read it.

One correction to the earlier reading of the scheduler warps: they are parked at the CLC throttle `bar.sync` (kernel offset +11968) waiting for a load-warp credit that never comes, and the reported PC is the following `TRYWAIT`. With that, every barrier count in both dumps reconciles (loads on the tile the MMA warp abandoned, scheduler one credit ahead).

Taken together with the SASS (only the load and scheduler warps wait before their first `cu_seqlens` load), I now put the PDL-stale-input mechanism well above the alternatives. The `cu_seqlens` read the monitoring agent added to the capture is the confirming measurement: on the next hang, the buffer should hold the boundaries the load warp used (`[0, 2220)` and `[2220, 4398)` in work-index units are 370 and 363 M-clusters of 256 rows) while the retired warps evidently used a set that ended around 723 clusters in total. Independently of that read, `use_pdl=False` on the three `quack_moe_cute` launchers, or the two-line wait in the MMA and epilogue warps, is the change to trial at the next relaunch.

🤖 The September 18 UTC stall at step 118837 followed an InfiniBand port failure. Its RAS signature differs from the earlier GPU hangs; no CUDA debugger was attached. The automatic retry restored checkpoint 118722 and resumed training. [Incident record](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/470). Monitoring continues with the two-minute threshold and the updated capture ready.

🤖 The September 18 stall after step 120206 was another permanent-checkpoint metadata deletion failure. Checkpoint 120000’s pending `DeleteObjects: AccessDenied` surfaced at the next checkpoint synchronization. The automatic retry restored 120000 and resumed training, rolling back 206 steps. [Incident record](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/473). The metadata commit incompatibility remains; this event provides no GPU-state evidence of an 8870 recurrence. Monitoring continues on attempt 3.

🤖 The September 19 interruption after step 124715 began with `CUDA_ERROR_CONTAINED` on task 14, local GPU 3, followed by GPU-reset-required and NVLink-mask node conditions. The error leaves invalid peer-memory access versus hardware/driver fault unresolved. No RAS or debugger capture is available, so this does not confirm another silent #8870 hang. Iris automatically retried from checkpoint 124642; attempt 1 resumed and later passed 127172. Evidence and recovery: [incident record](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/488).

Permanent checkpoint 126000 subsequently logged successful completion with the deployed metadata fix, and later temporary checkpoints also completed. This verifies permanent publication; restoring 126000 has not been tested. [Checkpoint incident update](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/473). The 120-second no-progress monitor is rearmed on attempt 1 with the updated capture ready.

The strongest discriminator now seems to be CLC rather than ragged A2A itself. Since the captured CTAs show scheduler/load warps alive after MMA/epilogue exit, please treat the PDL-off run as a separate mechanism test: it does not by itself rule out CLC scheduling.

A useful production-geometry matrix would be: (1) current QuACK with CLC, (2) 0.6.4 drain fix with CLC, and (3) identical 0.6.4 build with CLC disabled. Keep the same checkpoint, rack map, and capture trigger. If only (3) survives comparable exposure, that materially localizes the failure; if (2) and (3) both survive, capture state from (1) remains essential to distinguish the fix from timing.

🤖 The September 23 stall on `hero-fa4sm100-nomask-step146k` was traced to rank 0 waiting in an S3 `put_object` for checkpoint 146585’s `manifest.json`. Two host-thread captures showed the same stack. NCCL reported only rank 0 behind, unlike the previously captured rack-wide GPU hangs; no CUDA debugger was attached. Why the S3 call remained blocked is unresolved.

The existing watchdog terminated the stalled attempt, and Iris automatically started attempt 1. All 176 tasks were running by 00:00:27 UTC September 24. The retry restored temporary checkpoint 146355 at 00:01:55, rolling back 228 steps from the last observed metric, then resumed training through step 146366. The two-minute monitor is rearmed. [Incident and evidence](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/518).

topics.title: [inference] Adopt the qualified vLLM 0.30 GPU release
topics.body:
Adopt the published vLLM 0.30 GPU release with Torch 2.14.1+cu132 and CUDA 13.2.2/compiler 13.2.86. Both x86_64 and aarch64 use vLLM source commit `3a054c458ca8a32609ba2bc578c4d9b93eabb395` and the normal installer's architecture-specific dependency constraints. The pins are generated from [the released manifest](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/releases/download/marin-vllm-gpu-20261012-3a054c458ca8/marin-vllm-gpu-manifest.json), SHA256 `e8a9e8e11781e0c1021783c5b559b9de4f82d0b90ca496de48b208d81baeeb82`.

[Official run 38314409260, attempt 2](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/actions/runs/38314409260) built both wheels, passed their physical H100 and GB200 gates, and published [the qualified pair](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/releases/tag/marin-vllm-gpu-20261012-3a054c458ca8). Independent downloads match the run's wheel hashes, qualification records and GitHub asset digests. All Python model files and shared libraries match the [earlier staged 47b pair](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/releases/tag/marin-vllm-gpu-staged-candidate-47b411d5785d) on both architectures. Version metadata and the optional Rust executable differ; equivalence of that executable is unproved. The normal Python serving and trainer paths leave it disabled.

The Snowball serving-mesh fix is merged in #9401. Retain the regression comparing logits from identical weights on the canonical training and serving meshes. Fresh normal-install HF-export parity passed all 64 representative cases with Levanter on 8 H100s and vLLM on 8 and 16 H100s. Maximum logged absolute probability differences from stored references were 0.056754, 0.064367 and 0.055632, respectively, within the unchanged 0.075 Levanter/0.125 vLLM bounds. Both vLLM configurations passed exact runtime placement/stage checks and exact same-rank token/logprob repeatability on a 15,025-token sentinel with fresh recomputes. Cross-rank variation is diagnostic. These application results cover the standalone Transformers 5.18.0 profile.

Earlier Snowball and Hero runs passed fresh training, checkpoint restoration and HF export on H100 and GB200 against the 47b wheels in MarinSkyRL's combined profile (Transformers 5.12.1). Hero/GB200's driver finished before a worker pod was deleted during shutdown; four queued worker retries were canceled. [MarinSkyRL #944](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/944) reconciles the exact released wheel pins at `cb2565d6`; all six current CI checks passed. Its explicit applicability assessment retains the original four-case evidence with its source/lock and sampling limits. New normal frozen combined installation and repeated Hero ShortConv/FP32-bias weight publication checks passed on H100 and GB200. The separate [native Snowball checkpoint failure](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9400#issuecomment-6129427326) covers a different path from this HF-export parity gate.

The frozen MarinSkyRL training and serving package set retains Transformer Engine 2.20.2 and its other agreed native dependencies. The earlier Hero/GB200 comparison measured 56.37 seconds per native policy update for the refreshed [Torch 2.14.1 profile](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/c9def79c0ac7d043879c669722aab311532b3b03/uv.lock) versus 48.10 seconds for the shipping [Torch 2.13.0 profile](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/f85737fc366d1f077ce9216b179a2a98a0bf8d14/uv.lock), a 17.2% gap. Several dependencies differ between those profiles. That gap did not reproduce consistently as a TE-version effect. Follow-up Transformer Engine 2.19.0/2.20.2 repeats averaged 49.489/50.198 seconds over 18 warm updates per version, a descriptive 1.43% difference. Logical rank placement varied, and one process used a replacement allocation. The original cause and performance equivalence remain unproved. These measurements cover native policy updates; the [trainer handoff](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/944) owns the combined lock and its qualification.

The reviewed source landed through [vLLM #92](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/pull/92). Romain accepted its completed admin bypass as a one-time exception; no further bypass is authorized. [vLLM #93](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/pull/93) later changed only the cache-cleanup schedule; it is outside this release. The prior main `903f1cc6fb7bed4897bcebdcaa83487e07624edc` is retained at `main-backup/20261012/pre-903f1cc6fb7b`.

Keep this draft for final consumer review. Romain owns the Marin/MSRL merges. Consumer rollback is GPU release `marin-vllm-gpu-20260924-01911be34fac`, source `01911be34fac8715347962a8d791ca34a879e01e`. The [paired TPU refresh](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10023) remains parked with its separate environment, missing `vllm.distributed.aux_output_connector` module and unexecuted physical gate. The [release handoff](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10022#issuecomment-6093743002) records artifact identities, application results, trainer reconciliation and rollback; the old separate GPU activation/promotion commands are superseded.

topics.title: Explore Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA)
topics.body: Introduced in [DeepSeek-V2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.04434), now used in many other models, as noted by Sebastian Raschka: https://sebastianraschka.com/llm-architecture-gallery/mla/.

comments.body:
### Mathy explainers
- [Part 1](kexue.fm/archives/10091) and [Part 2](https://kexue.fm/archives/10907) by Jianlin Su (in Chinese)
- [DeepSeek's Multi-Head Latent Attention](https://liorsinai.github.io/machine-learning/2025/02/22/mla.html) by Lior Sinai
- [Understanding Multi-Head Latent Attention](https://planetbanatt.net/articles/mla.html) by Eryk Banatt

### Survey papers
- [A Survey on Large Language Model Acceleration based on KV Cache Management](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.19442) (2025)
- [Key, Value, Compress: A Systematic Exploration of KV Cache Compression Techniques](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.11816) (2025)
- [Efficient Attention Methods: Hardware-efficient, Sparse, Compact, and Linear Attention](https://attention-survey.github.io/) (2026)

Mentioned by @ClassicLarry at https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5151#issuecomment-4336418404 as a direction to explore, and again [on Discord](https://discord.com/channels/1354881461060243556/1516857141514997881) in relation to the GLM-5.2 release.

There was also a brief discussion of MLA in 2025 [on Discord](https://discord.com/channels/1354881461060243556/1380235124011958313/1397673126854267012), summarized by Claude:
  - What MLA buys you: willheld — "for MLA, the inference benefit is mostly in RAM… because you 
  don't need to save the KV cache, just the latent cache." The win is serving memory, not loss.
  - The RoPE incompatibility (the central design wrinkle for your issue): "RoPE would mean you 
  need to materialize the full K vectors and therefore make MLA bad. So DeepSeek and Kimi folks 
  do just a tiny bit of RoPE to add some positional signal with a smaller perf cost." (msg
  (https://discord.com/channels/1354881461060243556/1380235124011958313/1397673126854267012)) —
  i.e. the decoupled/partial-RoPE trick. He pointed at Jianlin Su's kexue.fm
  (https://kexue.fm/archives/10862) (the RoPE author, now at Kimi), and a follow-up post
  (https://kexue.fm/archives/11111) arguing partial RoPE should be theoretically better.
  - The evaluation problem (flagged by dlwh, still unresolved): "we need to figure out how to 
  evaluate these inference-time things. KV reuse, MLA, GQA, alternating SWA… we want to know the
  bpb hit, and inference time/space can be its own measurement." willheld concurred the
  partial-RoPE effect is "not too likely to show up in C4 loss" — so a fair MLA eval needs
  long-context signal plus a separate inference time/space measurement, not just BPB.
  - willheld said he "planned to run MLA" after his then-current work — but no run ever surfaces
  in the corpus, so this didn't land.

Also I had Mumwelt read through the [MLAfication](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17202) paper and compare it to our work on MLA: https://htmlpreview.github.io/?https://gist.githubusercontent.com/hammer/4bf21985183ebae3cbee1e3e0c9f2d70/raw.

> Ideas worth trying
> 1. Calibrated KNorm in Larry's MLA stack. This is the cheapest test, and it answers the QK-norm problem that both Larry and Will raised.
> 
> Experiment: train the fast-track MLA + Inkling model with per-head key norm, swap in the calibrated constants at the end, and measure the loss change. Compare against the current stack without QK-norm.
> Also compare against [QK-Normed MLA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16310), which [Larry cited](https://discord.com/channels/1354881461060243556/1527756652890161292/1551997294805520455) as another way to keep QK-norm under MLA. In the same thread Kaiyue Wen relayed Jianlin Su's concern that keeping QK-norm under MLA grows the KV cache. A fixed constant should not.
>
> 2. Pretrain with MHA, convert to MLA for serving. This is the route that would win back Larry's 15%.
> 
> Experiment: pretrain a fast-track MHA model (with QK-norm and half-RoPE) at d1024–d1280. Convert it to a latent the size of the GQA 4:1 cache (a 75% cut), and distil on about 1–2% of the training tokens.
> Success test: the converted model beats GQA 4:1 trained from scratch, at equal KV memory.
> The joint SVD initialisation may also be what the staircase lacked, since that run's latent steps started from random weights.
> It needs a Levanter port. The math is small: the norm constants, the weighted SVD, and attention-only distillation. Marin already runs distillation, including on-policy distillation ([#9920](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9920)).
> Precedent is mixed. The one previous surgery on a trained Grug MoE, tying expert banks across layers, [recovered most of the loss but missed its targets](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8032).

- 🟢 `Oct 16 16:32Z` Answered issue #6494: hero uses GQA; KDA/MLA are in fast_track experiments. https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6494#issuecomment-6220057604

🤖 No. The current Grug production hero (`hero-ctx16k-step257k`) uses GQA softmax attention, with 48 query heads, 12 local KV heads, and 6 global KV heads. Its [attention module](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L538-L578) has separate Q, K, and V projections; the [hero recipe](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/heuristic.py#L85-L115) selects the FA4 kernel. The recipe's `latent_dim=3072` is [LatentMoE](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1102-L1115): it compresses expert-parallel transport, not the attention KV cache.

The [MFU handoff](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9960) moved the hero to an optimized MoE stack; the earlier [FA4 handoff](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9378) changed its attention kernel. Neither switched its attention architecture to MLA or Kimi Delta Attention (KDA). The combination of KDA on local layers and MLA on global layers is being tested in the separate [`fast_track` ladder](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451), whose first version explicitly excludes hero-scale speed testing. The latest [hero handoff](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10101) changed context length and QK scaling while retaining the GQA recipe.

MLA is not on the hero- it is on Marin Belay and running at 28 MFU at hero scale. https://claude.ai/artifact/2ZfzxTKZBMF3HJ77xeSQb5.

So now that it has competitive MFU, can give it a fair shot for future runs. Will need to test further to see if its better. Interestingly, Western labs like Meta (at least their open release), reflection, and microsoft seem to be sticking with GQA. And then there is Deepseek who is off doing their own unique attention stuff.

I will test the conversion idea. I think for the scale of models we will train, qk-norm on MLA head may be fine.

topics.body:
`pallas_triton_flash_attention` now runs the Pallas kernels inside `shard_map` whenever the type of `q` names an Explicit mesh axis, including on a mesh whose axes all have size 1. Before, it called the kernels directly when no axis larger than 1 partitioned `q`, and `pallas_call` rejected the explicitly sharded inputs. The June synthetic benchmark on one MI350X (`--expert-axis 1 --attention gpu_pallas_triton_flash`) failed at the first step with `AssertionError: (2, P(('replica_dcn', 'data', 'expert'), None, 'model', None))`. The batch-sharded mesh test now also covers a data axis of size 1, and a new test runs the kernels on concrete arrays batch-sharded on a one-device Explicit mesh against reference attention. Both fail without the change.

topics.title: mini-swe-agent sandbox contains clean copies of SWE-smith task repositories
topics.body:
When Harbor runs the mini-swe-agent 2.1.0 adapter on a SWE-smith task, the agent's own Python environment is installed inside the task sandbox at agent setup (`/root/.local/share/uv/tools/mini-swe-agent/lib/python3.12/site-packages/`). That environment contains clean, unbroken copies of three packages that are also SWE-smith task repositories: pygments, pandas and tenacity. The agent can read the fixed source directly. The same class exists at the image level, independent of the agent: conda's package cache ships boltons in every conda image, pip and setuptools vendor chardet, tomli and inflect, and one testbed environment holds an installed dataset egg.

Observed: in a GLM 5.3 trial on `swesmith-00763` (jd/tenacity) with the mini-swe-agent adapter, the agent ran `sed -n 136,175p /root/.local/share/uv/tools/mini-swe-agent/lib/python3.12/site-packages/tenacity/retry.py`, called it "the reference", copied the logic and passed. A pre-agent audit of the task packages cannot see this environment, because it appears only when the agent is installed.

Scope in the DCAgent SWE-smith packages (`DCAgent/swesmith-sandboxes-with_tests-oracle_verified_120s`), measured with mini-swe-agent's dependencies pinned (identical 80 distributions across one image per repository): pygments 222 tasks, pandas 196, tenacity 30, boltons 21, chardet 10, tomli 23, inflect 27, dataset 13. In the 2,100-task shootout pool that was 542 tasks before replacement. A filename-only check produces false positives (pygments' `html.py` versus safety, IPython's `timing.py` versus alive-progress), so the check must compare module contents or names, not file suffixes.

Reproduce: start a trial with the mini-swe-agent adapter on any pygments, pandas or tenacity SWE-smith task, and in the agent phase list `/root/.local/share/uv/tools/mini-swe-agent/lib/python3.12/site-packages/<package>/`. For the image-level copies, build the task's `environment/Dockerfile` and search outside `/testbed` for directories named after the task repository's import name (for example `find / -path /testbed -prune -o -type d -name tomli -print`).

Impact: pass rates on those tasks are inflated and the resulting traces teach reading a library copy instead of fixing the bug. Terminus-2 is not affected by the tool-environment copy, because the Terminus-2 agent runs outside the sandbox, but the image-level copies affect every agent. Existing SWE-smith trace sets were generated with other agent setups, so their tool environments may differ; they have not been audited for these paths.

Expected: during the agent phase, no readable copy of the task repository exists outside `/testbed`. Either the agent environment lives outside the sandbox (as Terminus-2 does), or the adapter installs it on a path the agent cannot read, or task packages whose repository is a dependency of the agent or of the base image are excluded from training pools and flagged in evaluation.

Done when: Harbor's mini-swe-agent adapter keeps its environment out of the agent's reach or documents the limitation; a content-based image check for repository copies outside `/testbed` is part of SWE-smith package validation; and existing SWE-smith trace sets are audited for reads under these paths. The shootout pool (#10213) already excludes the eight repositories above, pins the agent's dependencies, and drops traces that read a library copy of the task repository; the method and per-repository evidence are in the pool manifest at `open-athena/Snowball-SFT-Shootout-Pool-2026.10`. Related: #10212 (git history left in the same packages).

comments.body:
🤖

# Research

Harbor's Mini-SWE setup puts its Python tool environment inside the task container; a GLM 5.3 trial read the installed `tenacity/retry.py` and passed using that reference ([probe](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10212#issuecomment-6227834962)). [Pool P v4](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10213#issuecomment-6228022768) excludes the affected repositories, and its row builder drops known library-copy reads, but those controls apply to this shootout rather than to future SWE-smith packages or older traces. Marin delegates agent execution to the pinned Harbor runtime, so the adapter, package validator, and trace audit need separate changes.

**Relevant code**
- [`trial_driver.py#L104-L116`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor/trial_driver.py#L104-L116) — Harbor agent selection.
- [`driver_config.py#L69-L80`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor/driver_config.py#L69-L80) — pinned external runtime.
- [`penfever_rollouts.py#L702-L708`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/datakit/download/penfever_rollouts.py#L702-L708) — one historical SWE-smith trace source.

# Proposal

Keep the v4 exclusions as the current safeguard. Add the following durable checks before treating other SWE-smith packages or historical traces as clean.

1. **Harbor adapter:** Move the Mini-SWE controller and its Python environment outside the task sandbox; send tool commands through Harbor's sandbox execution interface. Probe after agent setup, when the tool environment currently appears, and verify that the agent can edit `/testbed` but cannot read the controller's packages. If Harbor cannot support this boundary, document the limitation in the adapter and reject repository/agent pairs whose code ships in its pinned dependencies. The adapter change belongs in `marin-community/harbor`; Marin should pin the tested revision.
2. **Package validation:** Promote the [v4 image probe](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10212#issuecomment-6228022644) into the SWE-smith package build gate. Inspect agent-readable files outside `/testbed` in the built image and again after agent setup. Use repository import names and distribution metadata to find candidates, then confirm source overlap with content fingerprints; a matching filename alone must not reject a task. Record matched paths, files, image revision, and agent dependency pin in the manifest, and reject confirmed overlaps before publishing packages.
3. **Historical traces:** Inventory each existing SWE-smith trace source and its agent/setup revision, starting with the registered Penfever source and the Kimi traces noted in [#10212](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10212#issuecomment-6228022644). Join commands and observations to the task repository; flag reads from its copies in `site-packages`, `_vendor`, conda caches, eggs, Go module caches, and agent tool environments. Publish counts and example paths by dataset and repository, quarantine confirmed contaminated rows, and mark sources with missing command or environment provenance as unknown rather than clean. Run the audit where the traces are stored to avoid bulk cross-region transfer.

## Testing and rollout

Test the validator against the observed tenacity tool environment and vendored tomli, plus unrelated files such as Pygments' `html.py`; the latter must not trigger on its filename. Run one Mini-SWE task end to end with the new boundary and verify that setup, editing, and the verifier still work. Hand-check flagged and unflagged audit samples, publish the audit manifest and rejected counts, then require the validator result in future SWE-smith pool manifests.

## Costs and open question

Moving the controller changes Harbor's agent lifecycle and needs an integration test, while scanning built images adds package-build work. Can Harbor's current Mini-SWE adapter run outside the sandbox with its existing command transport? If not, the documented limitation plus enforced repository exclusions is the immediate adapter deliverable; the package gate and trace audit remain required.

🤖 **TL;DR:** in the existing SWE-smith trace sets, clean copies outside `/testbed` matter little for the testbed-format tasks, and mini-swe-agent's tool env never appears. They ran Terminus-2, not mini-swe-agent. The exception is AgentTrove's clone-format tasks: 1,142 of their traces read an installed release copy of the task's own package.

| Set (revision) | Traces | Agent command reads a library copy of the task's repo | Touches mini-swe-agent's tool env | Row-builder drop (copy or tool env anywhere in the trace) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `open-athena/Kimi-2.5-swesmith-...-maxeps-32k` (`1b87a9cf78`) | 9,356 | 2 (1 of 5,237 passes) | 0 | 6 |
| `laion/calibforge-relay-traces` `kimi_swesmith` (`66feab4d24`) | 4,392 | 1 (0 passes) | 0 | 3 |
| `DCAgent2/GLM-4.7-swesmith-...-maxeps-131k` (`e209a88db1`) | 9,437 | 3 | 0 | 10 |
| `open-thoughts/AgentTrove` swesmith rows (`b395a4307a`) | 78,246 | 1,157 (1,142 in clone tasks) | 0 | 1,598 |

- **Clone tasks:** the instruction makes the agent clone `swesmith/<mirror>` into an image that already has the package installed. The agents then `ls` or `cat` the installed copy (`/usr/lib/python3/dist-packages/<pkg>`, `/usr/local/lib/python3.12/dist-packages/<pkg>`, a venv's `site-packages`), and that copy is clean code. 106 repos are affected; cantools, pygments, oauthlib and python-docx lead. The same tasks also expose the full mirror history (see #10212).
- **Go module cache:** 2 traces read a Go repo's module-cache copy. The shootout lists no import names for Go repos, so this column is supplementary.

**Method:** the shootout row builder's own rules, used verbatim: `LIBRARY_LOCATION` plus the repo's import names, and `AGENT_TOOL_ENV`. They are applied to the agent's commands, and also to the whole trace, matching the builder's drop rule. Import names are the shootout's for its 38 repos and extended for the rest. Code and exact regexes: [`scripts/task215/`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/29a6fb1919/scripts/task215).

topics.title: [rl] Build mixed RLVR pivot arm datasets
topics.body:
`experiments.post_training.pivotrl.mixed_rlvr` builds the three datasets the mixed-domain RLVR pivot arms train on: RLVR1 alone, RLVR1 with #9933's selected SWE and Terminal pivots at λ = 0.65, and RLVR1 with random SWE and Terminal candidate turns (every turn the frozen policy was scored on). Validation is the same in all three: RLVR1's validation rows plus #9933's held-out SWE and Terminal turns.

Every row carries a top-level `teacher_route` (`rlvr`, `swe` or `terminal`), so MarinSkyRL's domain-weighted sampling (`data.sampling.kind=domain-weighted`) sets the pivot share per batch at launch and one dataset serves every share. `domain_weights` gives the per-batch counts, splitting the share evenly between SWE and Terminal because the two benchmarks weigh equally in the decision rules; at 20% of 512 prompts that is 410 RLVR, 51 SWE and 51 Terminal. RLVR rows come first and the sampler shuffles the `rlvr` pool before the others, so with one seed every arm draws RLVR prompts in the same order. Arm A uses domain-weighted sampling too, with `rlvr` alone.

The rows are adapted to MarinSkyRL's task sessions (since its #879). Their route moves from the retired `skyrl_gym` to `task_session`. Pivot rows carry `max_output_tokens` in their request at the 4,096 tokens their pass rates were sampled at, while RLVR rows keep the run's per-turn budget. Code generation, NeMo tool use, NVARC inductive and Lean rows are left out, because their sessions execute in a Docker task machine that Iris task pods cannot start, and so are rows with a blank text message, which task conversations reject; each manifest counts what it dropped. That leaves 63,590 RLVR, 25,792 selected SWE and 6,940 selected Terminal training rows.

RLVR1 is pinned to `open-athena/Nemotron-RL-Ultra-RLVR1-Cleaned-v3-2026-09-30@600262dd`. Built at `--version 2026.10.09`, the graph reuses #9933's stored pooled K = 16 pass rates and runs only the two selections and the three datasets.

Stacked on #9933. Part of #10214

topics.title: [rolloutengine] Replace task sessions with registered harnesses
topics.body:
RolloutEngine runs each task attempt through a harness, which owns the agent loop and calls the model only through a `RolloutRecorder`. `RolloutEngine(machine_factories, harnesses, *, observer=None)` holds the two registries, and `run_task(spec, model, *, run_id=None)` returns a `GradedRollout(rollout, grade)`. `Rollout` replaces `RolloutData`: it holds `run_id`, one `ConversationRecord` for each conversation of the attempt, the stop reason, metrics, and run outputs, and no longer carries `task_id` or the grade. Without a `run_id`, each attempt gets a new random ID, so the events of repeated attempts of a task stay apart.

A harness implements `Harness`: `check(task, limits)` rejects a task before any machine starts, and `run(context, recorder)` runs one attempt with a `HarnessContext(task, machine, events, cleanup, run_id)`. This replaces `TaskSession`, `TaskSessionFactory`, and `TaskGrader`. The recorder's `start(prompt)` begins a conversation, `reply(observations, token_ids=...)` continues it, and `record(observations=..., data=..., metrics=...)` adds to the step of the last turn. The recorder records the exact tokens and applies `max_turns`, `max_total_tokens`, the length stop, `model_turn_timeout`, `tool_turn_timeout`, and `total_turn_timeout`. The next request after a limit raises `LimitReached`, and a failed model request raises `RolloutEnded` with the model's error as its cause. After either, `record(data=..., metrics=...)` still adds to the step of the last turn until the record is final, for example a final reward. Without a turn, `record` raises the refusal again. A second `start` is a new conversation, so `Transition.reset` and the engine's reset rules are removed, and the rollout keeps every conversation. Harnesses do not grade. `SessionGrader` and harness grading are removed, the engine grades the last conversation that has a model turn with the task's grader, and a harness puts its own rewards in step data. Thus a new conversation whose first request fails leaves the earlier one to grade. `harness_rollout(harness, task, model, *, limits, machine=None, ...)` runs a harness without the engine, and `task_machine(task, factory, runtime, *, cleanup_timeout)` starts a task machine for it.

`shell_harness(command_timeout=..., shell_tool=..., tools=...)` takes the shell options and tool providers that were in the spec and the engine, so one engine can register several shell configurations. `step_harness(open_episode)` runs a step-style `Episode` (`prepare`, `advance`, `close`). `agent_harness(run)` replaces `AgentTaskSession`. Each `complete` call of the agent runs the recorder in the caller's task, with no queue and no request tasks. One model request can be open at a time. A call that is cancelled while the model generates loses that generation and does not change the record, and the last prompt again gets the same turn. After the attempt ends, calls wait until the cleanup, after grading, so a waiting agent does not change the task machine during grading. The cleanup then cancels the agent, and an agent that does not stop within `cleanup_timeout` is a cleanup error.

When the harness ends or a turn deadline expires, the record is final. The recorder cancels a model call that is still open, for example in an agent's HTTP handler, and ignores its result, so the grader and the returned rollout see the same record. A harness registers the close of its resources with `context.cleanup`. The closes run after grading, each within `cleanup_timeout`, and a failure is a cleanup error of the attempt.

`TaskRolloutSpec(task, harness, task_machine, verifier_machine, limits, trace, judge_connection)` replaces `LoweredTaskSpec`, `TaskRuntimeSpec`, and `TaskSessionSpec`. Its `limits`, a `RolloutLimits`, holds the turn, token, and time limits of `TaskSessionSpec`. `RolloutEngine.check(spec)`, which `run_task` also calls first, replaces `lower_task` and `validate_lowered_task`. `Prompt` replaces `SessionStart`. `ModelRequest.continuation`, a `Continuation(served_token_ids, assistant_message_index)`, replaces `prefix_token_ids` and `assistant_message_index`. A request has a continuation, pinned `prompt_token_ids`, or neither, and a `MESSAGES` rollout never has a continuation. Under `EXACT_TOKENS`, `reply` refuses pinned tokens that do not start with the served tokens before it sends the request. In `Transition`, `token_ids` replaces `next_prompt_token_ids`, and `next_options` is removed, so options change only with a new conversation. `reward`, `token_rewards`, `token_credit`, `reward_components`, and the per-step `grade` are removed from `Transition`. A harness can put such values in its new `data` field, which the engine keeps unchanged. A trainer that reads per-token rewards from it compares their length with the turn's `response_token_ids`; `RolloutStep.response_end` is the index of the turn's last response token. `check` also rejects, for every harness, a shell binding without a task machine, as it already did for the shell capability, and a graded `state` task, because the engine does not capture state.

A judge grader grades on the host through `grade_remote_judge_answer`, the function that the curation pipelines use, with `judge_connection` or with `VERIFYIT_JUDGE_BASE_URL` and `VERIFYIT_JUDGE_API_KEY`. It uses no verifier machine. `judge_connection` holds an API key, so `model_dump`, JSON, and pickle leave it out. `check` rejects a judge task with a verifier machine, a judge task with no connection and no `VERIFYIT_JUDGE_BASE_URL`, a judge task with no `JudgeSpec.model` and no `VERIFYIT_JUDGE_MODEL`, and a judge task whose answer is not in the conversation. The verifier deadline stops only the engine's wait for a host judge. Each judge request has `JudgeSpec.request_timeout`, and for every rubric except labels the OpenAI client retries a failed request up to two times (#10246).

An interrupted attempt raises `RolloutInterrupted(rollout, operation)` from `harness_rollout`, and `GradedRolloutInterrupted`, with the grade of the completed turns, from `run_task`. A model failure still grades the completed turns, and a harness that returns with no model turn fails with `prepare`. `RolloutContractError` means only a token-contract violation.

The token trace grows its loss mask and log probabilities as lists, and the rollout is built once at the end. With a fake model that costs nothing, engine time per turn falls from 2.4–2.5 to 1.0–1.1 ms at 129k tokens and from 4.7–5.0 to 2.6 ms at 257k tokens (three runs each against 24aa43cea).

MarinSkyRL pins rolloutengine at a Marin commit, so it keeps working until it advances that pin. Its port must:

- run its step-style sessions through `step_harness`, and put each old `grade()` result in the last step's data. A session that computes that result only at the end needs its own harness, which records it with `record(data=...)` after `LimitReached` or a failed model request
- give Nemotron its own harness, which calls `start` again for its correction turn
- read `rollout.conversations` when it builds training samples
- register one shell harness for each shell configuration
- build its `ChatContinuation` from `ModelRequest.continuation`
- read `result.rollout` and `result.grade` from `run_task`, and `grade` from `GradedRolloutInterrupted`
- take task IDs from its specs, and rebuild its stored task Parquet files, which hold `LoweredTaskSpec` JSON
- replace the grader of each stored task that has a `SessionGrader` (`kind: "session"`), which no longer parses
- drop `RolloutOperation.CLEANUP`, which the engine never raised

Observers get `run_id` instead of `run_key`, `ConversationStarted` for each conversation instead of `SessionPrepared`, `TransitionCompleted` without `reset_conversation`, and the cleanup steps `episode_close`, `agent_stop`, and `tool_provider_close` instead of `session_close`.

Part of #10187.

🤖 One question on grading while this is a draft, from the Taskforge side; nothing here needs to block the PR.

`Harness.grade` now grades only a `SessionGrader` task, and `_grade_rollout` grades every other task with the task's grader: in process when a verifyit grader has no environment, otherwise in the verifier machine. A verifyit `JudgeSpec` grader must carry an environment, because the judge mode has no in-process grader (`Mode.JUDGE` has no candidate entry in `verifyit/spec.py`, so `candidate_spec` refuses it), so every judge task goes to a verifier machine, and `check_spec` requires one. TaskCompendium's own entry grades the same task differently: `runtime/task_grading.py` `grade_task` sends any `JudgeSpec` grader to `grade_remote_judge_answer(task, attempt, judge_connection)` on the host before it looks at the environment, and the task-curation verification and controls pipelines use that path.

Would a host-graded judge fit this shape as a third registry? Something like `RolloutEngine(machine_factories, harnesses, judges)`, with `RolloutSpec.judge: str | None` naming the registered judge (a callable from task and `GradingAttempt` to `GradeResult`, the default built from `grade_remote_judge_answer` and a `JudgeConnection`), `check_spec` accepting `verifier_machine=None` for a `JudgeSpec` grader when a judge is selected, and `_grade_rollout` running it under `asyncio.to_thread` like `grade_answer`. The task definition stays unchanged and nothing in it names a service, which keeps #10021's line. If you would rather take it as a follow-up PR after this one lands, I can draft it against this branch's shape; a word on which you prefer is all I need.

Context: Taskforge's decision-model verifier (judge graded on the host through a service the lowering selects) cannot be validated through the engine until a judge grades host-side, and today no engine test exercises a `JudgeSpec` grader.

**Before.** At 98c7e15, the engine ran the turn loop itself. It called `session.prepare()` and then `advance(turn)` on a `TaskSession`. A session could reset the conversation through `Transition.reset_conversation`/`next_options`, and per-token rewards had to pass `trace.check_transition`. Grading went through a `TaskGrader` callback, and a `SessionGrader` task graded itself. `validate_lowered_task` returned early for every session other than `"shellbox"`, so custom sessions skipped the workspace and resource checks. `AgentTaskSession` connected an agent to the engine through a one-slot queue.

**After.** The harness owns the loop. The recorder applies `max_turns`, `max_total_tokens`, the length stop, and the model and tool turn deadlines. It records exact tokens per conversation, so a second `start` replaces `reset_conversation`, and `Rollout.conversations` keeps every conversation. `check_spec` now applies to every harness. Judge graders grade on the host through TaskCompendium's `grade_remote_judge_answer`, the path `grade_task` already used, and need no verifier machine. `check` rejects a judge task that has no service (`judge_connection` or `VERIFYIT_JUDGE_BASE_URL`) or no model (`JudgeSpec.model` or `VERIFYIT_JUDGE_MODEL`) before any model request. Rewards a harness computes go into opaque `Transition.data`. The length check that `check_transition` did moves to each trainer, which can compare lengths against `RolloutStep.response_end`. The token-budget formula and the start of `total_turn_timeout` at the first request are unchanged from the old loop.

**Evidence and limits.** Locally, `uv run --group test pytest tests` in `lib/rolloutengine` at this head gives 194 passed and 5 skipped (the skips are the root-only local-grading tests), and `lib/taskcompendium/tests/test_controls.py` passes. - **3. Related PR:** #10190 edits `agent_session.py`, which this PR deletes. At its current head it still adds a second judge surface, `RolloutEngine(..., judge_connection=...)`, and a `ResponseAbandoned` stop (`RESPONSE_ABANDONED_STOP_REASON`) for cancelled agent requests. Both overlap this PR's `TaskRolloutSpec.judge_connection` and the recorder's rule that a cancelled call changes nothing. MarinSkyRL pins #10190's branch. Land #10190 first so the pin is reachable from main. Then, in this PR, delete its engine-level `judge_connection`, `ResponseAbandoned`, and `RESPONSE_ABANDONED_STOP_REASON` in favor of this PR's mechanisms, so main does not end up with two judge-connection paths.
- **4. Related PR:** #10181 adds `experiments/post_training/pivotrl/compendium.py`, which imports `LoweredTaskSpec, TaskRuntimeSpec, TaskSessionSpec` from `rolloutengine.spec` and writes `LoweredTaskSpec` JSON rows. Its `test_pivotrl.py` calls `LoweredTaskSpec.model_validate_json`. Whichever PR lands second must port `lowered_pivot` to `TaskRolloutSpec(task=..., harness=<registered shell harness>, ...)` with `max_turns=1`, and update the Parquet column and its reader.
- **5. Related PR (changed):** #10078 (`agent_session.py`, `contracts.py`, `engine.py`), #10115 (`engine.py`, `grading.py`), and #10032 (`grading.py`) edit code that this PR rewrites. #10078 also adds `closure_repair.py` on top of `TaskSession`. topics.title: [post_training] Add SFT shootout arm verification and progress tools
topics.body:
`validate_pilot.py` builds the requested SFT shootout arms from real traces into a dry-run prefix. Each row is re-decoded independently to check that trained spans match the GLM turns, loss excludes padding and tokens beyond the row's content, and held-out status matches the arm. The pilot reports wall time and peak memory for each build. Dry-run prefixes carry a `DRY_RUN_NOT_FOR_TRAINING` marker and never receive `_SUCCESS`.

`verify_arms.py` re-reads production prefixes and checks markers; every file and row hash against the manifest; row counts, steps, and padding; and per-family token totals. It also checks that held-out tasks contribute no rows, every epoch contains plain's replay rows, plain's epochs contain the same rows in different orders, and RS-multi's epochs are within 1% of B on plain's task slots. Verification passed on the pool v5 plain and RS-multi prefixes.

`progress.py` dry-builds plain, RS-multi, and relay over every finished generation shard. `progress_table.py` renders a dated table with that summary and per-family projections, flagging B above the replay ceiling, relay below parity, an unknown drop reason, or a capability-token drop.

Stacked on #10253.

Part of #10213

topics.title: [eval] Run each evaluation as a StepSpec
topics.body:
Run each evaluation as a StepSpec with its own lock, success cache, and result record. Evaluations in one launch share a candidate server and optional hosted judge. Cached evaluations are skipped on restart; a fully cached launch starts no servers. A group StepSpec locks the launch before starting inference so duplicate orchestrators cannot provision duplicate servers.

Evaluators run sequentially by default. `--max-concurrent` allows concurrent evaluators on shared inference, but omits per-evaluation server metrics because server-wide counters include sibling traffic. Server startup failures write infrastructure-failure records for all pending evaluations.

Pipeline retries derive run IDs from the pipeline artifact path and resolved model, evaluator, runtime, judge, and policy settings, preserving completed evaluations across orchestrator resubmissions. CLI launches and mutable pipeline versions (`dev` or `*-dev`) create fresh runs. Verified policies retain their pinned benchmark sources and Harbor/Evalchemy commits.

EvalDash withholds scores until each evaluation's StepSpec succeeds. Historical records without step status keep their existing display. A crash after writing a record but before StepRunner marks success can rerun that evaluation. The success cache prevents completed steps from being overwritten on ordinary restarts, addressing the failure in the [October 6 incident](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/627).

🤖 Holistic review of bc3348d1398a4b8fd3170feb49265dc165ee509f.

The PR runs each evaluation as an inline StepSpec under a group StepSpec lock inside the CPU orchestrator, so an Iris preemption retry of the same orchestrator skips evals that already succeeded. EvalDash withholds scores until a step reaches `SUCCESS`. The core mechanism is sound: StepRunner continues past a failed step and raises at the end, startup failures record every pending eval, and the changed runner, launch, and policy tests pass locally (17 passed). Nothing blocks merge. The items below are about where the code lives and how much it caches.

**Should fix**
1. `experiments/evaluation/pipeline.py:104` `run_eval_pipeline_step` calls `prepare_evaluation_batch`, which mints fresh random run IDs on every call. When `eval_step` reruns after a failed or preempted pipeline task, every eval runs again, including ones that already succeeded. The README admits this (lines 205-208), but it is the case rjpower raised in review ("can we have the eval.step itself do the right thing"). Fix: derive `group_id` and each `run_id` deterministically from `config.artifact_path` plus the eval key, so a rerun of the pipeline step reuses the per-eval StepSpecs. Keep the timestamp prefix that EvalDash parses in `_next_verification`.
2. `lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/runner.py:475` `run_evaluation_steps` takes a `build_steps` callback and exports the `EvaluationStep` type alias only because `build_evaluation_steps` and `run_evaluation_group` landed in `experiments/evaluation/launch.py:355,391`. Both functions use only `marin`/`rigging` imports (`StepSpec`, `ModelConfigRef`, `model_config_digest`, `prefix_join`). Move them, plus the Iris submission formerly at `submit_evaluation_batch`, back into `runner.py` and have `run_evaluation_steps` build its steps directly. That deletes the callback parameter, the type alias, the `partial(run_evaluation_steps, batch, partial(build_evaluation_steps, batch))` chain, and the experiments-to-StepRunner coupling, and keeps orchestration in the library.
3. `experiments/evaluation/launch.py:368` `hash_attrs` carries the model digest, eval ref, runtime, judge digest, and policy version, but the step path is pinned by `override_output_path` to a random `run_id`, and these steps have no fingerprint, so `check_drift` returns `False`. These attributes never affect caching. They only duplicate `record.json` into `.executor_info`. The PR body's "Step identities include the resolved model and evaluator configuration, runtime revisions, judge configuration, and policy version" describes no behavior the code has. Fix: reduce `hash_attrs` to `{"run_id": ...}`, drop the `model_config_digest` import, and remove that sentence from the body and the README "step identity records" paragraph (line 169).
4. `lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/runner.py:484` repeats the `max_concurrent < 1` guard from `build_evaluation_batch` (`launch.py:273`), and the CLI already enforces `IntRange(min=1)`. Keep the guard at the batch boundary and delete this copy.

**Tests to drop**
5. `tests/evaluation/test_eval_policy_launch.py:107-118` (the `changed_config`/`changed_runtime` block in `test_verified_launch_rejects_changed_source_before_contacting_iris`): the `run_id !=` assertions hold for any two calls because `_run_id` uses `uuid4`, and the `eval_ref`/`eval_runtime` inequalities project the monkeypatched inputs back out. It does not fail when step identity is wrong.
6. `test_step_cache_skips_completed_eval`: redundant. `test_evaluation_restart_skips_completed_step_without_serving` already reruns a completed single-eval batch and asserts the record is unchanged and the status is `SUCCESS`. `test_evaluation_restart_only_runs_unfinished_evals` covers the execute-once case for a mixed batch.

**Related PRs**
7. #10169 (in-orchestrator recovery after inference preemption) rewrites the same `_run_one_evaluation` and is written against the pre-#9813 `evaluate_batch` / `_EvaluationExecution` / `_record_unstarted` structure that this PR deletes. Its body also restores "mark the current and remaining evaluations as infrastructure failures", which this PR replaces with per-step failure records. The two are complementary: #10169 handles inference restarts and #9813 handles orchestrator restarts. Land #9813 first, then rebase #10169 onto `run_evaluation_step`. Under per-step semantics, a permanent inference loss should fail the current step and let the remaining steps record infrastructure failures through the startup-failure path.
8. #9897 (EvalDash model selection) edits `app.py`, `metrics.py`, `tests/test_local_store.py`, and `web/src/types/api.ts`, where this PR switches status fields to `display_status` and adds `step_status`. Expect textual conflicts only; whichever lands second must route any new status reads through `display_status`.

topics.title: [grug] Close FA4 SM100 review follow-ups
topics.body:
Close the open review items from #9332.

The native SM100 FA4 dispatch now rejects unsupported layouts in both directions. Before, with `sm100_backward` set, the backward quietly fell back to the port kernel for shapes outside BF16, D128 and GQA ratios 4, 6 and 8, using the placeholder port fields of the SM100 config. One `validate_sm100_layout` check now defines the supported shapes for the entry point, forward and backward.

`gpu_fa4_cute_sm100` and the native tile sweep accept every compute capability 10.x, matching upstream FA4, which runs its SM100 kernels on all of them, and the removed `gpu_fa4_cute_wide` backend. SM103 (GB300/B300) has not been validated on hardware.

The native SM90 backward now passes the context-parallel query offset to its kernel mask; it previously passed zero while its sparse metadata used the real offset. The frontend no longer swaps H100 sequence-sharded attention onto the 64×64 segmented backward.

Left out: hoisting the per-layer sparse-metadata rebuild out of the layer scan. At the hero's per-device shape (B=16, S=4096), a forward-plus-backward metadata build takes about 0.3 ms on CPU. The hero does about 144 builds per step, which comes to roughly 5 ms, or 0.03% of a ~15 s step on 64 GB200s. Sequence sharding would also need per-shard precompute, because the backward block lists cannot be sliced from one global build.

GPU validation is pending: the SM90 context-parallel path needs the sequence-sharded parity test on H100, and the SM100 paths need the FA4 GPU tests on GB200.

topics.title: [gpu] Unify the managed GPU stack on CUDA 13 and audit version pins
topics.body:
## Goal

Use a supported PyTorch CUDA 13 build alongside JAX CUDA 13, and keep only the direct version pins that protect a demonstrated compatibility boundary. The uv lock should provide reproducibility; package requirements should use ranges where safe.

## Current blocker

`marin-core[gpu]` currently resolves:

- JAX on CUDA 13 with `nvidia-cublas>=13.2.0.9`.
- PyTorch 2.11 from the cu128 index with separate CUDA 12 runtime packages.

The PyTorch cu130 wheel cannot replace cu128 as-is: it requires `cuda-toolkit[cublas]==13.0.2`, which pins `nvidia-cublas==13.1.0.3` and conflicts with Marin’s B200 cuBLAS floor.

## Work

1. Find a supported PyTorch CUDA 13 resolution that retains Marin’s H100 NCCL and B200 cuBLAS guards. Prefer a newer compatible release over overriding an upstream exact CUDA-library dependency.
2. Audit the direct GPU requirements for `torch`, `torchvision`, and the CUDA libraries:
   - Document why each exact pin or bounded range is necessary.
   - Replace exact application-level pins with compatible ranges where the lockfile and upstream dependency metadata are sufficient.
   - Keep hardware safety floors such as cuBLAS/NCCL until validation proves they are obsolete.
3. Update the PyTorch index selection and uv lock.
4. Validate imports, device execution, matmul, and collectives on H100 and B200; run the existing H100 GPU canary.

## Acceptance criteria

- `marin-core[gpu]` installs one coherent CUDA 13 environment without per-job overrides.
- PyTorch and TorchVision resolve as a compatible pair.
- The resolved cuBLAS and NCCL versions retain the existing B200 and H100 fixes.
- Every remaining direct exact pin has a nearby compatibility rationale; otherwise it is expressed as the narrowest validated range.
- H100 and B200 smoke tests pass, and the H100 GPU canary passes.

<details>
<summary>Why the current constraints exist</summary>

- **Torch 2.11:** selected in #5379 because Torch 2.10 cu128 pinned NCCL 2.27.5, which reproduced a CoreWeave H100 all-to-all failure. Torch 2.11 cu128 brought NCCL 2.28.9, which passed the probe.
- **TorchVision 0.26:** this is the native-extension compatibility pair for Torch 2.11. PR #6346 demonstrated why changing Torch without changing TorchVision is unsafe.
- **cuBLAS floor:** `nvidia-cublas>=13.2.0.9` was added in #5428 after older CUDA 13 builds warned on B200. Marin does not directly exact-pin cuBLAS; uv records the selected version in the lock.
- **cu128 index:** retained because the available Torch cu130 metadata exact-pinned cuBLAS below that B200 floor.
- **vLLM:** the selected vLLM revision also pins its build/runtime Torch and TorchVision pair exactly. Relaxing Marin alone may therefore not be enough for GPU vLLM; any required fork change belongs with #7135.

</details>

Blocks #7135. The downstream `marin-serve --gpu` integration remains tracked by #7111.

topics.title: [finelog] Increase forwarding throughput for dense log backlogs
topics.body:
Increase regional Finelog → hub forwarding throughput so dense log backlogs drain faster and delayed task logs reach Iris. Forward up to four namespaces concurrently and read up to one million log rows per read-and-send cycle. Requests retain their byte limit, and chunks remain serial within the log namespace. The saved source cursor records completed progress and cannot advance past a pending or retryable request.

Encode each candidate chunk once. If its payload exceeds 150 MiB, split it in half and process each half the same way. Process the left half first to preserve source order. Source scans keep separate row-count and segment bounds, and oversized single rows retain their existing handling. Release the decoded Arrow batch before waiting for acknowledgements. Slow-cycle diagnostics separate source reads, chunk encoding, and RPC compression/transport/durable acknowledgement from cursor persistence.

During the October 17 incident, RNO2A was roughly 395 million regional sequence positions behind. Forwarding counters showed about 24,000 accepted positions/sec before deployment and 87,000–107,000/sec over successive 71- and 65-second samples after deploying namespace concurrency and larger reads. A dense source sample contained about 77,000 rows per second of event time; this measures production density. Sequence positions can include gaps and filtered rows, so those counters are not exact row counts. By 17:56 UTC, backlog was down to 91 positions and all 417 rows for the affected task were present on the hub. The chunk-splitting follow-up remains undeployed.

A local benchmark on one million synthetic NCCL-shaped rows with six log columns and 294 MB of Arrow IPC output reduced serialization attempts from seven to three compared with the deployed sizing search. Bytes serialized, including discarded attempts, fell from 1,010 to 589 MB; both versions produced two requests. With 100,000 narrow rows followed by 100,000 wide rows, halving produced nine requests against eight with the packing search. Halving accepts underfilled requests to avoid the sizing search. These measurements describe serialization work; they do not establish an end-to-end throughput improvement.

A bounded million-row regional read took 1.32 seconds initially and 0.19 seconds on repeat. Later live scans took 5.4–8.2 seconds in 12–16-second cycles, including a 128-segment window returning only 424,000 rows. Read cost varies with segment geometry and cache state. An isolated local server capped at four CPUs acknowledged compressed 500,000-row writes in 0.70–0.78 seconds. Live hub samples showed about three active cores on a four-core VM, compaction/index work, and near-zero disk I/O wait. The largest resolved perf symbols involved copying, comparisons, and page faults; stripped Rust symbols limited attribution. These probes do not fully apportion live cycle time; the added stage timings expose the remaining waits.

[Incident record](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/780).

topics.title: [levanter] Add plateau dropping as a train_lm option
topics.body:
Add plateau_dropping to train_lm. With it set, a supervised token leaves the
loss once its loss has stopped changing: from its third visit on, a token is
dropped when both visit-to-visit relative changes, including the current
visit, are below 10% (each relative to the earlier loss, floored at 0.05 nats).
The token stays in the input, its loss is still measured, and it is trained
again as soon as its loss moves. The loss is the mean over kept tokens, and
each step logs kept and dropped token counts and loss sums. The rule follows
the write-up in #10028; the defaults are configurable.

History is kept per row on the host, keyed by a hash of input_ids and
loss_weights, so it does not depend on loader order and survives per-epoch
permutations. It is written beside every checkpoint as
plateau-updates-<N>.npz, and a resumed run refuses to start without the file
for its restored update count. A resume reproduces the uninterrupted run's
training metrics and history bit for bit, and on a 2-way context, 4-way expert
CPU mesh the per-epoch dropped counts equal a mesh without context
parallelism. PlateauTrainer plugs into two new Trainer.train_step overrides,
one adding per-step inputs and one consuming metrics before the step's hooks
run.

Microbatching and z-loss are rejected with plateau dropping. Multi-host
gathering of the per-token losses and host memory (about 16 bytes per
supervised token) are untested at scale.

Part of #10213

topics.title: [post-training] Mix PivotRL pivots into broad RLVR for SWE and terminal gains
topics.body:
## TL;DR

Three matched mixed-domain RLVR runs from the Grug Datakit SFT (October 5) test whether a share of [PivotRL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.21383) pivots improves SWE-bench Verified and OpenThoughts-TBLite without hurting the other domains, and whether pivot selection matters: RLVR alone, RLVR with selected SWE and Terminal pivots at 20% of prompts, and RLVR with random SWE and Terminal turns at the same share. Two optional arms move the selected share to 10% and 30%. Every arm stops at 12 steps. Status: prerequisites done; a two-step smoke run of B is running.

## Hypothesis

Pivots that the SFT policy's own pass rates select (#9933), rewarded by #9933's deterministic verifiers, improve SWE-bench Verified and OpenThoughts-TBLite at 20% of prompts while broad holdout accuracy stays within noise. Random SWE and Terminal turns at the same share help less. Training pivots alone has been hard to stabilize; mixing them into broad RLVR keeps the rest of the policy anchored.

## Setup

- **Start:** [open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Datakit-SFT-262K-2026.10.05](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Datakit-SFT-262K-2026.10.05), a pure SFT checkpoint. #9933 measured its SWE and Terminal pass rates on this policy, so the selections apply unchanged, and the RLVR data is unseen.
- **RLVR data:** [Nemotron-RL-Ultra-RLVR1-Cleaned-v3](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Nemotron-RL-Ultra-RLVR1-Cleaned-v3-2026-09-30) (84,403 train / 94 validation rows; 24% single-step tool use, 14% instruction following, 9% code, 13% math, no SWE or Terminal rows). Any SWE or terminal change between arms is therefore attributable to the added turns.
- **Recipe:** the #9735 reference/KL arm (frozen reference, KL 0.01, sequence-mean loss, entropy 0.001, router replay), 512 prompts × 16 samples per step, at most 12 steps, the same seed in every arm. SFT starts in #9735 collapsed after 12 to 20 steps. Asynchronous rollouts with staleness up to 2, TIS correction, a 102,400-token request window with 49,152 tokens per turn, and thinking on, as #9933 measured the pivots' pass rates.
- **RLVR blend as trained:** 63,590 of RLVR1's rows. MarinSkyRL now runs every Nemotron Ultra row as a task session, and code generation, NeMo tool use, NVARC inductive and Lean sessions execute in a Docker task machine that Iris task pods cannot start, so every arm omits those four agents (about 20% of RLVR1, including #9735's code domain). Rows containing a blank text message, which task conversations reject, are dropped too (3,991 RLVR, 59 Terminal). Validation keeps 67 of RLVR1's 94 rows.
- **Pivot prompts:** the runtime drops earlier assistant turns' reasoning from pivot prompts, which #9933's pass-rate measurement kept.
- **Pivots:** #9933's long-format SWE and Terminal candidates, selected at λ = 0.65 (1 to 10 passes of 16) from the pooled K = 16 pass rates already measured on this policy (`users/dml/pivotrl/{swe,terminal}/pass-rates/grug-67b-a2b-datakit-sft-262k-20261005+seed-1@2026.10.09`). That selects 25,792 of 72,434 scored SWE turns under `nemo` and 6,999 of 36,107 Terminal turns.
- **Reward:** `nemotron_ultra` grades pivot rows through MarinSkyRL#992 with #9933's verifiers: NeMo Gym argument comparison (`nemo`) for SWE and Terminus-2 keystroke similarity without a judge (`string_90`) for Terminal. #10000 uses the same graders. Pivot replies are capped at 4,096 tokens, the cap the pass rates were sampled at.

## Arms

| Arm | Data |
| --- | --- |
| A | RLVR1 |
| B | RLVR1, with selected pivots replacing 20% of prompts |
| C | RLVR1, with random SWE and Terminal candidate turns replacing 20% of prompts |
| B-10, B-30 (optional) | As B, at 10% and 30% |

The batch stays at 512 prompts, so added turns displace RLVR prompts. Each step carries 102 added turns, 51 SWE and 51 Terminal, because the two benchmarks weigh equally in the decision rules; MarinSkyRL's domain-weighted sampling fills every batch to these counts from route-tagged pools and draws each pool uniformly. RLVR rows come first and their pool is shuffled first, so with one seed B's and C's RLVR prompts are a prefix of A's draw order. Twelve steps use 612 of each pool (25,792 SWE and 6,999 Terminal pivots), so no turn repeats.

### Why 20%

Only groups with mixed outcomes produce a gradient, and RLVR1 groups already mostly do: `reward/informative_group_fraction` was 0.79 at the first step from the Datakit SFT (Datakit v4, #9735) and fell to about 0.55 by step 12. Resampling the stored K = 16 pass rates, 88% of selected SWE pivots and 81% of selected Terminal pivots come back mixed, against 58% and 24% of random candidate turns. Pivots' share of the gradient is therefore only 1.1 to 1.5 times their share of prompts, and C carries about half of B's pivot signal at the same share.

Pivot-only RL on this SFT, with the same policy learning rate (4e-6) and gradient clip, bounds the dose. One update of 64 SWE pivot groups raised SWE-bench Verified from 26.0% to 29.4% (146 vs 129 of 496 matched tasks, against a historical base run) with AIME24 unchanged; five updates raised held-out pivot accuracy from 0.29 to 0.38. Forty Terminal updates cost 36 points on AIME24 and 9 to 10 on GPQA Diamond, MMLU-Pro and Math500, and ninety SWE updates collapsed agentic behavior (1 of 248 SWE-bench Verified trials solved, 0 of 190 TBLite) while held-out pivot accuracy kept rising.

Counting a mixed step as its pivot gradient share of a pivot-only update, with RLVR1's informative fraction averaging about 0.68 over the first 12 steps, a first-order approximation that ignores RLVR and KL counteracting drift:

| *p* | Pivot prompts per step | Pivot gradient share | Equivalent pivot-only updates by step 12 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 10% | 51 | ~12% | ~1.5 |
| 20% | 102 | ~24% | ~2.9 |
| 30% | 154 | ~35% | ~4.2 |

With at most 12 steps, 10% delivers about one pivot-only update, the dose that gained about 3 points on SWE, below what the benchmarks resolve. 20% places the dose in the middle of the range where pivot-only training helped, about 14 times below where it did damage, with RLVR still about three quarters of the gradient. B-10 and B-30 bracket it.

## Measurements

- At steps 0, 4, 8 and 12: pass rate on #9933's held-out validation turns graded in process, broad holdout pass@1 and normalized verifier score, and per-domain reward.
- Per step and per source (RLVR, SWE, Terminal): informative group count and mean response length, so B and C are compared by delivered pivot signal and any pull toward shorter RLVR answers shows up early. Pivot replies are capped at 4,096 tokens, the cap their pass rates were sampled at, through each pivot row's request; the sequence-mean loss weights them like full RLVR answers.
- At step 0 and each arm's step 4, 8 and 12 checkpoints: full SWE-bench Verified (500 tasks, mini-swe-agent 2.1.0) and OpenThoughts-TBLite (Terminus 2), three runs each, compared per task between arms, plus AIME24, GPQA Diamond, MMLU-Pro and Math500, the benchmarks pivot-only training hurt.
- Checkpoints are selected by the broad holdout and pivot validation, never by the benchmarks. A paired comparison on 500 SWE tasks has a standard error of about 2 points; on 100 tasks it is about 4.4, too wide for the effects expected here.

## Decision rules

- B beats A on SWE-bench Verified or OpenThoughts-TBLite by more than two paired standard errors, with the broad holdout and the four reasoning benchmarks within noise: pivots help in mixed RLVR. Next, test RL-then-merge against the Campaign 3 merge recipe (#9975).
- B ≈ C: selection does not matter at this share; random turns are enough. B > C partly reflects C's smaller pivot signal, so the logged informative group counts qualify the comparison.
- B beats A on pivot validation only: the verifier reward does not transfer to the benchmarks. Revisit the reward component (`exact`) or the generation cap.
- An arm collapses: report its best checkpoint before the collapse and compare arms only at matched steps.

## Prerequisites

1. Per-agent `pivot_reward`, declared among the Nemotron Ultra session settings: MarinSkyRL#992.
2. Selection artifacts at λ = 0.65 from #9933's stored K = 16 pass rates: built, 25,792 SWE and 6,999 Terminal pivots.
3. Arm datasets: #10215 builds RLVR1 (`open-athena/Nemotron-RL-Ultra-RLVR1-Cleaned-v3-2026-09-30@600262dd`) alone, with the selected pivots, and with every scored candidate turn, each row tagged with its route. Rows move from the retired `skyrl_gym` route to `task_session`, which MarinSkyRL grades Nemotron Ultra rows on since its #879. Validation in every arm is RLVR1's 94 rows plus #9933's 508 held-out SWE and 503 Terminal turns.
4. A two-step smoke run of B on 6 nodes (64 prompts with B's composition, 32K window) confirming that every agent's rows load and grade.

## Links

- PivotRL candidates, pass rates and selection: #9933; SFT baselines on the same pivots: #10000; TaskSpec versions of the candidates: #10181
- Prior broad-domain RLVR: #9359, #9735
- Paper: [PivotRL (arXiv 2603.21383)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.21383)

topics.title: [grug] Add a Triton flash attention for AMD GPUs
topics.body:
Add `gpu_triton_flash`, an opt-in fused causal attention for Grug on AMD GPUs, where Grug had no fused kernel. Existing backends are unchanged. The forward, dQ and dK/dV kernels are Triton kernels launched through `jax_triton`, like the top-k and Sonic MoE kernels. Earlier revisions of this PR used the Pallas Triton backend. JAX 0.11 deprecates it and tells Triton users to switch to the official Triton bindings and `jax_triton`; its other route, Pallas on Mosaic GPU, does not target AMD GPUs.

The kernels reduce each mask to one inclusive key lower bound per query, `max(segment start, q - W + 1)` for window `W`. Key blocks outside `[lower bound, q]` are skipped, and blocks fully inside it skip the mask computation. GQA indexes the shared KV head instead of repeating K/V, for any ratio that divides the heads. The dK/dV kernel computes `K Qᵀ`, so P and dS come out of their matmuls already transposed for the dV and dK matmuls. Under a mesh, including Grug's one-device mesh, the kernels run inside `shard_map`; batch and heads may be sharded, sequence and head_dim may not.

One layer's forward plus backward at the June model's per-GPU shape (8 x 4096 tokens, 20 query heads, 5 KV heads, head_dim 128, bf16), median of three interleaved rounds in one process (jobs 457836, 457837):

| Mask | GPU | reference | Pallas Triton (earlier revision) | `gpu_triton_flash` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| window 2048 | MI350X | 20.19 ms | 6.77 ms | 5.11 ms |
| causal | MI350X | 22.26 ms | 10.04 ms | 8.38 ms |
| window 2048 | MI300X | 31.17 ms | 12.04 ms | 10.17 ms |
| causal | MI300X | 32.32 ms | 17.28 ms | 15.25 ms |

Pallas hands its Triton IR to XLA's bundled Triton, while `jax_triton` compiles with pip triton 3.6. With the Pallas revision's tiles, the port ran 11-13% slower than Pallas, so the tiles were swept again on both GPUs. MI350X (gfx950) runs the forward with two pipeline stages and MI300X with one; the other tiles are shared.

Value and gradient parity tests against `reference_attention` pass on MI300X and MI350X. CI has neither a GPU nor jax-triton, so it skips them. All dots run at IEEE precision: by default Triton runs float32 dots as xf32 on MI300X, which failed the float32 tests. Float32 inputs get smaller tiles, because the bf16 tiles overflow MI300X's 64 KiB of shared memory.

On ROCm the kernels need jaxlib 0.11.1 or newer with jax-triton 0.3.1 and triton 3.6; jaxlib 0.11.0 never loads `jax_rocm10_plugin`'s Triton launcher. The measurements above used jax 0.11.1, jax_rocm10_plugin 0.11.1+rocm10.1.0, jax-triton 0.3.1 and triton 3.6.0. #9989 moves the HPC Fund venv recipe to these versions.

Each run of equal segment IDs is one document, so a segment ID that reappears after a different ID starts a new document; `reference_attention` lets the two runs attend to each other. Masks that carry FA4 precomputed bounds, as moe_hero_ep and moe_hero_fsdp build them, supply the lower bounds directly; padding queries then attend only to themselves.

jax-triton kernels fail today when one process drives several AMD GPUs: on a kernel's first launch, jaxlib 0.11.1 reads the compiled hsaco from a temporary file and deletes it without holding its cache lock, so all but one GPU fail and the step stalls at the next collective (repro in https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9853#issuecomment-6090140907). #10014 lands the Pallas-Triton version of these kernels in the meantime; this PR replaces it once AMD's jax fork fixes the race.

Part of #9812
