| Arm | Context | `--qk-mult` | `--qk-mult-long-scale` | Global / local QK |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A1 | 16K | — | — | 1.48 / 1.48 (default) |
| A2 | 16K | 1.58 | — | 1.58 / 1.58 |
| A3 | 16K | 1.68 | — | 1.68 / 1.68 |

A2 and A3 bracket the all-layer value above the default: 1.58 is close to DeepSeek-V2's mscale coefficient (about 1.57) and 1.68 is the squared YaRN form.

**Possible follow-up waves**, decided after wave 1:

| Arm | Context | `--qk-mult` | `--qk-mult-long-scale` | Global / local QK |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| G1 | 16K | 1.3 | 1.1386 | 1.48 / 1.3 |
| G3 | 16K | 1.3 | 1.2964 | 1.68 / 1.3 |

- G1 and G3 scale only the global (full-causal, no-RoPE) layers. The local layers keep a 2048-token window at both lengths, so their number of keys per query grows by at most about 25% (fewer queries sit near a sequence start), against 4× for the global layers. On the 67B, a global-only arm did worse; that run started from 1.3 at 8K, so its arms sat at different values from these. They are most useful if a higher all-layer value wins in wave 1, to check whether the gain comes from the global layers alone.
- A second seed for A1 and the best other arm, if wave 1's differences are close to the noise bar (decision 2).

**Shared settings.**

- 100 steps per arm at the production schedule (390251 steps), tokens per update (4,194,304 per rack, batch 2816 at 16K), and gate/router weight decay 0.02. The optimizer config is identical at 4K and 16K.
- Eval every 50 steps, so at N+50 and N+100. Eval packs at the training context, 16K. The mid-run eval exercises eval followed by more training, including memory after the dropless 16K eval, which has not run on GPUs yet.
- One checkpoint save and resume in at least one 16K arm.
- Capacity factor 1.15 in every arm, from `HERO_MODEL`. Expert drops at 16K were 16× the 4K value on one rack (3.1e-3 against 1.9e-4 on the current stack); the sweep records them, and a capacity change would be a separate decision.

**Reading the results.** The default is 1.48 on all layers. Another arm replaces it only if it is better on both Uncheatable and the Paloma macro without PTB and WikiText at 16K packing, by a margin clearly above the noise, with no worse loss stability. bethehand's 2× pooled-SD bar is the guide, and the N+100 eval is the scoring point, since the arms are still converging at N+50; the final call is made by people, not by the rule. Also compare:

- step-by-step training loss against A1 on the shared batches;
- total grad norm, spikes, and loss stability over the 100 steps;
- per-parameter grad norms, only for parameters that reproduce across same-seed reruns (`output_proj` and the final norms), or for differences well above the 6–28% per-step rerun spread;
- expert drop fraction, tokens/s, and peak memory, which also set the rollback bands for the production run.

The hero's own steps before the handoff are the no-switch reference for loss stability, grad norm, drops, and throughput; a 4K arm would read different batches from the 16K arms, so its loss and evals would not line up with theirs either. A 4K-packed retention check of the 16K arms, since `qk_mult` changes the model at every length, needs a separate eval of each arm's final checkpoint; the launcher has no eval-only mode.

**Decisions needed**

1. **Racks.** On 11 racks (Larry's preference) each arm is about 22 minutes of training at 13–14 s/step, plus a 3–5 minute restore, a cold compile of about 30 minutes (the 16K executables and each `qk_mult` value are new to the compile cache), and two evals, so about 60–70 minutes per arm. Wave 1's three arms pause the hero for roughly 3–3.5 hours plus the hero's own restart, and each follow-up arm adds about an hour. On the one spare rack the hero keeps training, but each step has 11× fewer tokens, and the arms run one at a time.
2. **Noise bar.** With one seed per arm, the seed-to-seed SD of eval differences is not measured. Options: add a second seed for A1 and one other arm, or use the hero's eval-to-eval noise (SD of the change 0.0026 for the 14-subset Paloma macro, 0.0012 for Uncheatable).
3. **Handoff checkpoint.** It must be permanent and at a multiple of 50 steps, so the trial evals land at N+50 and N+100 (resumed runs skip the first-step eval). For the production switch, it should also sit a few hundred steps before a 3000-step eval boundary, so the first 16K eval comes soon after the deploy.
4. **Retention check.** Whether the 4K-packed eval of the 16K arms is worth adding eval-only tooling before the switch, or can be skipped given that the production run will train at 16K from here on.

🤖 Plot of the 67B YaRN 20-step probe from #6811 ([table](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6811#issuecomment-4931724369)): `train/cross_entropy_loss` per step for the six arms, resumed from step 39,000 at seq 65,536 and batch 1,024. All arms read the same batches. Color is the coefficient (grey 0.0, blue 0.1, orange 0.2); solid lines scale qk on all layers, dashed lines scale only the long (global) layers and keep the short layers at 1.3. The bottom panel subtracts the `all_00` control. The two controls are identical, so their lines overlap.

![67B YaRN 20-step probe: per-step training cross-entropy, six arms](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/4886ea7987a1237df1ecd85db511e5db23f3c8b2/qk16k/yarn_20step_xent_6811.png)

- Long-only coef 0.2 (long qk 1.84, short 1.30) is lowest at almost every step, about 0.005–0.008 below the control from step 39,005 on.
- All-layer coef 0.2 (qk 1.84 everywhere) starts 0.010–0.015 above the control and only crosses below it around step 39,006.
- At step 39,019 the four scaled arms sit within 0.003 of each other, 0.002–0.005 below the control.

Note: that probe started from 1.3 at 8K, so its qk values (1.57, 1.84) are not the same points as the hero's 4K → 16K arms.

Artifact showing attention entropy as a function of position in document, qk_mult on local, qk_mult on global, layer, and head: https://claude.ai/artifact/53wrjEW1Ep4uPahyjf47pK. Entropy on local layers stays flat, regardless of global layer context length.

Comment above shows the earlier results from the 67B run. Long only is slightly better on train loss- evals may have some noise. Will see what results are for long only qk mult 1.68 on hero, estimating that will look best.

@ClassicLarry @mcwitt Paired per step on the shared batches, the arms separate more clearly than the eval totals in #10101 do, and this supports keeping 1.48: A2 roughly ties it, while A0 and G3 are behind at every step after step 20.

- A0 (1.3): +0.0164 at step 0, before any update, then +0.0022 over steps 1–49, +0.0012 over 50–99 and +0.0009 over 100–107, still closing slowly. At N+100 it is worse on Uncheatable (+0.0009) and on 15 of the 16 Paloma subsets (all but gab).
- G3 (1.68 on the global layers only): 0.0008 lower at step 0 and level through step 19, then behind: about +0.0005 over steps 30–89, +0.0008 over 90–99 and +0.0011 over 100–107. It is worse on all 16 Paloma subsets at both evals, and on Uncheatable (+0.0002, +0.0003).
- A2 (1.58): +0.0022 at step 0, closing to +0.0002 by step 10, then level (+0.00001 over steps 10–99; +0.0001 over 100–107).

For scale, the three same-seed 16K restores from step 180k that I compared above differ by under 0.0001 on average over steps 30–89, and are positive on 30–35 of those 60 steps; G3 is behind A1 on all 60.

On the hero, G3 and A1 were still level at step 19, where the 67B probe stopped, and the gap built up only from about step 25, so a 20-step run here would not have shown it. Later switches may need arms of 100 steps or more.

A2's +0.0012 at N+100 on the Paloma macro without PTB and WikiText is mostly twitterAAE; the other 13 subsets average +0.0002. Over the hero's last 30 evals before step 252k, twitterAAE accounts for 58% of that macro's eval-to-eval variance, so it may be worth reporting the macro without it as well.
Going with 1.48 on all layers. Seems slightly better than 1.3, but this field is pretty insensitive at only a 4x context extension.

16k extension has been deployed.

topics.title: [grug] Switch the hero to 16K context with qk_mult 1.48
topics.body:
Switch the hero from 4K to 16K context with `qk_mult` 1.48 on all layers. The new run `hero-ctx16k-step257k` forks `hero-mfu30-step231k` at its permanent `step-257553`, where the parent stopped on 2026-10-13. Tokens per rack per update, the 390251-step schedule, and the optimizer stay the same, so the batch drops from 11264 to 2816 sequences on 11 racks.

`HERO_MODEL` gets `max_seq_len=16384` and `qk_mult=1.48`. `HERO_CONTEXT_PHASES` records the 4K phase ending at step 257553, and `HERO_FLOPS_BASELINE_TOTAL` is 1.7792877262736668e24, the parent's `throughput/total_gflops` × 1e9 at W&B `_step` 257552 (`global_step` 257552). `trigger_hero.sh` hands off from `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/grug/hero-mfu30-step231k/2026.08.19.2/checkpoints/step-257553` (permanent, `metadata.json` step 257553) and forks W&B at `hero-mfu30-step231k?_step=257552`; `current_run.py` names the child.

`build_ladder_run` now uses the checked-in history for d6144 by itself instead of relying on `main()`, and it refuses an explicit `num_steps` while a history is in effect, because the prior phases' data stages are rebuilt from the schedule length. The diagnostics launcher and restore benchmark take their default batch from the hero's tokens per rack at the model's context length (256 sequences per rack at 16K); the old fixed 1024-sequence default would have put four times the hero's load on a rack. `HERO_EP_BATCH_SIZE` is replaced by `HERO_TOKENS_PER_RACK` and `hero_rack_batch_size` in `hero_recipe.py`.

In 100-step arms at 16K from permanent `step-252000` on the 11 hero racks (#9615), the dropless eval loss after step 252100 was 1.81349 at `qk_mult` 1.3, 1.81156 at 1.48, 1.81200 at 1.58, and 1.81282 for 1.68 on the global layers only. The differences are within eval noise, so we keep the YaRN-style value 1.3 × (0.1·ln 4 + 1). Those arms also ran the 16K dropless eval on 11 racks at 123.4 GiB peak memory, about 30.6% MFU, and a drop fraction falling to about 1.2e-3.

A dry build of the exact `trigger_hero.sh` launch gives 16K, `qk_mult` 1.48/1.0, capacity 1.15, batch 2816, eval at the training length every 3000 steps, `FlopsBaseline(257553, 1.7792877e24)`, and a rebuilt 4K phase with stages [0, 108000, 312192] at batch 11264. The optimizer config is identical to main's 4K build and to the parent's logged config, and the rebuilt phase's mixture, shuffle, and seed match what the parent trained with. An independent review found no blockers; its findings are fixed here except the vibe-check sampler, filed as #10100.

- Run `trigger_hero.sh fork-wandb` right after merge. Until the child exists and logs its config, the hourly completions workflow fails at `hero_checkpoint_paths`.
- The parent stopped at the handoff, so there is no same-batch control window. The agreed gates: the first logged step is 257553 and cross-entropy stays below 1.25 over the first 10 steps; cross-entropy in 1.09–1.15; MFU at least 29% after warmup; drop fraction below 2e-3 by step 257633–257652; peak memory 123–124 GiB; no retries, watchdogs, or runtime errors; the first 16K eval at step 258000 completes.
- Rollback relaunches `f2bc69bf6c` under `hero-mfu30-step231k`, which resumes `step-257553`.
- Eval packs at 16K from the child onward, so the `eval_dropless/*` series step down at the switch, and `eval_regressed` may fire once.
- Comparison report: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/reports/Hero-16K-cutover:-hero-ctx16k-step257k-trial--VmlldzoxODEwNzE3Mg==

@ClassicLarry for review.

Part of #9615

topics.title: Preserve evaluator-owned metrics after infrastructure failures
topics.body:
Preserve Evalchemy's metrics after infrastructure failures. Marin's per-sample averaging loses benchmark-specific scoring, metric names, and breakdowns.

Accept partial results only when Evalchemy's reported scored count matches the valid archived samples. Partial-result recovery requires [Evalchemy #214](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/pull/214).
topics.head: 9a3e045d55db0a7d165dfdde20b7e82e94fe23f2

comments.body:
🤖 Holistic review of 83842b7e152d14bd409e23e0390d6edd99784a9c.

The PR removes Marin's per-sample metric rebuilding. When a task has transport failures, `run_evalchemy` now keeps Evalchemy's aggregate only if the reported `scored_count` equals the number of valid archived samples. Otherwise it raises `INFRA_FAILED`. The direction is sound and the shared-path check now covers `eval_step` (26 evalchemy/aggregate tests pass locally). The open issue is the order in which this lands relative to the Evalchemy pin.

**Should fix**
1. `lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/evalchemy/runner.py:322` This PR alone makes every run with any transport failure end as `INFRA_FAILED`. The runs Marin used to recover now fail. The pinned Evalchemy (`EVALCHEMY.commit` c2548fe6 in `lib/marin/src/marin/external_dependencies.py:68`, `EVALCHEMY_COMMIT` c131e5ab in `eval_policy.py:20`) still uses `_scored_count`, which falls back to `generated_count`. That count includes the failed rows, so the count never matches. marin-community/evalchemy#214 is the change that subtracts the excluded rows, and it is open and unmerged. Nothing in this PR exercises a real Evalchemy output whose counts match. Land #214 first. Then bump both pins in this PR, with a policy version if that identity requires one. If the PR merges before that, the description should say that partial runs fail closed until the bump.
2. `lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/evalchemy/runner.py:389` `EvalchemyExecutor` calls `outcome.result.task_metrics()` a second time. `run_evalchemy` already read and validated the same metrics at `runner.py:299`. The executor then copies `coverage` and `canonical_metrics` into locals that only forward them. Add `metrics` to `EvalchemyOutcome` and build `EvaluationOutcome` straight from the outcome fields. That removes a second archive scan, and the executor's metrics are then guaranteed to be the ones the consistency check approved.

**Tests to drop**
3. `test_evalchemy_executor_rejects_native_transport_failure_when_rebuilding`: duplicates `test_run_evalchemy_rejects_partial_aggregate_with_inconsistent_scored_count`. Both cover one generation sample with a transport failure, where the fixture's default `scored_count` equals the document extent. The `source_metric` / `benchmark_name` parametrization fed the deleted `_apply_recovered_canonical_metrics` projection and no longer reaches different code. The "when_rebuilding" name describes the removed behavior.
4. `test_evalchemy_executor_preserves_evaluator_partial_aggregates[WeightedTask-weighted_score-0.7]`: redundant matrix. Both cases are an opaque pass-through of the evaluator's results dict, so one case covers the behavior.

**Related PRs**
5. #10169 (same author): renames `run_evalchemy` to `_run_evalchemy_once` and repoints `EvalchemyExecutor` at it, over the same lines. The validation block this PR moves into `run_evalchemy` has to follow into `_run_evalchemy_once`, and the post-hoc `run_served_evalchemy` path must keep it. Land this PR first, then rebase #10169.
6. #10033: its hunk sits next to `_apply_recovered_canonical_metrics`, which this PR deletes, and it changes the `run_evalchemy`/`_run_evalchemy_child` signatures (`model` → `session`). It does not depend on this PR. Whichever lands second has to resolve the textual conflict.

<!-- marin-holistic-review:83842b7e152d14bd409e23e0390d6edd99784a9c -->

🤖 Removed a duplicate transport-failure test and redundant aggregate case. Evalchemy now passes validated metrics to the executor without a second archive read; the shared scored-count key and test name are consistent. Focused tests (31) and changed-file checks pass.

17 validate_local.py:163 ml-overloaded-function: fixed; write_pool and write_fixtures (returning a Fixtures NamedTuple) build the inputs. The secret traces moved to their own file: a build with them must be refused by the input token gate, and the drop rule is checked by calling candidates() directly. Before this change the validator failed at that gate.

topics.title: FP8 loss-curve validation: bf16 (main) vs FP8 (PR #7079) at row-13 scale on 64x H100
topics.body:
<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

This experiment validated the FP8 changes from PR #7079 against a bf16 control at the row-13 Grug MoE scale, using identical seed and data order and a full 24,000-step schedule on H100s. After smoke debugging reduced the run to one 8-H100 node per arm and fixed allocator fragmentation with `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_ALLOCATOR=cuda_async`, both arms completed cleanly. The loss-curve gate passed: FP8 ended with a matched-step gap of about +0.0040, flat through the cooldown tail and inside the <=0.01 acceptance bar, while running about 5.5% faster by throughput. The campaign also found two follow-ups that do not block the gate: BFC allocator fragmentation can silently deadlock training collectives without `cuda_async`, and FP8 currently uses about 1.66x the bf16 transient step arena because XLA keeps cast/transpose FP8 operands resident for backward GEMMs.

### Helpful links
- [Final result comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7298#issuecomment-5010209991)
- [W&B overlay group](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/groups/fp8-loss-val-7079)
- [Final comparison artifact](https://claude.ai/code/artifact/99ec4cac-2537-494c-b9e2-1b285311fa32)
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

Part of #6699. Validates PR #7079 (FP8 expert GEMMs + FP8 EP wire + FP8 dense GEMMs for attention/shared-expert) against a bf16 control on real data — the loss-curve gate flagged in the PR before FP8 defaults can flip.

**Motivation:** before FP8 can become a default, we need evidence that enabling it does not perturb the training loss at production scale. This experiment runs a bf16 control (main) and an FP8 test arm (PR #7079) in parallel on the CoreWeave H100s from identical init and data order, saving the full per-step loss trajectory for both, and compares them. The run is sized (~8 h, cached in-cluster dataset, full LR schedule) to show substantial loss movement while resolving 0.01-level precision deltas — using the cluster-resident SlimPajama cache to avoid cross-region data costs and staying within a 64-H100 budget.

## Design

Two arms in parallel on cw-us-east-02a, 4 nodes / 32 H100 each (64 total):

| arm | code | precision |
|---|---|---|
| `fp8val-bf16-*` | `research/mcwitt/7079-fp8-loss-val-ctl` = main + launcher | bf16 |
| `fp8val-fp8-*` | `research/mcwitt/7079-fp8-loss-val` = PR #7079 merged with main + launcher | `GrugFp8Config(wire=True, dense=True)` |

- **Model:** row-13 flagship shape — d2560, 26 layers, 64 experts top-4 (+shared), MHA 20×128, seq 4096, sliding window 2048, qk_mult 1.3, ~18B params; `ring` MoE backend, EP8 intra-node, FSDP over 4 nodes, `gpu_fa4_cute` attention, `recompute_all` remat. Identical in both arms; seed 0 in both (same init + data order).
- **Optimizer:** production MuonH (`lr=1e-3`, `adam_lr=1e-4`, warmup 10%, cooldown to 0) run through the **full schedule** — #6486 showed precision gaps surface in the cooldown tail, so a truncated schedule can show false parity.
- **Data:** SlimPajama-6B llama3-tokenized cache already materialized under this cluster's `MARIN_PREFIX` (`s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin`, in-cluster LOTA endpoint) — zero cross-region traffic. Feistel block shuffle.
- **Budget:** ~11k steps × 128 seqs × 4096 tok ≈ 5.8B tokens/arm, sized from measured H100 throughput to finish inside ~8 h (final step count calibrated by a short smoke run). Precedent: #6486 resolved 0.01-level loss deltas at 1.4B tokens.
- **Trajectory:** W&B project `marin_moe`, group `fp8-loss-val-7079`, `log_every=1` (per-step `train/loss`).

**Acceptance:** matched-step train-loss overlay; gap ≤0.01 at end of schedule (the #6486 threshold for a meaningful difference), with specific attention to the last 10% (cooldown tail). Divergence, NaNs, or a growing gap fails the gate.

Logbook: `.agents/logbooks/7079-fp8-loss-val.md` on `research/mcwitt/7079-fp8-loss-val`.

Note: not filed under the #4281 recipe-ablation family — this is infra/precision validation for #6699, not a recipe-change experiment.

comments.body:
🤖 Full A/B launched 2026-07-17 13:32 UTC after nine smoke rounds: `/mwittmann/fp8val-bf16-full1` vs `/mwittmann/fp8val-fp8-full1` on cw-us-east-02a.

**Final configuration** (revised from the issue body's design during smoke debugging — full trail in `.agents/logbooks/7079-fp8-loss-val.md`):

- 1 node × 8 H100 per arm (16 total), EP8, **batch 16** × seq 4096, **24000 steps ≈ 1.57B tokens/arm** (≥ the 1.44B that resolved 0.01-level deltas in #6486). Model/optimizer/data/seed as designed (row-13 shapes, MuonH full schedule to zero LR, SlimPajama-6B cluster-local cache, seed 0 both arms).
- Tracker: json_logger (per-step `train/loss` in job logs) — no WANDB key was reachable on the submit host; trajectories will be harvested and plotted here.
- No periodic checkpoints (`FP8VAL_CHECKPOINTS=local`).

**Operational findings from the smoke ladder** (each cost a round; logged for reuse):
1. Multi-host XLA sharded-autotuning rendezvous hangs the 4-node compile → `--xla_gpu_shard_autotuning=false`.
2. `experiments/grug/dispatch.py` forwarded only `XLA_FLAGS`, silently dropping `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION` → train tasks ran at the 0.75 default pool and OOM'd; forwarding widened to `XLA_*` (+ `TF_GPU_ALLOCATOR`) on both experiment branches — candidate for upstreaming.
3. Row-13 (26 unrolled layers) does not fit 4-node FSDP (`data=4`) or 2-node EP16 at B64 on 80GB H100s (program peak 89 GiB; matches the June spike's "B64+L26 HBM wall").
4. **FP8 needs ~4 GB more than bf16 at B32** where the pre-merge bench harness fit — possible memory regression from the main merge or a real-trainer×FP8 interaction; open follow-up.
5. **The 10-minute async time-checkpoint deadlocks the run against training collectives** (all bf16 "NCCL clique stalls" and one FP8 step-10 OOM sit exactly at the first save; reproduced on three different nodes). Avoided here by disabling periodic saves; deserves its own issue.
6. bf16 also stalls NCCL comm-init at mem fraction 0.95 but not 0.90; FP8 needs 0.95. Arms run their proven fraction (allocator pool size does not affect numerics).

ETA: fp8 ~6h, bf16 ~6.7h + ~15 min compile. Results (matched-step deltas, final-loss gap vs the ≤0.01 acceptance bar, cooldown-tail zoom) to follow at completion.

🤖 **Root cause of every training wedge found — and it is neither log reads nor checkpoint saves.**

Full-history post-mortems of all terminal runs (smoke9, full1–full3b) show one identical signature in all five wedges: a **BFC allocator failure to allocate the train step's contiguous scratch chunk** — `bfc_allocator.cc ran out of memory trying to allocate 22.66GiB` (bf16 arms) / `40.68GiB` (fp8 arms) on 1–5 of 8 GPUs — followed ~10 s later by the permanent `Acquire clique` rendezvous stall. Allocator dumps show the pool only ~40% occupied at failure: **fragmentation, not exhaustion**. The device threads whose allocation fails never join the 8-way clique rendezvous, so the remaining ranks wait forever — a silent XLA deadlock instead of a raised OOM.

Both earlier theories are retracted with evidence:
- **Log reads (FP8VAL-003b): refuted.** `iris job logs` is served by the standalone finelog server over on-disk parquet (fed by the logship sidecar); it never enters the task process (the in-task uvicorn is the metrics telltale). Timeline agrees: bf16-full2 *survived* the heavy 400k/600k-line harvests at 18:08 UTC and wedged at 19:09 with no heavy read within 10 min; the blamed 900k harvest ran at 19:19 — after the stall.
- **Checkpoint saves (FP8VAL-003c): demoted to a perturbation.** Single-node saves have no barrier/collective; their alloc/free churn just re-carves the pool (both save-adjacent wedges landed 3–11 s after the commit callback). Checkpoint-less arms died identically after hours of slow fragmentation.

Side finding, now quantified: **fp8's largest step temp is 40.68 GiB vs bf16's 22.66 GiB at the identical B16 config** — the fp8 memory regression to bisect, and why fp8 arms always wedged first (needs 57% of the ~72 GiB pool contiguous).

Mitigation for any resubmit: `TF_GPU_ALLOCATOR=cuda_malloc_async` (VMM-backed, immune to BFC fragmentation — the allocator's own hint). full4 (running) predates this finding and has no such flag; recovery commands are pre-staged with it. Details in logbook entry FP8VAL-004.

🤖 **fp8 memory regression attributed** (compile-only probe, one 8×H100 node, AOT-compiles the exact row-13 step bf16 vs fp8 without running it).

`compiled.memory_analysis()`:

| arm | temp arena | args/output/alias |
|---|---|---|
| bf16 | 22.65 GiB | 29.88 GiB |
| fp8 | 37.67 GiB | 29.89 GiB |

Persistent state (args/output/alias) is **byte-identical** — fp8 adds nothing to params/grads/opt-state. The whole **+15.0 GiB is transient peak** in the single fused train step.

Per-dtype arena composition (from XLA `buffer-assignment.txt`; Δ = fp8 − bf16):

| dtype | Δ (GiB) | what |
|---|---|---|
| f8e4m3fn | **+5.0** | forward fp8 operands |
| u8 (fp8-as-u8) | **+3.3** | transposed dual-write fp8 operand copies |
| f8e5m2 | **+0.8** | backward fp8 gradient operands |
| f32 | +4.1 | scale / dequant / amax / accumulation scratch |
| bf16 | +4.0 | extra intermediates around quantize ops |

**The bf16 arena contains zero float8 tensors; the fp8 arena adds ~9 GiB of float8-family data.** XLA materializes each large linear's quantized operand *and its transposed layout for the backward GEMM* and keeps them resident across the fused forward+backward, rather than requantizing in each GEMM prologue. The +4 f32 and +4 bf16 are the requantization scaffolding. So this is dual-write/mixed-dtype operand residency — **not** custom_vjp remat-pinning (bf16 grew only ~4 of the 15 GiB).

Highest-leverage reduction: recompute the transposed fp8 operand in the backward instead of stashing it (the e4m3 + u8-transpose pair is ~8.3 GiB). Real fp8-wiring overhead, tracked as a follow-up separate from the loss validation. Probe: `experiments/grug/moe/fp8val_mem_probe.py`; logbook FP8VAL-005.

Separately, the training wedge (FP8VAL-004) is fixed by `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_ALLOCATOR=cuda_async` (VMM allocator, no contiguity requirement — note this is the JAX var, not TF's `TF_GPU_ALLOCATOR`). bf16 control now clears the fragmentation cliff; both arms running.

🤖 **RESULT: loss-curve gate PASSED.** Both arms completed the full 24,000-step schedule (1.57B tokens/arm) cleanly on the `cuda_async` allocator — `fp8val-fp8-full4` and `fp8val-bf16-full6`, seed 0, identical data order.

**Matched-step train loss (FP8 − bf16), all 23,998 steps:**
- mean **+0.0039**, median +0.0038, σ 0.0028, max single-step |Δ| 0.14 (noise)
- no growth: first 2k +0.0034 → mid +0.0029 → **cooldown tail (last 10%) +0.0040**
- final 200-step mean loss: **bf16 3.084 / FP8 3.088 → +0.0040**

**Verdict: PASS** — final matched-step gap **+0.0040**, well inside the ≤0.01 bar (#6486), flat through the cooldown tail (the region #6486 flagged as where precision gaps surface), no NaNs/Infs. Enabling FP8 (wire+dense+grouped GEMMs) does not perturb the training loss at row-13 scale.

**Throughput:** 70.1k / 73.9k tok/s (**1.055×**), MFU 15.09% / 15.92%. On wall-clock (x rescaled by ∫1/throughput), FP8 reaches any given loss ~4.4% sooner and finished 24k in **6.03h vs 6.31h** (~17 min ahead).

Final artifact (4 panels — loss vs step, loss vs wall-clock, Δ with ±0.01 band, throughput): https://claude.ai/code/artifact/99ec4cac-2537-494c-b9e2-1b285311fa32

**Two infra findings from the campaign (both tracked, neither blocks the gate):**
1. Every training "wedge" was a **BFC fragmentation OOM → silent NCCL clique deadlock** at ~42% pool occupancy — *not* heavy log reads or checkpoint saves (both investigated and exonerated). Fix: `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_ALLOCATOR=cuda_async` (VMM allocator, no contiguity requirement). Worth landing as the default for FP8 grug runs.
2. FP8's transient step arena is **1.66× bf16** (+15 GiB), attributed by a compile-only probe to the **cast-transpose dual-write** (caching the transposed FP8 operand for the backward) — a deliberate TE-style speed optimization, bounded and sharding-friendly, not a blocker. Follow-up for #7079 if a memory-marginal config adopts FP8.

Logbook `.agents/logbooks/7079-fp8-loss-val.md` (FP8VAL-006) sealed with full TL;DR.

🤖 **W&B:** the two validation trajectories are now in `marin-community/marin_moe`, group `fp8-loss-val-7079` (full 24k-step per-step `train/loss` + throughput + MFU, history CSVs attached as artifacts):

- bf16 control: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/fp8val-bf16-control
- FP8 (PR #7079): https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/fp8val-fp8
- group (both overlaid): https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/groups/fp8-loss-val-7079

Backfilled post-hoc from the harvested json_logger histories (the runs used `json_logger` at train time — no `WANDB_API_KEY` on the launch box). Reproducible via `experiments/grug/moe/fp8val_wandb_backfill.py` on `research/mcwitt/7079-fp8-loss-val`. Final losses match the reported values (bf16 2.909 / FP8 2.911 at step 23,999).
@dlwh Added a managed experiment TL;DR block summarizing the FP8 loss-curve pass, key W&B/artifact links, and the two non-blocking infra findings.

topics.title: SWE-smith Harbor packages expose the fix through git history in the agent container
topics.body:
The SWE-smith Harbor task packages in `DCAgent/swesmith-sandboxes-with_tests-oracle_verified_120s` (and the same layout in `mlfoundations-dev/swesmith-sandboxes-with_tests`) leave the repository's full git history in the agent's container. The image built from `environment/Dockerfile` keeps a local `main` branch with the unbroken code and about 944 other branches, so the agent can print the fix with `git diff HEAD main -- <package>` or `git show main:<file>`. `/tests` and `/solution` are correctly absent from the image.

Reproduce: build `swesmith-00003`'s `environment/Dockerfile` from the package, run it with no network, then `git log --oneline` (three commits: Initial commit, Bug Patch, Remove F2P Tests), `git branch -a` (944 branches including `main`), `git diff HEAD main -- oauthlib` (the exact fix).

Impact on existing data: in `open-athena/Kimi-2.5-swesmith-sandboxes-with_tests-oracle_verified_120s-maxeps-32k`, 860 of 5,237 passing trials (16.4%) and 433 of 4,119 failing trials run history-reading commands (`git show main:<path>`, diffs against `main` or `HEAD~N`, checkout or restore from history, `git log -p`). Some are benign (a diff against `HEAD~1` shows only the removed tests); many copy the original file. So the reported pass rate on these packages is inflated, and trace sets built on them carry shortcut solutions: the Kimi set above, the `GLM-4.7` and AgentTrove swesmith streams, and the allkimi relay data (`laion/calibforge-relay-traces`, `kimi_swesmith` rows) that was DARE-grafted into Snowball v0 (`open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Merge-Campaign3-DARE-Linear-02-2026.10.12`). SWE-bench Verified is not affected: there the fix is not in the repository's past.

A plain squash is not enough, because `tests/test.sh` itself uses history (`git checkout <task branch>; git checkout HEAD~1`) to restore the removed fail-to-pass tests before running pytest.

Expected: during the agent phase the repository has one commit, no other branches, no remote and no reflog; the verifier restores the fail-to-pass tests from outside the agent's view (for example, ship the test files in `tests/` and copy them in, or keep a git bundle that only the verifier unpacks). For each task, the gold patch still passes, the unpatched repository still fails, and the history-reading commands above return nothing.

Done when: a fixed package build exists with that validation on a sample of tasks, existing SWE-smith pass rates and training sets built on the leaky packages are re-reported with history-reading trials removed or flagged, and the shootout pool in #10213 uses the fixed packages.

comments.body:
🤖

# Research

The reported `swesmith-00003` image retains the pre-bug `main` branch and earlier commits, so an agent can recover the fix from Git history. Removing old refs alone is insufficient if the object database still contains the clean tree; the current verifier also uses `HEAD~1` to recover fail-to-pass tests. The reported 860/5,237 passing and 433/4,119 failing history-reading trials are contamination candidates, not yet an audited count of trials that copied the fix. Marin consumes these external packages and traces, while the package builder is outside this checkout.

**Relevant code and artifacts**
- [DCAgent package release](https://huggingface.co/datasets/DCAgent/swesmith-sandboxes-with_tests-oracle_verified_120s) — affected task source.
- [Shootout #10213](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10213) — waits for stripped packages.
- [AgentTrove ingestion](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/datakit/download/agenttrove.py#L17) — SWE-smith trace consumer.
- [Relay source PR #10027](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10027) — registers Kimi SWE-smith rows.

# Proposal

## Outcome

Publish an immutable, revision-pinned Harbor package release whose agent image contains the bugged working tree in one new Git repository with one commit, one task branch, no `main`/remote/tags/reflog, and no recoverable old objects. Keep the fail-to-pass test payload in Harbor's verifier-only `tests/` area and copy it into the repository when scoring. Record the old and new package revisions and per-task content digests; do not overwrite the release used by existing trials.

## Plan

1. Change the package producer to create a fresh `.git` after applying each bug patch, rather than squashing the existing repository in place. Export required test files from the source package into verifier-only storage before discarding history. Make `tests/test.sh` restore those files without `git checkout` or `HEAD~1`; keep `solution/` and `tests/` out of the agent container.
2. Validate a stratified sample across repositories and test layouts in offline Harbor runs. In each agent image, require one reachable commit and no old refs, remotes, reflogs, or dangling objects containing the clean fix. Exercise `git show main:<file>`, `git diff HEAD main -- <package>`, `git show HEAD~1`, `git log -p`, and `git fsck --unreachable`; none may reveal the clean file. For each sampled task, the untouched bugged tree must score 0 and the gold patch must score 1 under the revised verifier. Publish task IDs, package digests, commands, and results with the new release.
3. Audit the Kimi, GLM-4.7, AgentTrove, and allkimi relay/Snowball v0 provenance at trial or row level. Classify history commands as benign inspection, fix recovery, or unresolved; report raw and unflagged success rates with denominators, plus counts by outcome and category. Publish flagged row IDs or a reproducible manifest and clean-filtered trace revisions where the source can be republished. Annotate existing model and dataset results; filtering rows cannot undo training already performed on Snowball v0.
4. Pin the fixed package revision in the #10213 SWE-smith pool and block the eight-attempt generation until the package validation passes. Keep the already stated pilot-trace history filter separate from the new pool validation. Coordinate Harbor release acquisition with [#10198](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10198); its cache work does not repair the package contents.

## Risks and open questions

The package producer and release permissions are external to this repository, so the new dataset revision needs an owner with access to that build pipeline. The verifier payload must be checked against every sampled task's required test files; a one-commit image can still give false rewards if a file is omitted. Excluding all history-reading trials gives a conservative subset, not an unbiased replacement for a fresh evaluation on fixed packages.

🤖 A fresh GLM 5.3 trial on the raw package used the history to check its fix.

**Setup:** `swesmith-00003` from `DCAgent/swesmith-sandboxes-with_tests-oracle_verified_120s` (revision 78b0d879), unchanged. Harbor at `marin-community/harbor@016dd78b`, mini-swe-agent 2.1.0 with a 32k context, Daytona sandbox, GLM 5.3 through the internal bulk service. The trial passed (reward 1, 16 model calls).

**History use in the trajectory:**
- Step 6: `git log --oneline -5 && git status` showed `Remove F2P Tests` / `Bug Patch` / `Initial commit`.
- Step 8: `git log --all --oneline -- oauthlib/oauth2/rfc8628/endpoints/device_authorization.py && git show 614b134:oauthlib/oauth2/rfc8628/endpoints/device_authorization.py`. The second command prints the pre-bug file (`614b134` is `Initial commit`).
- Step 17: `git diff 614b134 -- oauthlib/oauth2/rfc8628/endpoints/device_authorization.py && echo "IDENTICAL TO ORIGINAL"` printed `IDENTICAL TO ORIGINAL`. The agent confirmed that its edit matches the original file before submitting.

GLM made the edit itself at step 10, after reading the original file at step 8. So this pass is history-assisted, and a GLM pass rate on these packages would be inflated in the same way as the Kimi data.

**Visibility probe:** an oracle-agent probe printed the container state during the agent phase (no model calls).
- `/testbed`: 944 branches (`main`, the task branch, `remotes/origin/*` for every task), and `git log --all` lists every task's `Bug Patch` / `Remove F2P Tests` commits.
- `/tests`: absent.
- `/solution`: absent for model agents. Harbor uploads it only for the oracle agent.
- None of the other task files are present (`task.json`, `test_*_state.py`, `setup.sh`, `container.def`, `test_state.py`).

**Run folders:** `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/sft-shootout/generation/dryrun/swe-dry3` (trajectory: `swesmith-00003__LQ7xGdF/attempts/000/agent/trajectory.json`) and `.../dryrun/visibility1`.

**Consequence for the SFT-shootout teacher pilot (#10213):** the SWE-smith 200x2 pass-rate pilot will run only on the history-stripped packages.

🤖 Fixed SWE-smith packages for the #10213 pool, with validation on 20 tasks. The same class of leak is also present in TMax.

**Fixed packages.** `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/sft-shootout/pool/swesmith-packages.parquet` (sha256 `f004b109edf8aa9274693c07e01266d14469ec8c61fe695cc516aa1175117407`), 2,100 tasks. The schema is the same as the DCAgent parquet (`path`, `task_binary`), and the folder names are unchanged. The source is `DCAgent/swesmith-sandboxes-with_tests-oracle_verified_120s@78b0d879`. The upstream dataset is not modified. Code: [`experiments/post_training/sft_shootout_pool/`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/3bc613878c/experiments/post_training/sft_shootout_pool) on branch `task/206`.

- `environment/Dockerfile`: after the upstream `git fetch && git checkout <instance>`, the same `RUN` replaces the repository: `rm -rf .git && git init && git symbolic-ref HEAD refs/heads/main && git add -A && git commit -m "Initial commit" && git reflog expire --expire=now --all && git gc --prune=now`. This is a new `.git`, not a squash, so no old objects remain in the container's filesystem. The base image's lower layers still hold the old `.git`, but the container cannot read them.
- `tests/f2p_restore/`: the files that the upstream `git checkout HEAD~1` would change, at their parent contents, plus `deleted.txt`. They are computed from a bare clone of `github.com/swesmith/<repo>`. On `swesmith-00003` they match the image's own `git show HEAD~1:<path>` byte for byte.
- `tests/test.sh`: `git checkout <instance>; git checkout HEAD~1;` is replaced by `cp -a /tests/f2p_restore/files/. /testbed/` plus the deletions. The rest is unchanged. Harbor uploads `tests/` only to the verifier (checked in harbor 0.24.0 `verifier/verifier.py`; only `agents/oracle.py` uploads `solution/`).

**Validation** on 20 pool tasks, one from each of 20 repos, in local Docker following Harbor's phase order:

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Agent-phase repository: 1 commit, 1 branch, 0 remotes, empty reflog, no `HEAD~1`/`main~1`/`origin/main`/`master` | 20/20 |
| Gold patch (`solution/solve.sh`) then `tests/test.sh`: reward 1 | 20/20 |
| Unpatched tree: reward 0 | 19/20 |
| Leak commands (`git log --all -p`, `git show HEAD~1`, `git diff HEAD main`, `git diff HEAD~1`, `git fsck --unreachable --lost-found`, `git stash list -p`, `git show main:<every file>`) print a clean-only line | 0/20 (upstream `swesmith-00003` control: 2/2) |

- `swesmith-01094` (`ariga/atlas`) also scores 1 unpatched with the unmodified upstream package, so its verifier does not detect the bug. This is an upstream defect, and it means DCAgent's "oracle verified" does not imply that an unpatched run fails.
- "Clean-only line": a source line the Bug Patch removed that occurs nowhere in the bugged tree. 7 of the 20 tasks have none, so only the ref checks apply to them.
- The filesystem search found no git leak. It did find copies of clean lines in installed packages: `setuptools/_vendor/typeguard` is an older vendored typeguard, which is relevant for `agronholm/typeguard` tasks (57 in the pool). The `_pytest` (iniconfig) and `rapidfuzz` (thefuzz) hits are probably coincidental.
- Residual: `github.com/swesmith/<repo>` is public and keeps every instance branch, so an agent with internet access can still fetch the fix. In the Kimi traces this happened once (`git fetch origin; git show origin/main:<file>`).

Per-task results: `pool/swesmith-validation-20.jsonl` and `pool/swesmith-leak-probe-20.jsonl`.

**TMax: same class of leak, different mechanism.** In `allenai/TMax-SFT-16.5K@848e2182` `tasks.zip`, 221 of 2,200 environments build verifier assets into the agent's image (for example `/opt/oracle/<reference program>`, `/app/verifier/ground_truth_valid_events.txt`, `/home/user/oracle.py`), and `test_final_state.py` reads them. In 181 of the 221, the instruction never names the path. In the #202 Qwen3.6-27B success traces (`allenai/tmax-sft`), 63 trajectories across 18 tasks name one of these hidden paths in a bash command. That is a heuristic: naming a path doesn't prove the answer was copied. The pool excludes the 181 (`excluded.jsonl`, `leak_risk=hidden_verifier_assets`) and keeps the 40 visible ones. TMax's Harbor converter (`hamishivi/tmax@6d3d606c`) does not copy `task.json` (including its `truth` field), `solutions/`, `setup.sh` or `test_initial_state.py`; `test_final_state.py` goes only to `tests/`.

**Effect on #202's pilot training set:** 860 Kimi history-reading passes and those 63 TMax trajectories were removed before training (manifest `selection.swesmith_git_history_rule` and `selection.tmax_hidden_asset_rule`).

🤖 The public `github.com/swesmith` mirrors are now unreachable while the agent runs, and a second leak was found in mini-swe-agent's own install.

**TL;DR**
- During the agent phase, the sandbox can reach only the model proxy. github.com, PyPI, apt and every other host fail DNS, and direct-IP HTTPS (GitHub 140.82.112.3, 140.82.114.4; 1.1.1.1) has its TLS handshake cut. Setup and the verifier keep full network.
- mini-swe-agent 2.1.0 installs a tool env that the agent can read. It holds clean copies of three pool repos: pygments, pandas, tenacity. GLM read `tenacity/retry.py` from it and called it "the reference". The conda base in the images also holds boltons 23.0.0. All four repos (469 tasks) are excluded from pool P.

**Why not a whole-trial block:** Harbor sets the Daytona network policy once per sandbox. Both the mini-swe-agent install and the SWE-smith verifier (`tests/test.sh`) download uv from github.com releases (`astral.sh/uv/0.7.13/install.sh`), so a whole-trial allow-list without github.com breaks them.

**Mechanism** ([`harbor_agents/trial_agents.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1555295d4d5a233e1bb854c814b927c21889574c/experiments/post_training/sft_shootout/harbor_agents/trial_agents.py), `AgentPhaseNetwork`, branch `task/207` @ `1555295d`): just before the agent's run, the live sandbox is switched to `domain_allow_list=iris.oa.dev` (the proxy host). The run starts once that host resolves, and the task's own policy is restored before the verifier. Each trial writes the applied policy to `agent/agent_network.json`, and the run's `driver_config.json` records it under `agent_network`.

**Measured** (null agent on swesmith-00008, -00698, -00763; HTTPS HEAD from inside the sandbox):

| Target | Before | Agent phase | After |
|---|---|---|---|
| `https://github.com/swesmith` | 200 | DNS failure | 200 |
| `api.github.com`, `raw.githubusercontent.com`, `codeload.github.com` | 200 | DNS failure | 200 |
| `https://140.82.112.3/`, `https://140.82.114.4/` (GitHub by IP) | 200 | TLS handshake cut | 200 |
| `https://1.1.1.1/` | 403 | TLS handshake cut | 403 |
| `pypi.org`, `deb.debian.org`, `archive.ubuntu.com`, `www.google.com` | 200 | DNS failure | 200 |

On these unchanged trees the verifier completed afterwards and scored 0, as expected. With GLM (`swe-net2`), 3/3 trials passed under the limit, and all 76 proxy calls returned 200. In one trial GLM ran `pip install pytest ...` and saw `No internet`.

**Tool-env leak:** in `swe-net2/swesmith-00763` (jd/tenacity), GLM ran `sed -n '136,175p' /root/.local/share/uv/tools/mini-swe-agent/lib/python3.12/site-packages/tenacity/retry.py`. A probe ran mini-swe-agent's real setup on one task from each of the 36 repos (`toolenv2`). It found the same 80 distributions on every image. Only three of them are pool repos: pygments (222 tasks), pandas (196) and tenacity (30). Every conda-based image also ships conda's own `boltons-23.0.0` under `/opt/miniconda3/pkgs`, including the mahmoud/boltons image (21 tasks). The install is now pinned (`mini-swe-agent-2.1.0-constraints.txt`, sha256 `c67d1ee2…`, Python 3.12), so this set cannot drift between the pilot and the full run. SWE-smith ingestion also drops any trace whose commands or outputs touch `/root/.local/share/uv/tools/`.

**Run folders** (`s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/sft-shootout/generation/dryrun/`):
- `netprobe2`, `netprobe3`, `netprobe4`: network probes; `agent/network_probe.json` per trial.
- `swe-net2`: GLM trials under the limit.
- `toolenv2`: tool-env listing; union in `tool_env.json`.

🤖 More of the #10212 leak class: clean copies of the code the agent must fix, readable in the sandbox without git. The SWE-smith shootout pool is now at v4.

| Where | Found by | Pool repos affected |
|---|---|---|
| mini-swe-agent's own tool env, installed in the sandbox at agent setup (`/root/.local/share/uv/tools/mini-swe-agent/lib/python3.12/site-packages/`) | #207 run swe-net2: GLM read `tenacity/retry.py` there and called it "the reference". Then #207's probe ran mini-swe-agent's real setup with the pinned dependency set on one task per repo. | pygments, pandas, tenacity |
| conda's package cache in every conda image (`/opt/miniconda3/pkgs/boltons-23.0.0-*`) | the same #207 probe | boltons |
| pip/setuptools vendored copies and an installed egg in the base images | the base-image check: a suffix pass plus a name pass over every file outside `/testbed` | chardet, tomli, inflect, dataset |

What was removed in each version:

| Version | Repo or task | Tasks removed | Reason (`leak_risk`) | Where the clean copy lives |
|---|---|---:|---|---|
| v1 | 181 TMax environments | 181 | `hidden_verifier_assets` | verifier assets (oracle programs, ground-truth files) built into the image, not named in the instruction |
| v2 | `agronholm/typeguard` | 57 | `vendored_clean_copy` | `setuptools/_vendor/typeguard` |
| v2 | `swesmith-01094` (`ariga/atlas`) | 1 | `broken_verifier` | (no copy: the verifier scores the unpatched tree 1, upstream too) |
| v3 | `pygments/pygments` | 222 | `agent_tool_clean_copy` | mini-swe-agent's tool env, `/root/.local/share/uv/tools/mini-swe-agent/lib/python3.12/site-packages/` (installed at agent setup) |
| v3 | `pandas-dev/pandas` | 196 | `agent_tool_clean_copy` | same |
| v3 | `jd/tenacity` | 30 | `agent_tool_clean_copy` | same |
| v3 | `mahmoud/boltons` | 21 | `image_level_clean_copy` | `/opt/miniconda3/pkgs/boltons-23.0.0-*/` (conda depends on boltons) |
| v4 | `chardet/chardet` | 10 | `image_level_clean_copy` | `pip/_vendor/chardet` (base env, conda pkgs, `/usr/lib/python3/dist-packages`) |
| v4 | `hukkin/tomli` | 23 | `image_level_clean_copy` | `pip/_vendor/tomli`, `setuptools/_vendor/tomli` (testbed env, base env, conda pkgs) |
| v4 | `jaraco/inflect` | 27 | `image_level_clean_copy` | `setuptools/_vendor/inflect` (testbed env, conda pkgs) |
| v4 | `pudo/dataset` | 13 | `image_level_clean_copy` | `dataset-1.6.2-py3.10.egg` in the testbed env site-packages |

Defenses now in place:

- **Pool:** every repo above is removed from pool v4. The SWE-smith family is topped back up to 2,100 from the 28 remaining repos, which the base-image check found clean. The method and per-repo evidence are in `image-check-v4.jsonl` and `manifest.json` `clean_copy_probe` (`s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/sft-shootout/pool/`, mirrored at [open-athena/Snowball-SFT-Shootout-Pool-2026.10@ac4e9c3f](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-SFT-Shootout-Pool-2026.10/tree/ac4e9c3fee6612c1d8ceecb0aa22950c4bdd8a9a)).
- **Generation (#207):** mini-swe-agent installs with a pinned dependency set, so the tool env cannot drift. The agent phase runs without internet access (proxy host only), which also closes the public `github.com/swesmith` mirrors.
- **Training rows (#211):** the row builder drops any trace that touches mini-swe-agent's tool env, or that reads a library copy (site-packages, `_vendor`, conda pkgs, the Go module cache) of its task's own repo. Drops are counted per task.

Kimi and other existing SWE-smith trace sets were generated with other agent setups, so their tool environments may differ. A trace audit for these paths is still open.

🤖 Upstream task defect found while freezing the SWE-smith shootout pool (v5). These 7 packages in `DCAgent/swesmith-sandboxes-with_tests-oracle_verified_120s@78b0d879` have verifiers that cannot fail. The tree with the bug still in it scores 1. All 7 are in `paramiko/paramiko`. This is the same class as `swesmith-01094` above.

| Task | Repo |
|---|---|
| swesmith-06993 | paramiko/paramiko |
| swesmith-07209 | paramiko/paramiko |
| swesmith-07315 | paramiko/paramiko |
| swesmith-07539 | paramiko/paramiko |
| swesmith-07171 | paramiko/paramiko |

| swesmith-07659 | paramiko/paramiko |

- **How they were found:** #207 ran a pool-wide null agent (it changes nothing) on all 2,100 fixed SWE-smith packages. 2,093 scored 0 and these 7 scored 1. Records: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/sft-shootout/generation/integrity/swe-{null,added-null}/integrity.jsonl`.
- **Not caused by the history fix:** the unmodified upstream packages were then run in local Docker in Harbor's phase order (`validate_swesmith.py`). All 7 score 1 unpatched, and the gold patch also scores 1. So the defect is in the upstream verifiers, not in the `tests/f2p_restore` change.
- **Action:** all 7 are removed from pool v5 as `broken_verifier` and replaced outcome-blind (#10213). Anyone else using this DCAgent release should drop them too: a policy gets reward 1 on them for doing nothing.

🤖 **TL;DR:** existing SWE-smith trace sets use the git-history leak. 16–18% of passing Kimi-2.5 traces read git history, and in 94% of the testable cases the output showed a line of the fix. The same holds for the 2,665 passing `kimi_swesmith` trials in `laion/calibforge-relay-traces`, which went into the allkimi relay SFT grafted into Snowball v0: 491 of them read git history.

| Set (revision) | Traces | Passes | Passes reading git history | ...that saw a fix line (testable) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `open-athena/Kimi-2.5-swesmith-...-maxeps-32k` (`1b87a9cf78`) | 9,356 | 5,237 | 860 (16.4%) | 708 / 752 (94%) |
| `laion/calibforge-relay-traces` `kimi_swesmith` (`66feab4d24`) | 4,392 | 2,665 | 491 (18.4%) | 418 / 446 (94%) |
| `DCAgent2/GLM-4.7-swesmith-...-maxeps-131k` (`e209a88db1`) | 9,437 | no verdicts | 848 of 8,241 completed (10.3%) | 723 / 790 (92%) |
| `open-thoughts/AgentTrove` swesmith rows (`b395a4307a`) | 78,246 | Kimi-2.5 stream only (same 5,237) | 5,822 of all traces (7.4%) | not testable (task ids differ) |

- **Commands:** most hits are `git diff HEAD~1 -- <file>`, `git show <hash>`, `git show main:<file>`, `git diff main` and `git log -p`.
- **"Saw a fix line":** the terminal output after the history command contains a clean-code line from the task's bug patch (15+ characters, in a non-test file) that the agent had not typed earlier.
- **Relay set's own flags:** its `leak` and `hunt` flags are False on all 4,392 rows, including these 491.
- **AgentTrove clone tasks:** 40,590 of AgentTrove's swesmith rows (the GLM-4.6, GPT 5.1 Nano and Kimi K2.0 streams, and part of GLM-4.7) use a different task format. The instruction itself says "clone the repo `swesmith/<mirror>` and run `git fetch && git checkout <instance branch>`". Every one of those sandboxes holds the mirror's full history, including the clean `main`, by design. 8.8% of them then read git history.

**Method:** the shootout's own rules, used verbatim: `GIT_HISTORY_READ` from #202's selection, and the host prefix from chukar's `repository_pytest.py`. Each task's repo and fix lines come from DCAgent's packages (`78b0d879`). Code: [`scripts/task215/`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/29a6fb1919/scripts/task215); `audit.py` docstring and README list the exact regexes. Spot checks of random hits were all real history reads or real fix lines.

The shootout pool's fixed packages (one commit, no remote) and its no-internet agent phase close this path for new traces. Any SFT that used these sets' passes trained on traces that may have copied the fix.

topics.title: [RFC] On-policy distillation (OPD) teacher serving — system-design options
topics.body:
*Request for comment.*

> **TL;DR.** OPD needs a teacher model that returns per-token logprob targets in the training inner
> loop. The deciding factor is **how many logprobs per token** we need: our stack (MarinSkyRL) today
> does **top-K sparse forward-KL** (default **K=256**), *not* the full-vocab reverse-KL of the
> DeepSeek-V4 recipe. Top-K payloads are small and travel cheaply over a network; **full-vocab is
> ~300 KB/token → GB/step and is only tractable co-located.** That single fact reorders the options.
>
> **My lean: Option 3 (permanent marin-serve teacher endpoints on CoreWeave, top-K), plus Option 4
> (forward-only co-located teacher) reserved as a "full-vocab fast-track" if an ablation ever shows
> we need it.** Option 3 reuses the remote teacher-client MarinSkyRL already has, decouples serving
> optimization from the RL loop, and amortizes across OPD + judge + eval. Options 1 and 2 are
> prototyping and single-hero-run tools, respectively. **Tell me where this is wrong** — especially
> on (a) whether K≤20 provider ceilings are disqualifying, (b) whether full-vocab reverse-KL is worth
> building for at all, and (c) whether the forward-only teacher (Option 4) should be the default
> instead of Option 3.

## Context

On-policy distillation (OPD) is load-bearing in our post-training plan: the distillation stage
distills RL-trained experts into the student via OPD, *if* we have teacher-logit infra — otherwise we
fall back to the weaker off-policy SFT-distill path. The [#7074](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7074)
cost analysis sizes the pipeline as **RL K experts → OPD into the student** (Nemotron-style path),
where the OPD leg is student-rollout-dominated and roughly RL-scale in cost.

**Why this decision matters NOW:** OPD is a complex, jointly-optimized system — the teacher serving
path is tightly coupled to the training loop (the teacher is queried in the inner loop, per batch of
student-generated tokens). Getting it working reliably is hard, and once it works there is a strong
incentive to never touch the plumbing again. That makes the early architectural choices effectively
*sticky*. This RFC aims to make that choice a deliberate one, with eyes open about what each option
forecloses.

The core question: **how do we serve the teacher model that provides logprob targets during OPD?**

---

## The logprobs crux (the deciding technical factor)

OPD's distillation loss is a per-token KL between the student and teacher distributions over the
generated positions. The teacher must return a **probability distribution over tokens** at each
position — not a generated sequence or a reward score. *How much* of that distribution we need is the
crux, and it splits cleanly into two regimes:

- **Top-K (what our stack does today).** MarinSkyRL's `distillation_trainer.py` requests
  `cfg.teacher.top_k_logprobs` (default **K=256**, `config/ppo_base_config.yaml`), carries a
  `teacher_top_k_logprobs: [batch, seq, K]` tensor (`training_batch.py`), and computes the loss with
  `forward_kl_from_sparse` (`utils/distillation_utils.py`) — a **forward**-KL over the teacher's
  top-K support (`kl = Σ_k teacher_p·(teacher_logp − student_logp_at_k)`). A remote
  `TeacherInferenceEngineClient.score_sequences` (with student↔teacher retokenization) already exists.
  **Top-K logprobs are a small payload** (K values + K indices per token) and travel cheaply over a
  network — so top-K OPD is *not* gated by where the teacher lives.
- **Full-vocab (the DeepSeek-V4 aspiration).** V4's OPD is full-vocabulary **reverse**-KL
  (`L = Σᵢ wᵢ·D_KL(π_θ ∥ π_Eᵢ)`, trajectories sampled from the student). This is a **different loss in
  both support (full vs top-K) and direction (reverse vs forward)** from what MarinSkyRL implements
  today. It is strictly richer — but per the bandwidth wrinkle below, it is only tractable with a
  **co-located** teacher.

**The bandwidth wrinkle (why top-K is the practical default, and why providers only offer top-k).**
A full-vocab logprob vector is ~vocab (≈128–150k) × 2 bytes ≈ **~300 KB per generated token**. Across
an OPD inner-loop batch that is **on the order of GB/step moving over the network, every step** — WAN
is prohibitive, intra-DC is heavy, and only a co-located teacher on the same NCCL/IPC fabric makes it
free. This is almost certainly *why* hosted providers expose only top-k logprobs (OpenAI: top-20): the
full distribution is too expensive to serialize per token. **Consequence:** any *networked* teacher —
a provider (Option 1) or a permanently hosted endpoint (Option 3) — is effectively **top-K only**.
Full-vocab reverse-KL is available only to a **co-located** teacher (Option 2's in-cluster engines, or
Option 4's forward-only teacher). If we want full-vocab, we want an **OPD fast-track for co-located
jobs** alongside whatever we run for the common case.

**Working assumption for this RFC:** unless an ablation shows full-vocab reverse-KL is worth its cost,
we should **plan for top-K** (start at the K our stack already defaults to, and treat provider K≤20 as
the one hard ceiling to check). Full-vocab is then an opt-in co-located path, not the baseline that
gates the whole serving decision. *(We found no published "safe K" ablation in our notes — see Q1.)*

---

## Option 1 — serve the teacher from a cloud inference provider (Together / Fireworks / OpenAI)

The teacher is a hosted model behind an API. The OPD trainer calls the provider's completions/chat
endpoint with `logprobs` to get per-token distributions.

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| **Least new plumbing** — no serving infra to build or maintain; one less component to jointly optimize for throughput. | **Provider top-k ceiling vs. our K.** Providers cap logprobs low (OpenAI: top-20). Our stack defaults to **K=256**; whether K≤20 is adequate is an open ablation (Q1). Full-vocab reverse-KL is off the table on any provider. **This is the gating question for this option.** |
| **Maximum teacher flexibility** — swap teachers by changing a model name; no weight staging. | **Teacher availability is not in our control.** A provider can deprecate/drop a model mid-campaign; teacher selection follows their catalog, not our research needs. |
| **Fast to prototype** — an API key unblocks OPD-loop development today. | **No path to custom Marin teachers** — distilling from a Marin-trained checkpoint (the point of expert iteration) needs a separate deal / custom serving. |
| **Elastic capacity** — no fixed GPU commitment; pay per token. | **Per-token cost + throughput risk at scale.** OPD processes ~10⁹–10¹⁰ training tokens (#7074); provider pricing is expensive at that volume, and **rate-limit / tail-latency variance is an inner-loop hazard** — a single slow or throttled teacher call stalls the whole synchronous train step, not just a batch's cost. |
| | **Redundancy requires N integrations.** Each provider has a different API surface, logprob format, and rate-limit regime. Multi-provider fallback is real integration work, not a config flip. |
| | **Reproducibility risk** — providers may silently update served weights, breaking experiment reproducibility. |

---

## Option 2 — co-host the teacher with the student in a single large allocation

The teacher, student, and reference model all live in one Ray cluster / GPU allocation. The
teacher is a set of vLLM inference engines scheduled alongside the training actors. This is the
"everything in one Slurm job" model.

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| **Infra already partially built** — MarinSkyRL already co-hosts policy + inference engines in one Ray cluster; the teacher is "one more served model," and the remote teacher-client already exists. | **The FLOP-utilization dance.** OPD is a 3-stage pipeline: student generates → teacher scores → student trains. When the student generates, the teacher is idle; when the teacher scores, the student is idle. Balancing all three at high utilization must be re-tuned per model size / batch / pipeline change. (SkyRL's `fully_async` 2-stage pipeline is already hard to balance; a 3rd stage compounds it.) |
| **Full control of quantization + weights** — quantized teachers, custom architectures, Marin-trained checkpoints all work. | **Resource-intensive** — a 120B-class teacher + student + reference in one allocation is a large footprint per experiment → **fewer concurrent experiments**. Trades experiment parallelism for self-contained runs. |
| **Low-latency hop** — teacher scoring is on the same Ray fabric as rollout, so batching is tight. | **Still top-K if the teacher is a vLLM engine** — vLLM's API returns top-K, not the full logits tensor (see Option 3 caveat). Full-vocab here needs a custom serving hook, i.e. it collapses into Option 4. |
| **Bugs are patchable** — full source access; no provider dependency. | **Infra burden** — one more thing the RL-launcher/SkyRL stack must schedule, configure, and debug. |

---

## Option 3 — permanently hosted teachers via marin-serve on dedicated CoreWeave compute

A set of CoreWeave GPUs is dedicated to long-running teacher endpoints (marin-serve / vLLM), queried
over the network by any consumer — OPD trainers, LLM judges, coding agents, eval pipelines, vibe
tests. The teacher is "always warm." **Top-K by nature of the network hop** (per the bandwidth crux).

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| **Decoupled optimization** — the serving pipeline (continuous batching, prefix caching, quantization, KV-cache tuning) is optimized **independently** of the RL/OPD run. No joint-scheduling dance. | **Top-K only.** The network hop caps us at top-K logprobs (bandwidth crux) — fine for our current top-K forward-KL loss, but forecloses full-vocab reverse-KL. If the endpoint's K is enough (Q1), a non-issue; if we later want full-vocab, this option can't provide it (use Option 4). |
| **No top-*20* ceiling** — we run the model, so we set K (e.g. 256, matching our default) rather than being stuck at a provider's ~20. | **Resource-intensive** — dedicates GPUs full-time to hosting, removing them from the experiment pool. Trades raw training throughput for serving readiness. |
| **Multi-purpose amortization** — one hosted teacher serves OPD + the LLM-judge tier + coding agents + eval + vibe tests. The post-training plan already asks for "~10 hosted endpoints we can update quickly" — this *is* that infra, and concurrent OPD runs share it. | **High infra burden + single point of failure** — we own uptime, autoscaling, model-swapping, failure recovery. If the endpoint goes down, all dependent OPD runs stall. |
| **Marin-trained teachers work natively** — swap the hosted checkpoint; no provider deal, no API integration. Future-proof for expert-iteration. | **Forces teacher prioritization** — dedicated GPUs can't host every teacher at once; we commit to a small primary set, limiting experiment diversity. |
| **Faster wall-clock than Option 2** — continuous batching across all consumers + prefix caching means the teacher runs at high utilization *without* the pipeline-imbalance tax. | **Network latency** — same-region intra-DC RTT is sub-millisecond (negligible vs. WAN), but it is still a hop; per-batch latency is nonzero. |
| **Reuses existing plumbing** — MarinSkyRL's `TeacherInferenceEngineClient` already targets a remote scoring engine and returns top-K; Option 3 is the closest to what's built. Also exercises marin-serve / the Inference Server ([#6500](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6500)) under real load. | |

---

## Option 4 — frozen, forward-only teacher co-resident in the trainer

A distinct implementation of "co-located": the teacher is a **frozen, forward-only** module in the
**training framework itself** (FSDP/Megatron forward pass, no generation engine), with the teacher
logits fed **straight into the loss**. This is a common OPD/KD setup and the only option that cleanly
supports **full-vocab reverse-KL**.

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| **Full-vocab by construction, no serialization hop** — logits never leave the training mesh, so the ~300 KB/token bandwidth wall (and vLLM's top-K API limit) simply don't apply. The natural home for full-vocab reverse-KL. | **Teacher lives in the training allocation** — teacher weights occupy HBM in the same job; a 120B teacher + student + ref is a large single footprint (same experiment-parallelism cost as Option 2). |
| **No generation-serving stack to schedule** — no vLLM engine, no continuous-batching tuning, no separate endpoint. Just a forward pass, sharded like any frozen model. | **Teacher forward contends with training compute** on the same mesh; the forward FLOPs are inline with the step (though there's no idle-teacher pipeline-imbalance tax — the forward is a synchronous part of the loss). |
| **Simplest correctness story** — no cross-process logprob transport, no top-K renormalization approximation, no retokenization mismatch; teacher and student share the trainer's tokenizer/dtype. | **Least flexible swapping** — changing teachers means re-staging weights into the training job, not hitting a different endpoint. |
| **Exact reverse-KL** — student-sampled trajectories + full teacher distribution is precisely the V4 recipe. | **Not multi-purpose** — this teacher serves only the OPD loss and only for the run's duration; the "~10 hosted endpoints" need is unmet by this option (that's Option 3). |

---

## Cross-cutting considerations

### The teacher-oracle abstraction (delaying lock-in)

The core concern — early lock-in because OPD is hard to get working — applies to all four options. One
structural mitigation: **architect the OPD trainer against a generic `TeacherLogprobOracle` interface**
— given a batch of student-generated token sequences, return the teacher's logprob targets at each
position. The four options become four *backends* (API client, co-hosted vLLM, remote marin-serve
endpoint, in-trainer forward-only teacher). MarinSkyRL's `TeacherInferenceEngineClient` is already
close to this boundary.

This makes the serving decision **reversible** for the *networked, top-K* backends (Options 1, 2-vLLM,
3 are interchangeable behind the interface). **The one seam the interface cannot paper over is top-K
vs full-vocab:** a full-vocab reverse-KL loss (Option 4) changes the loss's shape and the data the
oracle returns, so it is not a drop-in backend swap — it's a second loss path. Decide the
top-K-vs-full-vocab question first (Q1); *within* top-K, the backend is a swap.

### Quantization parity

For RL scoring, a quantized teacher (FP8/AWQ) is fine — the reward signal tolerates small logprob
perturbation. For **distillation**, the teacher's logprobs ARE the target, and quantization is a
systematic perturbation that compounds token-by-token. Options 2/3/4 give full control over teacher
quantization (and the ability to validate parity against an unquantized reference); Option 1's
quantization is whatever the provider serves. Whether it matters depends on teacher size and the loss's
error tolerance.

### The small-model distillation angle

The plan also ships smaller sizes via strong-to-weak distillation **from the flagship**. This is a
*different* OPD use case (flagship → small model, not expert → student) but reuses the same teacher
serving infra, and it is long-context / high-throughput / high-value. Whichever option we pick should
handle both.

---

## Open questions for discussion

1. **What K is safe? (the pivotal question)** Our stack defaults to **K=256** top-K forward-KL. Is
   K≤20 (provider ceiling, Option 1) adequate, or do we need K≈256 (self-hosted, Options 2/3), or true
   full-vocab reverse-KL (Option 4)? We found **no published safe-K ablation** in our notes — this
   likely needs a quick internal ablation, and its answer determines which options are even eligible.

2. **Is full-vocab reverse-KL worth building?** It's the DeepSeek-V4 recipe and strictly richer, but
   it's co-located-only (bandwidth) and a second loss path (not just a backend swap). If K=256 top-K
   forward-KL is "good enough," we can drop full-vocab entirely and the serving decision simplifies to
   Options 1/3. If not, Option 4 becomes load-bearing.

3. **Teacher size envelope:** What is the largest teacher we plan to distill from? A 120B-class teacher
   makes the co-located options (2/4) expensive (the allocation balloons) and pushes the common case
   toward Option 3. A ≤70B teacher is more tractable everywhere.

4. **Concurrency:** How many OPD experiments run simultaneously? "Many, sharing one teacher" → Option
   3's amortization dominates. "One at a time" → Option 2/4's self-contained simplicity is fine.

5. **Marin-trained teacher timeline:** When do we first need to distill from a Marin-trained checkpoint
   (not a third-party model)? That's the hard deadline by which Option 1 must be replaced by 2/3/4.

6. **Is a hybrid viable?** Option 3 (primary/production, top-K) + Option 1 as elastic overflow + Option
   4 as a full-vocab fast-track for the one hero run that needs it. The oracle abstraction makes the
   top-K backends interchangeable; Option 4 is the deliberate exception.

---

## Suggested framing for a decision

Rather than committing to one option now, a **phased path** that hedges lock-in:

1. **Phase 0 (fast):** Settle Q1 with a small **K ablation** (top-20 vs top-256 vs full-vocab on a
   representative teacher/student) — this is the decision that gates everything. In parallel, harden the
   `TeacherLogprobOracle` boundary around MarinSkyRL's existing top-K teacher-client, and validate the
   OPD loop end-to-end against **Option 1** (API, top-20) for loop correctness — the loop, not the
   backend, is the hard part.
2. **Phase 1:** Stand up a dedicated **marin-serve teacher endpoint (Option 3, top-K, K≈256)** for the
   primary production teacher; point the oracle at it. This is also the LLM-judge + eval endpoint the
   plan already needs, so the infra investment is shared, not OPD-specific.
3. **Phase 2 (conditional):** If — and only if — the Phase-0 ablation shows full-vocab reverse-KL is
   worth it, build **Option 4** (forward-only co-located teacher) as the full-vocab fast-track for the
   runs that need it. **Option 2** (co-hosted vLLM) is worth it only for a single large hero run where
   even Option 3's intra-DC hop is intolerable and full-vocab isn't required.

The interface boundary means the *top-K* backends are swaps, not redesigns. The genuinely sticky
decisions are the two the ablation forces: **top-K-vs-full-vocab** and **forward-vs-reverse KL**.

topics.title: [grug] Add a one-GPU Grug attention layer benchmark
topics.body:
Add `lib/levanter/scripts/bench/bench_grug_attention.py`, which times one Grug attention layer on one GPU. For each mask (2048-token sliding window, global causal) and each implementation passed to `--impl`, it reports forward and forward-plus-backward time and the max absolute output difference against the first implementation. With `--sweep --sweep-part fwd|dq|dkv` it times a grid of tile sizes, warps and stages for one of the three Pallas-Triton flash kernels (forward, dQ, dK/dV) and keeps the defaults for the other two. `--block-q`, `--block-k`, `--num-warps` and `--num-stages` replace that kernel's default values for one axis of the grid. TFLOP/s counts only the FLOPs the mask needs over the allowed (query, key) pairs. Each time is the median of ten 0.2 s windows after a 1 s warmup. Results are printed as `RESULT {json}` lines.

Defaults are the June per-GPU shape at global batch 64 on 8 GPUs: 8 x 4096 tokens, 20 query heads, 5 KV heads, head_dim 128, bf16.

```bash
python lib/levanter/scripts/bench/bench_grug_attention.py --impl reference xla_flash gpu_pallas_triton_flash
python lib/levanter/scripts/bench/bench_grug_attention.py --sweep --sweep-part dkv --block-q 64 128 --num-stages 1
```

Forward plus backward time on one MI350X with jax 0.11.1 and the ROCm 10.1 plugin (job 460980):

| Mask | reference | xla_flash | gpu_pallas_triton_flash |
|---|---|---|---|
| window 2048 | 18.84 ms (96 TF/s) | 22.66 ms (80 TF/s) | 6.74 ms (268 TF/s) |
| causal | 20.89 ms (115 TF/s) | 22.89 ms (105 TF/s) | 10.02 ms (240 TF/s) |

In the same job, the dK/dV sweep with the window mask ran all 36 configs. The default tile, 128 queries x 64 keys with 4 warps and 1 stage, was the fastest at 6.80 ms.

The script imports `TritonFlashBlockSizes` and `pallas_triton_flash_attention` from `levanter.grug.attention._amd_pallas_triton_flash`, which #10014 added.

Part of #9812
