topics.title: Add `ManagedAgent`
topics.body:
`ManagedAgent` = `RolloutEngine` + `RolloutSpec`

`RolloutSpec` is roughly a generalization of a `TaskSpec` with an optional grader. `ManagedAgent` allows to deploy a swarm of agents (harness + model endpoint) to accomplish an arbitrary task.

comments.body:
🤖
# Research

`RolloutEngine.run()` currently executes one lowered `TaskSpec`; its caller owns concurrency and deployment. `TaskSpec` requires source, answer format, and a grader, although `NoGrader` already records an ungraded attempt, and `AgentTaskSession` already adapts an agent-owned tool loop. No `ManagedAgent` or `RolloutSpec` exists on current `main`.

**Relevant code**
- [`engine.py#L55-L71`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/d8ac9acfd4f1425e8e6caad28fae70b904e5c5bb/lib/rolloutengine/src/rolloutengine/engine.py#L55-L71) — one-attempt engine API.
- [`models.py#L854-L898`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/d8ac9acfd4f1425e8e6caad28fae70b904e5c5bb/lib/taskcompendium/src/taskcompendium/models.py#L854-L898) — required task fields.
- [`models.py#L617-L640`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/d8ac9acfd4f1425e8e6caad28fae70b904e5c5bb/lib/taskcompendium/src/taskcompendium/models.py#L617-L640) — session and absent graders.
- [`agent_session.py#L26-L59`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/d8ac9acfd4f1425e8e6caad28fae70b904e5c5bb/lib/rolloutengine/src/rolloutengine/agent_session.py#L26-L59) — agent loop adapter.
- [`task-rollouts.md`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/d8ac9acfd4f1425e8e6caad28fae70b904e5c5bb/docs/references/task-rollouts.md) — runtime and result contracts.

# ManagedAgent proposal

A `ManagedAgent` should run a bounded set of independent agent attempts from rollout specifications, using a named harness, model endpoint, and machine backend. Each attempt returns its transcript, declared output files, stop reason, and grade when one was requested. The manager owns admission, cancellation, and result delivery; `RolloutEngine` continues to own each attempt's model calls, machine lifetime, and grading.

## Challenges

A `TaskSpec` requires answer and provenance fields that arbitrary work may lack. Chat endpoints can also re-tokenize turns, so untrained agents need the messages trace mode proposed in [#10142](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10142); training rollouts must retain the exact-token contract. Parallel attempts need separate machines and stable IDs so a failed worker cannot mix its transcript or files with another attempt.

## Costs and risks

Generalizing the spec and lowering contract changes callers of `TaskSpec` and `LoweredTaskSpec`. Endpoint ownership is a separate lifecycle concern: starting model servers inside the rollout engine would couple an attempt to service deployment. The first integration should use Iris jobs for worker replicas and bind each worker to an existing model service through Iris endpoint discovery.

## Design and implementation sequence

1. Define `RolloutSpec` in TaskCompendium with the fields an attempt needs: ID, public context, environment, tool and output declarations, and an optional answer/grade contract. Convert existing `TaskSpec` values at one boundary; keep task source metadata and private verifier resources intact. Generalize lowering to a validated rollout plus explicit machine and session settings, then update current callers rather than running a second execution loop.
2. Add `ManagedAgent` above `RolloutEngine`. Its configuration names the harness factory, model endpoint, machine factories, worker count, and per-attempt limits. It accepts a stream of `RolloutSpec` values, runs at most the configured worker count concurrently, and emits one typed outcome per input ID. Cancellation closes active attempts and releases workers. Infrastructure failure stays distinct from an ungraded completed attempt (`Outcome.UNAVAILABLE`); a requested grade retains existing `GradeResult` behavior.
3. Add an Iris launcher that starts the configured worker replicas and binds them to a registered model endpoint. Use the existing endpoint registry for discovery and Iris job cancellation for shutdown. Keep verifier inputs private to the attempt's grader machine. Incorporate the in-flight rollout changes for [outputs](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10140), [progress events](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10139), [token budgets](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10143), and [messages trace](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10142) as they land; none is a parallel implementation of this manager.

## Testing and completion criteria

Exercise graded and ungraded specs through the same engine, two concurrent attempts with isolated workspace files, bounded admission, cancellation, endpoint failure, and exact-token versus messages traces. Then run one Iris-backed agent swarm against a served endpoint, verifying worker shutdown and that every admitted ID has one typed outcome. Document the public spec, launcher, and result contract in `docs/references/task-rollouts.md`.

## Open questions

- Should `ManagedAgent` launch the model service, or require an existing Iris endpoint and own only harness workers? The proposed first version uses an existing endpoint.
- Is a swarm only bounded parallel execution of independent specs, or must agents exchange messages or spawn child tasks? The proposed first version handles independent specs.

🤖 A proof of concept of `ManagedAgent` = `RolloutEngine` + `RolloutSpec`, cut from the agentic part of Taskforge's authoring code (`taskforge/capability-restack`), as a pointer for the ~300-line target. It is 285 lines with docstrings, 227 without blanks. It imports against the restack environment, type-checks, and a spec lowers through `rolloutengine.lowering.lower_task` with a ShellSim factory. An attempt has not been run end to end against the engine with a fake model, so the loop-inside-the-engine half is shape-checked, not run-checked. **Why it is small.** `RolloutEngine` already owns the hard parts: the task machine's lifetime, the exact-token contract, deadlines, grading in a verifier machine, and an adapter for an agent-owned loop (`rolloutengine.agent_session.AgentTaskSession`). The agentic part of the authoring code is also small: the tool loop (`taskforge.llm.agent.run_agent`) is about sixty lines of logic plus a tool type, a shell tool over a machine, and a stop callback. Everything else in the agentic author is authoring, not agency: the loader, build and grade tools, the submit protocol, hand-offs, revisions, records. **What the PoC adds, and nothing more.** - `RolloutSpec`: an opening conversation, an optional environment with files, declared output paths, limits, and an optional grader. `to_task` converts it to a `TaskSpec` at one boundary, with `NoGrader` when none is declared; the engine already records that attempt `Outcome.UNAVAILABLE` and keeps its rollout. - `Harness`: the tools an agent gets over the attempt's machine. `shell_harness` is the engine's own shell tool. - `_EngineModel`: a `ModelClient` over the engine's `AgentCompletion`, so the loop runs inside `AgentTaskSession` and every turn is the engine's `ModelTurn`. The rollout keeps exact tokens and the model endpoint stays the engine's model function, bound outside. - `ManagedAgent`: a semaphore and a task group. Bounded concurrency, one typed `AttemptOutcome` per spec id in completion order, cancellation by cancelling the iterator. No model servers, no agent-to-agent messages, no cross-process workers: a swarm on Iris is N jobs over a sharded spec stream, which Iris provides. **Three gaps to close in a real version.** - `AgentTaskSession.advance` compares the prefix it sent plus its turn with what the loop sends next; the loop replays the assistant message through Taskforge's wire builder, so the two must agree byte for byte or the session re-tokenises the conversation. For GLM both come from the same function. This is what an end-to-end run proves. - `run_agent` takes a Taskforge ledger for recording; the sixty lines move into rolloutengine without it. - A chat endpoint that returns no token ids needs the messages trace mode of #10142. Against the research comment above: generalising the lowering contract, a second spec type in TaskCompendium with every caller updated, and an Iris launcher are more than the problem needs. The PoC converts at one boundary and launches nothing.
managed_agent_poc.py (285 lines) ```python # Copyright The Marin Authors # SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0 """ManagedAgent = RolloutEngine + RolloutSpec, as a proof of concept (#10165). The engine already owns everything that is hard: the task machine's lifetime, the exact-token contract, deadlines, grading in a verifier machine, and the agent-owned loop adapter (``rolloutengine.agent_session.AgentTaskSession``). What #10165 adds is small: * ``RolloutSpec``: what an attempt needs and nothing more. A ``TaskSpec`` requires an answer type, an answer format, a grader and a source; a spec here has an opening conversation, an environment with files, declared output paths, limits, and an optional grader. ``to_task`` converts it to a ``TaskSpec`` at one boundary (``NoGrader`` when none is declared; the engine then grades the attempt ``Outcome.UNAVAILABLE`` and keeps its rollout). * ``Harness``: the tools an agent gets over the attempt's machine. The agent loop is Taskforge's ``run_agent`` (sixty lines: tool-call validation, execution in order, cut-off handling, a stop callback), driven through the engine's ``AgentTaskSession`` so every model turn is the engine's own ``ModelTurn`` and the rollout keeps exact tokens. * ``ManagedAgent``: a bounded set of independent attempts over one engine, one typed outcome per spec id, cancellation through the task group. What it does not do, on purpose: start model servers (the model endpoint is the engine's model function, bound outside), let agents talk to each other, or own workers across processes. Running N of these on Iris is N jobs with the same spec stream sharded, which Iris already provides. Line count, docstrings included, is the point: the logic is the loop, the adapter and the gate. """ import asyncio import json from collections.abc import AsyncIterator, Awaitable, Callable, Iterable, Mapping, Sequence from dataclasses import dataclass, field from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field from rolloutengine.agent_session import AgentCompletion, AgentTaskSession from rolloutengine.contracts import ModelRequest, ModelTurn, RolloutData, SessionStart, TaskSessionContext from rolloutengine.engine import RolloutEngine from rolloutengine.lowering import lower_task from rolloutengine.spec import LoweredTaskSpec, MachineRuntimeSpec, TaskRuntimeSpec, TaskSessionSpec from shellbox.machine import Machine, MachineFactory from taskcompendium.grading_result import GradeResult from taskcompendium.models import ( AnswerType, ConversationInput, EnvironmentRequirements, Grader, NoGrader, PlainText, ResourceGroups, Source, TaskSpec, TextMessage, ) from taskforge.llm.agent import NO_USAGE, AgentRun, AgentTool, run_agent, shell_tool from taskforge.llm.client import Completion, FinishReason, ModelClient, ToolCall from taskforge.llm.policy import LLMPolicy, Message from taskforge.llm.recording import CallLedger AGENT_SESSION = "managed_agent" """The session kind ``to_session`` selects: the engine runs the harness's agent loop under it.""" MANAGED_SOURCE = Source(dataset="managed-agent", revision="0", row="0", importer_revision="0") """A ``TaskSpec`` requires provenance; an arbitrary attempt has none worth recording.""" class AttemptLimits(BaseModel): """The budget of one attempt: model replies, per-command and per-attempt wall clocks.""" model_config = ConfigDict(frozen=True, extra="forbid") max_turns: int = Field(gt=0, default=48) command_timeout: float = Field(gt=0, default=120.0) attempt_timeout: float = Field(gt=0, default=3600.0) startup_timeout: float = Field(gt=0, default=600.0) cleanup_timeout: float = Field(gt=0, default=60.0) class RolloutSpec(BaseModel): """What one agent attempt needs: a conversation to open, a machine to work in, and what to keep. ``grader`` is optional: without one the attempt is recorded ungraded. ``environment`` is optional: without one the agent has no machine and only the tools the harness gives it. """ model_config = ConfigDict(frozen=True, extra="forbid") id: str = Field(min_length=1) messages: tuple[Message, ...] environment: EnvironmentRequirements | None = None resources: ResourceGroups = Field(default_factory=ResourceGroups) output_paths: tuple[str, ...] = () grader: Grader | None = None limits: AttemptLimits = AttemptLimits() @dataclass(frozen=True) class AttemptOutcome: """One typed result per spec id: the rollout the engine produced, or why there is none.""" id: str rollout: RolloutData | None error: Exception | None = None @property def grade(self) -> GradeResult | None: return None if self.rollout is None else self.rollout.grade @dataclass(frozen=True) class Harness: """The tools an attempt's agent gets over its machine; ``shell_harness`` is the one most attempts want.""" name: str tools: Callable[[Machine | None, RolloutSpec], Sequence[AgentTool]] def shell_harness(*, output_limit_bytes: int = 16_384) -> Harness: """A harness whose only tool is the engine's shell, run on the attempt's machine.""" def tools(machine: Machine | None, spec: RolloutSpec) -> Sequence[AgentTool]: if machine is None: return () return (shell_tool(machine, timeout=spec.limits.command_timeout, output_limit_bytes=output_limit_bytes),) return Harness("shell", tools) def to_task(spec: RolloutSpec) -> TaskSpec: """The ``TaskSpec`` the engine runs for ``spec``: the one place the two contracts meet.""" events = tuple(TextMessage(role=m["role"], content=str(m.get("content", ""))) for m in spec.messages) return TaskSpec( id=spec.id, context=ConversationInput(events=events), environment_requirements=spec.environment or EnvironmentRequirements(), output_paths=spec.output_paths, answer_type=AnswerType.TEXT, answer_format=PlainText(), grader=spec.grader or NoGrader(reason="no grader declared for this managed attempt"), source=MANAGED_SOURCE, resources=spec.resources, ) def to_session(spec: RolloutSpec) -> TaskSessionSpec: limits = spec.limits return TaskSessionSpec( task_session=AGENT_SESSION, max_turns=limits.max_turns, model_turn_timeout=None, command_timeout=limits.command_timeout, tool_turn_timeout=None, total_turn_timeout=None, attempt_timeout=limits.attempt_timeout, verifier_timeout=limits.attempt_timeout, cleanup_timeout=limits.cleanup_timeout, ) class _EngineModel(ModelClient): """``ModelClient`` over the engine's completion: every turn the loop asks for is the engine's ``ModelTurn``. The engine samples through its own model function (the endpoint), keeps the served token ids, and hands the message back; the loop replays that message verbatim, so ``AgentTaskSession.advance`` sees the prefix it sent plus the turn and appends the tool observations instead of re-tokenising the conversation. """ def __init__(self, complete: AgentCompletion, tools: Sequence[AgentTool]): self._complete = complete self._options = {"tools": [tool.definition() for tool in tools]} if tools else {} async def complete(self, messages: Sequence[Message], policy: LLMPolicy) -> Completion: turn = await self._complete(SessionStart(messages=tuple(messages), options=self._options)) return _completion(turn) def _completion(turn: ModelTurn) -> Completion: message = turn.message calls = tuple( ToolCall(id=c["id"], name=c["function"]["name"], arguments=c["function"]["arguments"]) for c in message.get("tool_calls") or () ) finish = FinishReason.LENGTH if turn.stop_reason == "length" else FinishReason.TOOL_CALLS if calls else FinishReason.STOP return Completion( content=str(message.get("content") or ""), reasoning=str(message.get("reasoning_content") or ""), tool_calls=calls, finish_reason=finish, usage=NO_USAGE, wall_time=0.0, ) def agent_session(harness: Harness, spec: RolloutSpec, policy: LLMPolicy, record: CallLedger): """The ``TaskSessionFactory`` for ``spec``: the harness's loop inside the engine's session lifecycle.""" def factory(context: TaskSessionContext) -> AgentTaskSession: tools = harness.tools(context.machine, spec) async def loop(complete: AgentCompletion) -> None: await run_agent(_EngineModel(complete, tools), policy, spec.messages, tools, spec.limits.max_turns, record) return AgentTaskSession(loop, context.require_task_grader()) return factory class ManagedAgent: """Run a bounded set of independent attempts over one engine and yield one outcome per spec. Args: model: The engine's model function, the model endpoint bound outside. factories: Machine factories by backend, as ``RolloutEngine`` takes them. harness: The tools every attempt's agent gets. place: The machines ``spec`` runs on, chosen by the caller (laptop ShellSim, Iris gVisor). policy: The sampling policy the loop sends with every turn. record: Where model and tool calls are recorded. workers: Attempts in flight at once. """ def __init__( self, model: Callable[[ModelRequest], Awaitable[ModelTurn]], factories: Mapping[str, MachineFactory], harness: Harness, place: Callable[[RolloutSpec], TaskRuntimeSpec], policy: LLMPolicy, record: CallLedger, workers: int, ): self.model, self.factories, self.harness, self.place = model, factories, harness, place self.policy, self.record = policy, record self.gate = asyncio.Semaphore(workers) def lower(self, spec: RolloutSpec) -> tuple[LoweredTaskSpec, RolloutEngine]: sessions = {AGENT_SESSION: agent_session(self.harness, spec, self.policy, self.record)} engine = RolloutEngine(self.model, self.factories, sessions=sessions) return lower_task(to_task(spec), self.place(spec), to_session(spec), factories=self.factories, sessions=sessions), engine async def attempt(self, spec: RolloutSpec) -> AttemptOutcome: """One attempt, admitted through the gate; an engine error is the outcome, not an exception.""" async with self.gate: try: lowered, engine = self.lower(spec) return AttemptOutcome(spec.id, await engine.run(lowered)) except asyncio.CancelledError: raise except Exception as error: return AttemptOutcome(spec.id, None, error) async def run(self, specs: Iterable[RolloutSpec]) -> AsyncIterator[AttemptOutcome]: """Every spec's outcome, in completion order; cancelling the iterator cancels the attempts.""" done: asyncio.Queue[AttemptOutcome] = asyncio.Queue() pending = 0 async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as group: for spec in specs: pending += 1 group.create_task(self._deliver(spec, done)) while pending: yield await done.get() pending -= 1 async def _deliver(self, spec: RolloutSpec, done: asyncio.Queue[AttemptOutcome]) -> None: done.put_nowait(await self.attempt(spec)) def shellsim_placement(backend: str = "shellsim") -> Callable[[RolloutSpec], TaskRuntimeSpec]: """The simplest placement: every machine on one backend, the verifier on the same when the grader needs one.""" def place(spec: RolloutSpec) -> TaskRuntimeSpec: machine = MachineRuntimeSpec( backend=backend, network="deny", cpus=None, memory_mb=None, storage_mb=None, gpus=0, user=None, startup_timeout=spec.limits.startup_timeout, cleanup_timeout=spec.limits.cleanup_timeout, ) verifier = machine if spec.grader is not None and getattr(spec.grader, "environment", None) else None return TaskRuntimeSpec(task_machine=machine if spec.environment else None, verifier_machine=verifier) return place ```

👨 I think I would use a slightly different interface for the "agent task" and maybe add `engine.run_agent`, but we can do that later.

🤖 A proof of concept of `ManagedAgent` on the harness API of #10203 works with no change to the engine. A Zephyr job on cw-us-east-02a ran 10 GLM-5.3 agents that reviewed #10203, each with one focus, and a lead agent that checked their findings against the code. All 11 attempts ended with `stop` and no failure.

Code: [`experiments/post_training/managed_agent/`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/rav/managed-agent-poc/experiments/post_training/managed_agent) on branch `rav/managed-agent-poc` (d74347f8d, on top of #10203 at d04b44ec8). Job: `/rav/managed-agent-poc-run-1`. Outputs: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/user/rav/projects/managed-agent-poc/run-1/` (`reviews.jsonl`, `lead_review.md`).

**Shape**

`ManagedAgent` is one `RolloutEngine`, one model, and a concurrency limit. It adds only admission: each attempt is `engine.run_task(spec, model)`, and `run(specs)` yields one `AgentOutcome(id, rollout, grade, failure)` for each spec, so that a failed attempt does not stop the others. `managed_agent.py` has 82 lines of code.

```python
harness = agent_harness(reviewer(pull_request, max_turns=limits.max_turns))  # the agent program
engine = RolloutEngine({}, {"reviewer": harness}, observer=ProgressLog())
manager = ManagedAgent(engine, ChatModel(glm_client, "glm-5.3", ...), concurrency=5)
specs = [agent_spec(agent_task(task_id, instructions), "reviewer", limits) for task_id, instructions in work]
async for outcome in manager.run(specs):
    ...  # outcome.answer, outcome.rollout, outcome.failure
```

- An attempt is a plain `TaskSpec`: the instructions in its public context, a text answer, and `NoGrader`. `agent_spec` gives it no machines and `TraceMode.MESSAGES`, because a chat endpoint renders its own tokens.
- The agent is an `agent_harness` program with its own tool loop and four read-only tools over the repository in the job bundle: `changed_files`, `file_diff`, `read_file`, and `search`. It sends the same options on each turn, so each request is a reply in one conversation.
- `ChatModel` (45 lines) serves each `ModelRequest` with an async OpenAI client, so the recorder can cancel a call at its deadline. It finds GLM through the Iris relay with `experiments/post_training/glm.py`.
- Zephyr shards the 10 specs to 2 workers, and each worker runs its shard with one `ManagedAgent` at concurrency 5. A second pipeline runs the lead agent. The workers get the GLM token from the job and find the relay themselves.

The engine already owns the hard parts: the limits, the record of each conversation, grading, cleanup, and events. Thus a managed agent needs no new `RolloutSpec` type, no new lowering, and no launcher. Zephyr and Iris place the workers.

**Run** (21:07 to 21:29 UTC: 10 minutes for the reviews and 10 minutes for the lead)

| agent | focus | turns | tool calls | prompt tokens | completion tokens |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `review-00` | the recorder: its limits, its deadlines, and the end of an attempt | 18 | 20 | 361 k | 80 k |
| `review-01` | the agent harness: concurrent completion calls, cancellation, and agent shutdown | 20 | 23 | 543 k | 67 k |
| `review-02` | the public API: names, signatures, and what a harness author must know | 20 | 26 | 647 k | 48 k |
| `review-03` | the exact-token contract and the messages trace | 20 | 27 | 463 k | 48 k |
| `review-04` | failure handling: the operation that an interrupted attempt reports, and what its rollout keeps | 13 | 17 | 242 k | 39 k |
| `review-05` | grading: the task's grader, the host judge, and output capture | 20 | 34 | 580 k | 43 k |
| `review-06` | the tests: whether they test behavior, and which behavior has no test | 20 | 24 | 707 k | 4 k |
| `review-07` | the reference docs and docstrings: whether each sentence agrees with the code | 20 | 32 | 662 k | 59 k |
| `review-08` | simplicity: code, options, and types that the pull request can delete | 12 | 21 | 252 k | 7 k |
| `review-09` | downstream impact: what MarinSkyRL and other callers must change, and what can break without an error | 17 | 29 | 435 k | 30 k |

| total | | 196 | 278 | 5.33 M | 533 k |

**What the agents found in #10203, after my check**

The lead confirmed 8 findings and rejected about 20, each with a reason. I checked the 8 against the code:

- 3 are false. `copy.deepcopy` and `model_copy` keep `judge_connection` (finding 6). `task_machine` does use `runtime.cleanup_timeout`, through `_prepare_machine` (finding 5). `TaskSpec` rejects a file or workspace answer with an in-process verifyit grader, so that grading failure cannot occur (finding 4).
- 1 is a documented limit: an agent that does not wait in `complete` can still run during grading. #10225 removes it.
- 4 are valid but small:
  - `record` after a refusal raises when no turn exists.
  - A pinned prompt that does not start with the served tokens is found only after the model answers, and the error blames the transport.
  - One sentence about the token budget is too strong.
  - No test has a host judge that hangs (#10246).

In the smoke run, the lead also reported a false finding about `SessionGrader`, which #10203 removes. Thus the lead review is a good triage of the 10 reviews, but each confirmed finding still needs a check.

**Gaps for a real version**

1. An `agent_harness` agent cannot read its `RolloutLimits`. Thus the reviewer gets `max_turns` two times: in the spec and in its closure. The agent harness can give the limits to the agent.
2. A reasoning model can use its whole token budget on its final turn and give no answer. In the smoke run, the one reviewer did this with `reasoning_effort=medium` and 32,768 tokens. The run uses the low effort for reviewers. An agent can also start a new conversation after a length stop, which the recorder permits.
3. `ChatModel` belongs in a library next to the engine, so that each managed agent does not write its own.
4. Arbitrary work fills the placeholders of `TaskSpec` (`Source`, `PlainText`, `NoGrader`). `agent_task` does this at one boundary, which is sufficient for now.

<details><summary>The lead review</summary>

# Review: [rolloutengine] Replace task sessions with registered harnesses

## Summary

The harness/recorder split is a real simplification: the recorder owns the model calls, limits, and token evidence outside the attempt deadline; the engine owns machines, grading, and cleanup; and the test suite asserts on recorded evidence rather than exit codes. Most of the deadline, refusal, and finalization logic I traced holds together exactly as documented. The confirmed problems cluster in four places: the agent harness can return while the agent task is still running (so the engine grades a workspace the agent may still be mutating), the documented "record a final reward after a refusal" pattern raises when the refusal was the attempt's first request, the pinned-token prefix contract is neither checked before sending nor checked at all in `MESSAGES` mode, and a check-time gap lets file/workspace-state answers with an in-process verifyit grader through to a guaranteed grade-time failure. Two doc/code contradictions (`task_machine`'s ignored `runtime.cleanup_timeout`, `judge_connection` dropped by `deepcopy`) and the budget wording round it out. No blockers.

## Confirmed findings

1. **Should fix — `lib/rolloutengine/src/rolloutengine/agent.py:55-66` (with `engine.py:187-189` and `docs/references/task-rollouts.md:220-222`).** When `completions.ended` wins the `asyncio.wait` race (a completion in another task — e.g. an HTTP handler — hit a model failure or limit), `run` returns while the agent task is still alive; the agent is only cancelled by the cleanup callback registered at `agent.py:58`, which runs *after* grading. Only calls inside `complete` are parked on `released`; an agent that is elsewhere can still run commands on `context.machine` while the engine captures `output_paths` and grades, contradicting the doc's safety claim, which covers only a *waiting* agent. Fix: when `ended` wins, cancel (or join, bounded by the cleanup deadline) the agent task before returning, so the record is final only when the agent is quiescent. (review-01 #1, review-02 #2)

2. **Should fix — `lib/rolloutengine/src/rolloutengine/recorder.py:221-246` and `248-263` (docstring at `harness.py:84-98`).** The documented pattern "After `LimitReached` or a failed model request, the harness can still add data and metrics … to the step of the last turn until it returns" raises `RuntimeError` when the refusal was the attempt's *first* request (`_add_to_ended_step` finds no step anywhere), so a harness written to the docs (`except RolloutEnded: recorder.record(data=reward)`) converts a `MODEL` failure into a harness `PREPARE` failure — and since grading is gated on `failure[0] == RolloutOperation.MODEL` (`engine.py:187`), the completed turns are then not graded. Also, `record` checks `_ended()` first (line 228), so a deadline that expires in that window raises `RolloutEnded` instead of the promised amend. Fix: make `record(data=..., metrics=...)` a no-op (or attach to a synthetic terminal step) when the refusal left no step, and narrow the docstring to what the code does. (review-00 #3, review-04 #3)

3. **Should fix — `lib/rolloutengine/src/rolloutengine/recorder.py:207-219` (docstrings at `harness.py:75-82`, `contracts.py:229-230`; check at `trace.py:73-74`).** `reply(..., token_ids=...)` documents that pinned tokens "must start with the tokens served so far" but never validates it. In `EXACT_TOKENS` mode the violation surfaces only after the model answers, as `RolloutContractError("Model transport changed the served token prefix")` — blaming the transport for a harness error — and is recorded as a model failure ("The model turn broke the token contract", `recorder.py:344-347`). In `MESSAGES` mode `_MessageTrace.append` performs no prefix check at all, so a wrong pin passes silently. Fix: check `token_ids[:len(trace.prefix)] == trace.prefix` in `reply` before sending and raise `RolloutContractError` directly, and either enforce or scope the doc sentence for `MESSAGES`. (review-03 #1 and #5, review-08 reply nit, review-09 #6)

4. **Should fix — `lib/rolloutengine/src/rolloutengine/grading.py:77-78` (with `checks.py:42-52` and `taskcompendium/grading.py:84-95`).** The in-process verifyit branch builds `GradingAttempt(conversation, stop_reason=...)` and drops `outputs`; `answer_submission` raises `TypeError` for any non-conversation, non-STATE answer. A task with `answer_type` FILE or WORKSPACE_STATE, a `VerifyitGrader` without an environment, and a selected task machine passes `check_spec` (only STATE and judge-with-non-conversation answers are rejected) and then interrupts *every* attempt with a `GRADE` failure. Fix: reject in-process verifyit graders on file/workspace-state answers in `check_spec`, as the judge branch already does, or pass `outputs` through. (review-05 #1)

5. **Should fix — `lib/rolloutengine/src/rolloutengine/machines.py:222-228` (and `docs/references/task-rollouts.md:428`).** The `task_machine` docstring (and the reference table) says "`runtime.cleanup_timeout`, when it is set, replaces `cleanup_timeout` for the machine's close," but the code builds `cleanup = _Cleanup(cleanup_timeout)` once and never reads `runtime.cleanup_timeout`; a caller relying on the sentence gets the argument deadline with no error. Fix: honor the override (e.g. `runtime.cleanup_timeout if runtime.cleanup_timeout is not None else cleanup_timeout`) or delete the sentence from both docs. (review-09 #1; the untested-claim half is review-06's task-machine nit)

6. **Should fix — `lib/rolloutengine/src/rolloutengine/spec.py:77-89` (with `grading.py:45-51`).** `__getstate__` also strips `judge_connection` from `copy.copy`/`copy.deepcopy`, not only from `model_dump`, JSON, and pickle as the field docstring and the reference doc claim. A worker pool that deep-copies specs silently loses the explicit connection and falls back to `VERIFYIT_JUDGE_BASE_URL`/`VERIFYIT_JUDGE_API_KEY` — potentially a *different* judge, with no error or diagnostic, which is exactly the round-tripping workflow the PR description calls out. Fix: keep the connection under copy/deepcopy (override `__deepcopy__`) or at minimum document that copy drops it, and consider recording when the connection came from the environment. (review-02 #4, review-09 #2)

7. **Nit — `docs/references/task-rollouts.md:445-448` (and `spec.py:47-49`, `recorder.py:348-352`).** The budget invariant "it never sends a request whose prompt alone reaches the budget" does not hold: the refusal test uses the just-completed request's prompt+response count as a stand-in for the next prompt, and the next prompt additionally contains the new observation tokens, so when the observations exceed the previous request's count, `spent_tokens + turn.request_tokens < max_total` can hold while the next prompt alone reaches the threshold. Fix: weaken the two doc sentences to say the check is a lower bound (or charge the projected next prompt), and clarify the recorder comment, which also does not say the current request is counted twice. (review-07; comment clarity from review-03 #3)

8. **Nit — `lib/rolloutengine/src/rolloutengine/grading.py:70-76` and the judge tests in `lib/rolloutengine/tests/test_rollout.py` (~2922).** The judge tests exercise only a server that answers every request immediately with 200, so the documented bounds on the host-judge path — the verifier deadline stopping the engine's wait for a hanging judge, `JudgeSpec.request_timeout`, and the retry count — have no test. Fix: add a test with a handler that never responds (bounded by `verifier_timeout`, reported as a grading timeout) and one that fails so the retry count is observable in `judge_server.requests`. (review-06 #1 and #2)

## Rejected findings

- **review-00 #1 (total-turn timeout armed only at the first `start`):** the reference already documents that the total-turn deadline excludes the harness's work before its first request (`task-rollouts.md:430`), and the engine bounds that window with `attempt_timeout`; standalone `harness_rollout` documents that attempt deadlines belong to the engine.
- **review-00 #2 (tool deadline wins over the total deadline):** the two timeouts share one task and the first to fire cancels it, so both cannot be expired when the checks run; the ordering is unreachable in practice.
- **review-00 #4 (close leaves an expired model call's task awaiting forever):** speculative — it requires a transport that swallows the `model_turn_timeout` cancellation and never returns; the `call.expired()` guard itself is required because `reschedule` raises once expired.
- **review-01 #2 (cached turn returned after the record is final):** the cached return is guarded by `not self.ended.done()` with no await between the check and the return; any residual hazard of the agent running late is finding 1.
- **review-01 #3 (stop's release-then-cancel window):** `released.set()` and `agent.cancel()` run with no await between them, so the cancellation is already pending before the woken agent can run.
- **review-01 #4 and review-08's deletion suggestions (`ModelTurn.text`, `RolloutRecorder.limits`, `AgentCompletion`, `NO_TOOLS`, `_ShellToolSession.close`, double `judge_connection` call, docstring deferral):** style/API-surface preferences, not behavior the code gets wrong.
- **review-02 #1 (shell capability without a machine passes `check`):** `check_spec` rejects any non-empty environment requirements — including the shell capability — when no machine is selected (`checks.py:59-61`), so the `ValueError` in `_ShellHarness.run` is unreachable through the engine.
- **review-02 #3 (length-stop comment in `start`):** the comment explains why LENGTH is excluded from the explicit start-check; `_refusal` refuses any `start` after a length stop regardless, and the `start` docstring makes no contrary promise.
- **review-02 #5 (`command_timeout` without a default):** a deliberate API choice, not a defect; the doc example passes it explicitly.
- **review-02 #6 and review-09 #8 (`ADVANCE_INCOMPLETE` and last-step-only metrics in `Rollout.metrics`):** both are documented behavior (`task-rollouts.md:464-465`; "The last step's metrics").
- **review-03 #4 (`stop_at_turn_deadline` naming):** the tool-deadline-interrupts vs. total-timeout-stops distinction is documented (`task-rollouts.md:438`).
- **review-04 #1 (tool deadline demotes a model error):** the tool deadline is disarmed for the whole model request (`recorder.py:299`) and rearmed only on success, so `model_error` and `tool.expired()` cannot hold together when the checks run.
- **review-04 #2 (length stop leaves the tool deadline armed):** same disarm — `_send` clears the tool deadline at line 299 and the `GenerationLimitReached` branch raises before any rearm.
- **review-04 #5 (`delivery` unbound in `run_task`):** an exception inside the `try` propagates after the `finally`; the code after the `try`/`finally` never executes, so `delivery` cannot be unbound there.
- **review-05 #4 and #6 (judge capture overhead; verifier timeout covering capture and grading):** the single `verifier_timeout` covering output capture plus grading is documented in the deadlines table (`task-rollouts.md:426`); the capture-overhead point is a minor optimization.
- **review-09 #3 (old `RolloutEngine(model, factories)` order):** no in-repo caller passes the old order; an `isinstance` assertion is speculative migration aid, not a defect in this PR.
- **review-09 #4 (judge grader's `environment` ignored):** documented design — the judge grades on the host, so no machine is used for its environment (`checks.py:38-39`).
- **review-09 #5 (`record(observations=...)` then `start` allowed):** intended — the recorded observations end the earlier conversation's last step and `start` begins a new conversation, exactly as the `start` and `record` docstrings describe.
- **review-09 #7 (agent check misses provider tools):** `check` rejects every task with `tool_providers` (`agent.py:51`); only the error message names action interfaces rather than tool names.
- **review-05 #2/#3/#5, review-06 #3-#6, review-03 #2:** real but marginal polish (observation overwrite, a missing `TransitionCompleted` on the total-timeout path, empty standalone `outputs`, untested `harness_rollout` failure path/`response_end`, judge fallback key wording, `response_token_ids` mode wording) — dropped for rank, not disputed.

topics.title: [grug] Flatten MLP tokens locally under context parallelism
topics.body:
The hero's shared and routed MLPs now flatten `[B, S, D]` into tokens locally on each device instead of with a global `(b s)` rearrange. With the sequence sharded over context and more than one row per batch shard, the global rearrange is an all-to-all in each direction, forward and backward, in every layer. Without context sharding nothing changes: each device already holds whole rows, so the local and global token orders are the same.

`_flatten_tokens` reshapes each device's block of rows and sequence shard in a `shard_map`, and `_unflatten_tokens` inverts it and restores the residual layout. Under context parallelism the experts then see tokens shard-major. Routing is per token, so the only order-dependent effect is which tokens a full expert drops first. A CPU test checks that CP2 logits equal CP1 logits on the same parameters when no token drops; the compiled CP2 forward goes from 8 all-to-alls to the 4 of the expert transport.

On one GB200 NVL72 rack restored from hero step 240000 at 65K context on CP4/EP16 (same rack, 106 scored steps per arm), step time goes from 15.938 s on main to 15.586 s (+2.26% tokens/s). The drop fraction falls from 1.17% to 0.23% and loss is 2.3e-3 lower. The old flatten gave each expert-parallel group whole 65K rows, so a single-document row put a large share of the group's tokens on one document's preferred experts; the local flatten splits each row across the four groups and mixes slices of every row into each. With #10121's row balancing on top, CP4 runs at 14.626 s against 15.137 s and 1.94% drops on CP1, so CP4 becomes the faster and more faithful 65K layout.

At 262K with the documented recipe (batch 16, CP4/EP16) each device holds one row's sequence shard, which is already its block of the global order, so this change compiles to the same program there. At CP8/EP8 main fails to trace (the MoE unflatten reshape is not supported for that sharding); with this change the step traces but runs out of memory at the first step when NCCL allocates its all-to-all buffers, so CP8 at 262K needs separate memory work.

https://claude.ai/code/session_01V7n2oqJz61dkhYLBwNWYj9

topics.title: Add the Smartie joint-domain RL campaign
topics.body:
Add the Smartie campaign for joint training on structural closure, competitive coding, SWE-smith, NL2Bash, TaskForge and CalibForge tasks. Version the admitted data, fixed validation panels and saved training configurations. New runtime revisions use fresh run identities; submitted configurations remain immutable.

Pin MarinSkyRL to eedfec34799dd35ba3e19733d9e70efedc4730e1, which includes concurrent native/Harbor evaluation and benchmark task caching. The continuation starts from run 2026.10.15.32 step 14, the best surviving checkpoint by recorded inline validation score, shuffles training data, retains ten checkpoints, and uses 112 H100s. Run 2026.10.16.43 finished its initial validation pass with 621 of 663 attempted tasks graded; optimizer updates and post-update validation remain unverified. Before merging this PR, repin to the merged runtime repair commits on MarinSkyRL main, including [#1019](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/1019).

RolloutEngine accepts an explicit remote judge connection, propagates caller cancellation during cleanup, and checks replay prefixes after history transitions. Preserve grading after a conversation reset or an abandoned completion request; exclude undelivered responses from training records. RL coordinators reject missing declared secrets, and colocated SkyRL jobs reject expert-block weight synchronization. Local Shellbox execution rejects non-Linux hosts; curation image builds enforce tracked inputs only inside Git worktrees.

Offline closure audits reuse Verifyit's training scorer, including typed JSON comparison and signed-zero equality. Parsing accepts a numeric JSON scalar before a tool delimiter; structural content rewards still require the expected object. Marin's test environment includes RolloutEngine and the Daytona backend.

[Evaluation design](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10043#issuecomment-6214235547). Part of #10043.

🤖 Holistic review of 805e4468778daf2f6c7dfbb5814393a8f8f16eaa.

Adds the Smartie RL campaign (data splits, validation panel, saved-config launcher), the structure-closure experiments, a remote-judge path in RolloutEngine, and re-pins MarinSkyRL. The library changes are small and tested; the changed test files pass locally (rolloutengine 222, marin-core with CI extras 140). Two problems: the MarinSkyRL pin points at an unmerged PR head, and the PR adds a second copy of the closure scorer that already lives in VerifyIt, and the two copies disagree on results.

**Blockers**
1. `config/external/MarinSkyRL/pyproject.toml:15` The uv source changes from `branch = "main"` to `rev = "ea93af58…"`, which is the head of MarinSkyRL#1007. That PR is open and unmerged. MarinSkyRL squash-merges (b5287591, 03c9bf78 and 06a1b564 are single-parent commits), so this SHA will never be on the fork's `main`. `docs/dev-guide/forking-policy.md` (Promotion) says isolated projects "restore their uv source to `main` and relock at that same SHA". Once #1007 lands, Marin `main` would run an unreviewed branch commit that branch cleanup can orphan, and the `2026.10.16.33.yaml` header already says "submit only after runtime PR #1007 merges green". Fix: merge #1007 first, then point `pyproject.toml` back at `branch = "main"`, relock at the squash commit, and set `MARIN_SKYRL.commit` (`lib/marin/src/marin/external_dependencies.py:88`) and the config's `launcher_commit` to that commit.

**Should fix**
2. `lib/rolloutengine/src/rolloutengine/closure_scoring.py:107` This file copies `verifyit.closure_scoring` from before #10093 (merged in this PR's base). The copy compares canonical `json.dumps` strings; VerifyIt uses `json_values_equal(..., NumericTypePolicy.STRICT)`. They already disagree: with reference `{"a": 0.0}` and output `{"a": -0.0}`, VerifyIt scores success and this copy scores failure. The pinned MarinSkyRL computes the training reward with `verifyit.closure_scoring` (`skyrl_gym/closure_task.py`, `skyrl_train/closure_training.py`). Meanwhile `benchmark.py:14`, `eval_audit.py:15`, `tool_prompt_probe.py:12` and `training_prefixes.py:13` score with the rolloutengine copy, under the same `closure_region_v1` scorer id. Offline benchmark numbers can therefore disagree with the training reward. Fix: import `verifyit.closure_scoring` in those four modules (pass `terminal_markers=` to `closure_response_content` the way MarinSkyRL does), then delete `rolloutengine/closure_scoring.py` and `lib/rolloutengine/tests/test_structure_closure.py`, which duplicates `lib/verifyit/tests/test_structure_closure.py`.
3. `lib/rolloutengine/src/rolloutengine/closure_repair.py:105` Nothing in Marin's runtime uses this module. Its only caller is `experiments/post_training/structure_closure/test_token_data.py:7`. MarinSkyRL keeps its own `skyrl_train/closure_repair.py` and imports that copy, so this 235-line module plus its 380-line `test_closure_repair.py` is a third implementation inside a generic rollout library. Fix: delete it and its test, and drop the `verified_closure_target` assertion from `test_token_data.py`. If Marin really needs a shared copy, move it to VerifyIt next to `structure_closure` and have MarinSkyRL import it, so only one copy exists.
4. `experiments/post_training/structure_closure/evaluate_checkpoint.py:20` Six launchers (`evaluate_checkpoint`, `evaluate_native_tools`, `evaluate_parity`, `evaluate_parity_checkpoint`, `evaluate_tool_prompt_probe`, `evaluate_varied`) are 25–45-line click wrappers around `evaluate.build_evaluation` (`evaluate.py:85`). Each one hardcodes a single dataset/model pairing. Fix: one `evaluate.py` command with `--data {cohort|uri@version}` and `--model {base|checkpoint uri/version/identity}` options deletes five files. The `CHECKPOINTS` table belongs in the record, not in a module that another launcher imports.

**Related PRs**
5. #10078 (same author, open): adds the same `experiments/post_training/structure_closure/*` tree and the same `rolloutengine/closure_{scoring,repair}.py` that this PR carries. This PR supersedes it. Close #10078, or fold anything it adds that this PR lacks (`rolloutengine/structure_closure.py`, `tool_protocol.py`) into this branch first.
6. #10115, #10032, #9838, #9799: each edits `rolloutengine/grading.py` or `engine.py`, which this PR also edits (new `judge_connection` keyword on `_grade_rollout`). They have no semantic dependency on this PR. Whichever lands second rebases onto the new `_grade_rollout` signature.

topics.title: Add harbor launch configs for the cybersecurity safety suites
topics.body:
Add one launch config per ported cybersecurity suite for the evaluation
launch CLI: AgentHarm, AgentThreatBench, AgentDojo, InterCode-CTF, 3CB,
Cybench, CVE-Bench, GDM in-house CTF, CyberSecEval 2 (judge suites and
vulnerability_exploit), and CyberSecEval 4 (threat_intelligence, mitre,
mitre_frr, multilingual prompt injection). Each points at the task-dir
dataset published on the Hugging Face Hub for its suite and pins the retry
policy that keeps Daytona DinD dockerd flakes ("Cannot connect to the
Docker daemon", a bare RuntimeError) from failing a whole run; before this,
one flake class outside the default retry taxonomy could kill an eval after
minutes.

The judged suites declare their complete verifier env. Harbor resolves every
env placeholder a task toml declares strictly, so the configs must name
OPENAI_API_KEY, OPENAI_BASE_URL, JUDGE_MODEL, and the per-suite extras
(REFUSAL_JUDGE_MODEL, EXPANSION_MODEL). They route the judge through
Together's OpenAI-compatible endpoint with gpt-oss-120b because the paper
gpt-4o judges need an OpenAI credit path we do not have; swapping back is a
three-line edit per config.

All fourteen configs ran live on cw-rno2a against Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and
produced the baseline scores recorded in the cybersecurity tracker. The
adapters that generate these task datasets are in the companion harbor PR.

topics.title: [eval] Resume evaluations after inference preemption
topics.body:
When model or judge inference is preempted, stop the evaluator, wait for inference to become ready, and retry inside the same evaluation StepSpec. Harbor preserves completed trials; Evalchemy reuses saved generation responses. Completed StepSpecs stay cached.

If inference ends permanently, unfinished evaluations receive infrastructure-failure records. Evalchemy rejects resumed runs containing saved transport failures: native resume replays those failures without making new requests. The error names the affected archive and tells the operator to remove it before retrying.

comments.body:
🤖 Holistic review of e7b8dcb8e8f2a67e7ba8e7d17fdac56b4a11a128.

The PR moves inference-outage handling from the Harbor runner into a shared `run_with_inference_recovery` loop. Harbor and Evalchemy now stop their child work, wait for the backends, and resume against the same output directory. The shared loop fits the existing `EvalExecutor` seam, and the changed unit tests pass locally. One consequence of the transport-failure rejection needs an operator path, and one write is redundant. #10033 is a competing fix for the same failure and should be reconciled before either PR lands.

**Should fix**
1. `lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/runner.py:426` `resuming_archive` is true for any non-empty archive at `output_dir`, not only for archives this process interrupted. `run_served_evalchemy` uses the step's deterministic `out_path` (`experiment/evaluation.py:77-79`), and StepRunner or orchestrator retries reuse it. Suppose a first attempt saved even one transport failure that the fresh-attempt branch at :437 and the coverage gate at :505-514 accepted. Every later rerun of that step then fails as `INFRA_FAILED`, and no retry can clear it. The message at :440 does not name the archive or say what an operator must do. Put `output_dir` and the remedy (delete the archive to rerun) in the `EvaluationError` message. Add the same sentence to the README paragraph that this PR adds, so the permanent failure has a documented exit.
2. `lib/marin/src/marin/experiment/evaluation.py:117` `write_artifact(result.result_payload(), output_dir)` duplicates the record write in `_lower`'s step fn (`lib/marin/src/marin/execution/lazy.py:376-388`). That fn writes the full `ArtifactRecord` at the same path from `result.result_payload()` after `run_served_evalchemy` returns. Since `FineStoreEvalchemyResult` now carries `jobs`, the step record already persists them. The manual write adds a window in which a minimal record exists with no name, version, fingerprint, or provenance. Delete line 117 and the `write_artifact` import at :37.
3. `lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/evalchemy/result.py:58` and `lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor/runner.py:201,262` The docstring rewrites are unrelated to preemption recovery, and they remove invariants that the code still depends on. `EvalchemyResult` lost the note that historical reports persist its type name, so the class is part of the durable decoding contract; without it, the class reads as deletable. `_attempted_trials` lost the reason it returns `None` rather than the number of trials found: a found count would certify an interrupted run as complete. `_aggregate` lost the reason it divides by scored trials. Restore those three docstrings, or move these hunks to their own PR.

**Related PRs**
4. #10033: competing fix for the same incident (Evalchemy losing a re-registered serve). It rewrites the same `_run_evalchemy_child` wait loop and signature (`model` → `session`, a `_wait_while_serving` loop) and edits `experiment/evaluation.py`, so the two PRs conflict textually. They also overlap in design: #10033 follows re-registration through a loopback relay, while this PR cancels the child and resumes it. Choose one owner for Evalchemy recovery. If this PR lands first, reduce #10033 to the Iris `endpoint_relay` and drop its Evalchemy runner hunks.
5. #9813: makes each evaluation a StepSpec, with StepRunner owning retries at each result path, and edits `evaluation/runner.py` and `experiments/evaluation/README.md`. Those StepRunner retries hit item 1 on every evaluation that saved a transport failure. Land this PR first; #9813 then needs to handle the permanent `INFRA_FAILED` from item 1 when it rebases.

topics.title: [grug] Route QBRoutedMoE through the jax_triton top-k kernel
topics.body:
QBRoutedMoE now selects experts with `levanter.grug._moe.topk.top_k_indices`, called per token shard inside `shard_map`, in place of `jax.lax.top_k`. That is the jax_triton kernel from #9830, which the hero model already uses. `jax.lax.top_k` still handles rows of 1,024 or more (XLA:GPU runs its own top-k kernel on those), non-float32 inputs, non-GPU backends and environments without jax-triton.

On AMD, jax-triton 0.3.1 with triton 3.6.0, Levanter's GPU pins, compiles the kernel for ROCm with jaxlib 0.11.1 or newer. jaxlib 0.11.0 never loads `jax_rocm10_plugin`'s Triton launcher, so there the kernel falls back to `jax.lax.top_k`.

Time per call in ms, from 16 calls on distinct inputs in one executable, median of 5 runs. The shapes are the router logits per call of the hero model and of the June Snowball model:

| shape, k | GPU | `lax.top_k` | jax_triton (this PR) |
|---|---|---|---|
| [65536, 384], 9 (hero) | GB200 | 0.837 | 0.0754 |
| [65536, 384], 9 (hero) | H100 | 1.107 | 0.0954 |
| [65536, 384], 9 (hero) | MI300X | 0.847 | 0.0665 |
| [65536, 384], 9 (hero) | MI350X | 1.000 | 0.0570 |
| [32768, 256], 5 (June) | GB200 | 0.229 | 0.0207 |
| [32768, 256], 5 (June) | H100 | 0.308 | 0.0238 |
| [32768, 256], 5 (June) | MI300X | 0.351 | 0.0246 |
| [32768, 256], 5 (June) | MI350X | 0.402 | 0.0167 |

The AMD rows ran on jax 0.11.1, jax_rocm10_plugin 0.11.1+rocm10.1.0, jax-triton 0.3.1 and triton 3.6.0, with the AMD HPC Fund cluster's ROCm 7.2 libraries on the library path, as `experiments/amd/hpcfund/run_gpu.sh` leaves them. The `lax.top_k` baseline depends on that: with only the wheel's own ROCm libraries loaded, `lax.top_k` on MI350X takes 2.4 ms (hero) and 1.7 ms (June), while the kernel times do not change. The kernel code is unchanged since #9830; the NVIDIA rows are earlier measurements of it with the same harness.

On NVIDIA, the models that use QBRoutedMoE (`experiments/grug/moe`, `experiments/grug/moe_hero_fsdp` and `experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe`) now run the kernel, because Levanter's GPU extra installs jax-triton. In the optimized HLO of the June training step on H100 and GB200, the 4 `sort` ops of main's routing become 2 `triton_kernel_call`s, and the all-gathers, all-reduces and reduce-scatters are unchanged. Step time does not change measurably. June model at full width with 4 layers and sequence length 4096, ring expert parallelism over the node, `xla_flash` attention and XLA `ragged_dot`; median of steps 2-19 per run, runs alternating between main and this PR:

| GPU | Tokens per GPU | Runs per side | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4x GB200 | 8,192 | 4 | 0.5742 s (0.5723-0.5759) | 0.5740 s (0.5719-0.5760) |
| 8x H100 | 16,384 | 5 | 1.457 s (1.403-1.508) | 1.513 s (1.336-1.539) |

On H100, step time varied between runs of the same code: main's five runs spanned 1.403-1.508 s (7%) and this PR's 1.336-1.539 s (15%). Five runs per side cannot separate the two. Scaled to these shapes, the per-call times above put the saving below 0.1% of a step. At 16,384 tokens per GPU on GB200, runs of both variants intermittently hung in a training step or ran out of memory, so those runs are left out. TPU step time was not measured; there `top_k_indices` falls back to `lax.top_k` inside the same `shard_map`.

On MI300X and MI350X the kernel's indices equal those of `lax.top_k` computed on the CPU, for widths 37 to 1,023 and k up to 37, on random, tied, constant, ±0, ±inf and NaN rows. ROCm's own `lax.top_k` ties -0 with +0 and orders NaN payloads differently, while the kernel follows XLA:CPU and CUDA. The GPU tests therefore check the kernel's output against `lax.top_k` run on the CPU backend.

The AMD venv recipe in `experiments/amd/hpcfund/README.md` still installs jaxlib 0.11.0 without jax-triton, so runs from it silently keep `lax.top_k` until that recipe moves to 0.11.1.

topics.title: [iris] GPU jobs default to NCCL_DEBUG=INFO and flood log forwarding
topics.body:
Every Iris job that requests a GPU extra gets `NCCL_DEBUG=INFO` with `NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS=INIT,BOOTSTRAP,ENV,NET,GRAPH,TUNING,RAS` from the default environment in `lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/types.py:779`. Marin's training launcher sets `NCCL_DEBUG` to `WARN` only when nothing is preset (`lib/marin/src/marin/training/training.py:418`, `setdefault`), so the Iris default wins for every training job.

On 2026-10-17 four 32-GPU SFT jobs (`/karan/task203-lr*`, cw-rno2a) emitted about 80,000 log lines per second, mostly `NCCL INFO` per-collective output, while log forwarding accepts about 34,500 lines per second; the hub fell about 90 minutes behind on that cluster's logs.

Reproduce: submit any GPU job without setting `NCCL_DEBUG` and read its task log; `NCCL INFO AllReduce: ... Algo TREE proto LL ...` lines appear for every collective.

Expected: GPU jobs default to `NCCL_DEBUG=WARN` (abort and transport errors remain visible), with INFO and the subsystem list set only by jobs that are debugging NCCL (for example the recovery or wedge repro experiments, which already set INFO explicitly).

Done when: the Iris GPU default is `WARN` without a subsystem list, Marin's training launcher no longer needs to guess, and the two call sites that want INFO set it themselves.

topics.title: [finestore] Merge sorted runs and resolve versions in Arrow
topics.body:
FineStore compaction, scans, and `iter_rows` now resolve primary-key versions in Arrow instead of row by row in Python. Compaction becomes a sorted-run merge whose output shards hold disjoint, ascending key ranges.

Compaction used to order input row groups by their first key, keep the newest version of every key in a Python dictionary one row at a time, and then hand each output row to the shard writer as its own slice. `scan` and `iter_rows` also compared versions per row in Python. Version resolution therefore dominated compaction time, and a key could recur across one compaction's output shards.

`finestore.merge` selects the newest row per key with one Arrow sort and a key-change mask, using the existing order: a greater `(_commit, _seq, _gen)` wins, a missing `_seq` counts as zero, and null keys sort last and compare equal. A key column that no row sets is null for every row. `merge_sorted_runs` keeps a sorted buffer per run and merges by a frontier: buffered rows below the smallest last key among the runs are final and are sorted once as they leave, and only the runs at the frontier read their next table. Memory holds about one table per run.

Compaction reads each sorted input a row group at a time. An unsorted input, such as a flush with a row missing a key column or a shard migrated from format 1, is sorted whole in memory, so a compaction holds all of its unsorted inputs at once; these are expected to be rare. Output shards are cut at about `target_bytes`. `iter_rows` streams the same merge, and `scan` uses the vectorised selection while keeping its row order; `scan` also resolves versions when a key column is absent, as `iter_rows` does.

Local root, 16 overlapping level-zero shards of 20,000 rows each (320,000 rows, 95,874 live keys), against main on the same machine:

| | main | this change |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `compact_table`, 1,024-row row groups | 51.7 s, 79 MB Arrow peak, 33 MB Python peak | 0.9 s, 4.7 MB, 0.4 MB |
| `compact_table`, default row groups | 43.6 s | 0.15 s |
| `scan` | 0.78 s | 0.11 s |
| `iter_rows` | 1.69 s | 0.5 s |

Object-store traffic is unaffected: the 16-writer simulated S3 benchmark issued 1,772 requests, against 1,789 on main.

This is the merge half of P2 in the FineStore concurrency proposal (Loom session bth4qn4d, artifact `finestore-improvements`). The proposed `_version` column is not added: while every commit goes through one `HEAD`, `(_commit, _seq, _gen)` is already a total order, and `_version` only becomes necessary with per-writer heads (P3), so it should land with that format change.

comments.body:
🤖 Holistic review of 4fddb8ab9d4371931e3c467731bbea1e2a1a24d0.

This change moves FineStore's newest-version selection from per-row Python into Arrow and turns compaction into a sorted-run merge. Reads and compaction now share one module, `finestore/merge.py`. Since the last review, the merge keeps a separate buffer for each run and no longer re-sorts carried rows. One problem remains: compaction holds every unsorted input shard fully in memory at the same time.

**Before.** Compaction ordered input row groups by their first key through `heapq.merge`, kept the newest version of each key in a Python dict, and flushed that buffer as a sorted output shard each time it passed `target_bytes` (the bound added in #10188). Keys could appear in more than one output shard. `iter_rows` merged per-shard Python row streams, and `scan`'s `_deduplicate` sorted indices in Python.

**Design.** `newest_indices` sorts by key ascending (nulls last), then by `(_commit, _seq→0, _gen)` descending, and keeps the first row of each key using a key-change mask. A key column that is absent or null-typed is skipped, since it is null in every row. `merge_sorted_runs` keeps a `_RunCursor` buffer for each run with contiguous key arrays. Each round takes the buffered rows below the smallest `last_key` among the active runs, resolves versions on only those rows, and pulls the next table only for runs at that frontier. Before a pull, leftover versions of the frontier key shrink to one row. Compaction feeds `_sorted_run(shard)` into the merge, then into `table_row_groups`, and cuts output shards near `target_bytes`. Its output shards cover disjoint key ranges.

**Evidence and limits.** The 249 finestore tests pass locally at this head. They include a randomized merge-vs-dict oracle (40 seeds) and compaction tests for disjoint output ranges, an unsorted flush, and a key column that no row sets. That last test reproduces Codex's `ArrowInvalid` report. My microbenchmark of `merge_sorted_runs` (2M int keys, one run as a single table, the other in 1,024-row tables) took 7.2 s at 57ae77bc and takes 0.13 s now. I did not reproduce the benchmark table in the PR body.

**Findings**

- **1. Should fix (open):** `lib/finestore/src/finestore/compaction.py:223` still holds every unsorted input shard in memory at once. `_RunCursor.__init__` calls `pull()` (`merge.py:111`), so constructing the merge reads the first table of every run. For an unsorted shard that table is the whole shard, because `sorted_by_key` (`merge.py:49`) runs `list(tables)` over it. Peak memory is therefore the decoded size of all unsorted inputs together, where #10188 bounded it to about `target_bytes`. Every shard migrated from format v1 is unsorted (`migrations/m0001_manifest.py:249` builds `Shard(...)` without `primary_key_sorted`), and `compact_table` has no input budget. An explicit or leveled compaction of a migrated archive would therefore decode every legacy shard into memory together. Sort unsorted inputs one at a time before the merge, for example by rewriting each into a sorted temporary run, so peak memory is one shard. Add a test that compacts two unsorted shards and checks they are not materialized together. (`iter_rows` already buffered unsorted shards this way before this PR, so the regression is limited to compaction.)

Earlier findings: 2 resolved in 4fddb8ab; per-run buffers sort only rows that have become final, so a whole-shard run no longer gets re-sorted every round.

<!-- marin-holistic-review:4fddb8ab9d4371931e3c467731bbea1e2a1a24d0 -->

🤖 Removed the merge module's caller list and the compaction docstring's hard byte-limit claim in 5769d365e5. Pre-commit and 208 FineStore tests passed. The review's two behavior-changing findings remain with the PR author.

<!-- marin-deslop:57ae77bc6088cecf11a3365efa7580ef6957d9ca -->

🤖 Both findings are addressed.

1. Unsorted inputs are no longer held together (2f9e4d331e). Before the merge, each unsorted shard is read a row group at a time into chunks of at most `target_bytes` decoded bytes. Each chunk is sorted and written to a local temporary Parquet file, which the merge reads as another sorted run. `test_compaction_sorts_unsorted_shards_one_at_a_time` compacts 2 and then 6 unsorted 8 MiB shards. Peak Arrow memory is 25 MB in both cases, where the previous code grew from 56 MB to 152 MB and fails the test.
2. The carried remainder is no longer re-sorted each round (4fddb8ab9d, also Codex's finding). Each run keeps its own sorted buffer, a round binary-searches every buffer for the rows below the frontier, and only those rows are sorted. One 400,000-row run against 400 tables of 1,000 rows now merges in 0.36 s, down from 2.2 s. Slicing the sorted table is unnecessary with buffers, because a large buffer costs one binary search per round.

🤖 Reverted the spill in c62881fb6a. Unsorted inputs come only from flushes with a row missing a key column and from shards migrated from format 1, which may no longer exist. Temporary-file handling isn't worth carrying for that case. A compaction again sorts its unsorted inputs in memory and holds them together, and the README now says so.

topics.title: [fast-track] Marin Belay v1: hill-climb the scaling ladder (Paloma macro loss, 8 min on 8×H100)
topics.body:
This issue tracks iterative improvements to the Marin pretraining scaling ladder (`experiments/grug/fast_track`) using the **Marin Belay** process. It is a twist on autoresearch: an agent runs experiments in batches, and anyone can steer it with research directions. > **To suggest a research direction, comment on [Marin Belay Intake (#9514)](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9514).** Suggestions a maintainer approves (👍 from a `marin-devs` member) are copied into this thread automatically, and the agent acts only on this thread. This thread holds the agent's batch reports and maintainer steering. ![fast_track MoE ladder: Marin 535B baseline, clean KMA and candidate 9](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/9697c11ef215ec0f9d536a1bceb0876f768fcf26/v1/ladder_scaling.png) The Marin 535B compute-optimal baseline follows `L(C) = 1.2 + 59.0·C^(−0.0843)` over four data-matched rungs. Clean KMA, the current baseline (★), is 0.022 lower at d512, 0.049 lower at d768, 0.040 lower at d1024 and 0.033 lower at d1280, which is about 1.14×, 1.43×, 1.40× and 1.35× the baseline's compute efficiency. Its dashed curve is fit to all four points: `L(C) = 1.2 + 64.8·C^(−0.0870)`. The **?** marks the open question this issue is chasing: how much further down each point can go. The red diamonds are the current best recipe, candidate 9 (Status below): **2.977 / 2.725 / 2.515 / 2.397** at d512 / d768 / d1024 / d1280. d512 and d768 are seed means, and the bigram table follows rule A. d768–d1280 are data-matched; d512 sits at its fixed-time step count (2817 vs 2383 steps), so it's plotted slightly to the right. That is 0.157 / 0.098 / 0.078 / 0.074 below clean KMA. Its dash-dot curve is fit to all four points: `L(C) = 1.2 + 55.0·C^(−0.0847)`. Its slope is a little shallower than clean KMA's, so the gap narrows with compute: projected to **1e24 FLOPs, 1.710 vs clean KMA's 1.727, about 1.48× clean KMA's compute efficiency and 2.95× the 535B baseline's**. Because the fixed-time d512 point flattens the fitted slope, that projection is probably conservative. The right panel is clean KMA's training MFU at each rung on one 8×H100 node: 9.5% at d512 and d768, 12.2% at d1024, and 13.0% at d1280. FLOPs are counted from KMA's own layers (KDA, MLA + Inkling, AttnRes), as 3× forward with no recompute. The trainer's logged `throughput/mfu` uses the baseline architecture's FLOP formula, so it is slightly off for KMA. ## Objective **Minimize Paloma macro loss (`eval/paloma/macro_loss`, final step) at the d512 rung after a fixed 8 minutes of 8×H100 train-step time.** - **Fixed time, not fixed tokens.** Faster code trains on more tokens within the 8 minutes, so a pure speedup counts as a win. - The LR schedule depends on the step count, so fix steps before each run: `num_steps = round(480 s × ex/s ÷ batch)`. - Measure ex/s with a short `--no-eval` probe (~30 steps) on the same cluster, and use the steady-state throughput. - Compile, evals and startup are excluded from the 8 minutes. - **Numerics changes are allowed** (e.g. FP8, precision changes, approximate kernels). They count as ordinary wins; no parity check needed. - **Noise.** Differences under ~0.005 are noise. A win must beat the current best by more than 0.005. ### Gates (both relative to the current baseline, same fixed-time rule at each rung) - **Gate 1:** beat the baseline at d512 and d768. - **Gate 2:** also beat it at d1024 and d1280, **and** project to lower Paloma macro loss at 1e24 FLOPs. Fit a power law of final loss against training FLOPs across the four rungs, for both the baseline and the variant, fixing the asymptote to 1.2. ### Fixed - Training data, the 16k BPE tokenizer, and the eval sets. - Sequence length 4096. - One 8×H100 node per rung. - The FLOP accounting used for the gate-2 projection. ### Judgment calls - **Hero-scale speed is out of scope for v1, so use discretion.** - Robust target criteria would also check training speed and inference speed at hero scale. Marin Belay v1 skips those checks. - Judge whether a change's d512 gain would carry over to hero scale, and avoid changes whose gain comes from d512-only effects. Two examples: - Dropping MoE for dense would be a clear win at d512 because dense gets ~5× higher MFU there, but that MFU gain would not carry over at hero scale. - A much larger KV cache would also be a clear win at d512, but it would hurt long-context inference speed. - **Avoid magic numbers.** - Prefer changes with few new tuned constants. A tuned constant is justified when its gain is above the noise threshold and holds as a pattern across scales. For example, a 2× LR on one parameter group qualifies if it clears the noise threshold and the gain shows up consistently at larger rungs. - The higher a change's risk of curve fitting, the more scales it must be validated at before it counts as a win. - **Spend effort in proportion to an idea's likelihood of improvement.** - Promising ideas deserve several attempts. Long shots can be tried once and dropped. - A first run is not a verdict for a large change. If you try a new architecture or component, tune its optimizer assignment, LR, init and other key hyperparameters before concluding it doesn't work. The baseline's settings were tuned for the baseline, not for the new idea. ## Architecture (current best, d512) The diagrams below show **clean KMA**. The current best recipe adds the components listed under **Status → Current best recipe**: MLA key norm and key offset, a gated bigram-memory AttnRes source, ReLU² experts, and optimizer, schedule and logit changes. The diagrams show d512; the other rungs differ in the Shape table only. **1. Layer stack and Block Attention Residuals.** Every sublayer reads its input through its own AttnRes gate, a per-token softmax over the residual history. At d512 each layer closes an AttnRes block, so the history at layer *i* is the embedding plus one sum per earlier layer. [¹](#arch-note) ```mermaid flowchart TB tok["token ids

Values are for d512 unless noted; the code is `experiments/grug/fast_track/{model,optimizer,heuristic,launch}.py`. **Shape** | Rung | Width D | Layers | Local (KDA) / global (MLA) layers | Heads × head dim | Batch | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | d512 | 512 | 6 | 4 / 2 | 4 × 128 | 128 | | d768 | 768 | 8 | 6 / 2 | 6 × 128 | 128 | | d1024 | 1024 | 12 | 9 / 3 | 8 × 128 | 256 | | d1280 | 1280 | 14 | 10 / 4 | 10 × 128 | 256 | - Every 4th layer and the last layer are global; all other layers are local. - The run uses a 16k vocab and sequence length 4096 with packed documents. Every ShortConv and the KDA state respect document boundaries (the KDA state resets at each document start). - Weights are initialized with std 0.5/√D. Compute is bf16. **Embedding and output** - Token embedding → RMSNorm → GatedNorm. The result is AttnRes source 0. - Output path: final AttnRes gate → RMSNorm → GatedNorm → untied lm_head (`output_proj`). - The fused lm_head + cross-entropy loop uses a vocab tile of 8192. - GatedNorm (every GatedNorm in the model) is `x · sigmoid(W_up · SiLU(W_down · x))`, with a rank-128 bottleneck. **Block (every layer)** - **Attention sublayer:** input = its AttnRes gate mix → RMSNorm → GatedNorm → mixer (KDA or MLA). - **MoE sublayer:** input = its AttnRes gate mix → RMSNorm → GatedNorm → MoE → ShortConv on the MoE output. - Each ShortConv is a 4-tap causal depthwise conv. **Local layers: Kimi Delta Attention** (Kimi K3's layer) - **Projections:** q/k/v are D → N·128 with full heads (no GQA). Each goes through a ShortConv followed by SiLU. q and k are L2-normalized, and q is scaled by 1/√128. - **Decay:** per-channel log-decay `g = −5·sigmoid(exp(A_log)·(x·W_a_down·W_a_up + dt_bias))`. - The gate projection has rank 128. - `A_log` is one value per head, initialized to 0. - `dt_bias` is one value per channel, initialized so the decay rate spans 0.02–0.5. - **Write strength:** `β = sigmoid(x·W_β)`, one value per head. - **Recurrence:** `S_t = (I − β·k·kᵀ)·Diag(exp(g))·S_{t−1} + β·k·vᵀ`, read out as `o_t = S_tᵀ·q_t`. - It runs as chunked Pallas kernels, with a stable block-doubling inverse inside each chunk. - **Output:** per-head RMSNorm with a learnable 128-wide scale shared across heads → full-rank per-channel gate `sigmoid(x·W_g)` → `W_o`. - No positional encoding, no window, no XSA, and no ShortConv on the branch output. **Global layers: MLA + Inkling relative position** - **q:** full-rank, D → N·128 (no Q latent). - **k and v:** k = `W_uk · RMSNorm(x·W_dkv)` and v = `W_uv · RMSNorm(x·W_dkv)`. - They share one 512-wide KV latent, with a learnable RMSNorm on the latent. - Heads are 128 wide with no RoPE part. - There's no ShortConv on K, so the up-projections can be absorbed at inference. - **Scaling:** no QK-norm; `qk_mult` = 1, i.e. standard 1/√128 logit scaling. - **Position — Inkling relative-position bias**, added to the pre-softmax logits in place of RoPE: - `bias[h,i,j] = R[i,h,:] · P[:, i−j]`, where `R = x·W_r` is 16 values per head. - `P` is a bank of shape [16 × 1024] shared across heads. The relative extent is 1024. - It runs inside the FA4 attention kernel (forward, backward, and the SM90 backward pass). - **XSA** (exclusive self-attention): subtract the component of each head's output that is parallel to its own value vector. - **Output gate:** per head, `2·sigmoid(x·W_gate)`. `W_gate` is zero-initialized, so the gate is 1 at init. - The branch output also gets a ShortConv. **MoE sublayer (LatentMoE with quantile-balanced routing)** - **Experts:** 384 routed experts, top-8. Each is a SwiGLU with hidden size D/2. - **Latent space:** experts operate in a D/2-wide latent. The input goes through `W_latent_down` → RMSNorm, and the combined expert output goes back up through `W_latent_up`. - **Router:** reads the full-width token and computes logits in fp32. - Experts are selected by top-(8+1) on bias-adjusted logits, where the 9th logit is the threshold α. - Combine weights are the sigmoid of the unbiased logits, renormalized to sum to 2.5. - **Quantile balancing:** each step, each expert's threshold β is the global (1 − K/E) quantile of the logit margins (logit − α), read from a 10k-bin histogram. The router bias is set to −β. - The router bias is not trained by gradient. - **Capacity:** capacity factor 1.15, with pooled-wave expert-parallel dispatch. Receiver ranks are sort-based and the expand backward is gather-based. - **Shared experts:** 2 shared SwiGLU experts that bypass the latent: D → D/2 hidden → D. - **Fused projections:** - The router, latent-down, and both shared experts' gate/up projections run as one GEMM. - The shared experts' down-projections run as one GEMM. **Residual stream: Block Attention Residuals** - **Sources:** the embedding source, one running sum per completed block of sublayer outputs, and the running partial sum of the current block. - The model has 8 blocks. Block sums use the raw sublayer outputs. - **Gates:** every sublayer (attention and MoE) has its own gate, and there is one final gate before the output norm. Each gate has one learned pseudo-query `q ∈ ℝᴰ`, zero-initialized so every gate starts as a uniform average. - **Mixing:** per token, `logitᵢ = q · rms_norm(sourceᵢ)`, using a parameter-free (frozen) RMS key norm, then `softmax` over sources and a weighted sum of the raw sources. - **Implementation:** - Each completed block is scored once against every gate that reads it. - Backward: at d512 the layer's forward intermediates are saved.
